H.title: Named For Making Water
H.text: Hydrogen's name comes from the Greek words hydro (water) and genes (forming), meaning 'water-former.' The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier coined it in 1783 after showing that burning the gas produces pure water. Earlier, in 1766, Henry Cavendish had isolated it and called it 'inflammable air' without realizing it was a distinct element.

H.title: The Lightest Of All
H.text: With just one proton and one electron, hydrogen is the lightest and simplest element in the universe. A single hydrogen atom has a mass of about 1.67 x 10^-27 kilograms, roughly 1,836 times lighter than nothing you can hold. Because of this it tops the periodic table and is the only element whose most common form has no neutron at all.

H.title: Three Quarters Of The Cosmos
H.text: Hydrogen makes up about 75 percent of all ordinary (baryonic) matter in the universe by mass. It was the first element to form, appearing just minutes after the Big Bang during a phase called Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Stars like our Sun shine by fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium in their cores.

H.title: It Has Named Twins
H.text: Hydrogen is the only element whose isotopes have their own names: protium (no neutrons), deuterium (one neutron), and tritium (two neutrons). Deuterium, discovered by Harold Urey in 1931, earned him the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. 'Heavy water' made with deuterium is used to control reactions in some nuclear reactors.

H.title: The Powerhouse Of The Sun
H.text: Every second, the Sun fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that lights and warms our planet. This proton-proton fusion converts a tiny fraction of mass directly into energy, following Einstein's E=mc squared. The same process is what scientists are trying to recreate on Earth in fusion reactors like ITER in France.

H.title: A Metal Hidden In Giants
H.text: Under the crushing pressures deep inside Jupiter and Saturn, hydrogen is squeezed into a strange state called metallic hydrogen that conducts electricity like a metal. Researchers believe this liquid metallic hydrogen generates these planets' powerful magnetic fields. Creating it in the lab requires pressures of millions of atmospheres and remains one of physics' hardest challenges.

H.title: Fuel With Only Water Exhaust
H.text: When hydrogen burns or reacts in a fuel cell, its only by-product is water, making it an attractive clean energy carrier. Hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles convert the gas into electricity to drive motors, emitting nothing but water vapor. The catch is that most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, so 'green' hydrogen from renewable-powered water splitting is a major research goal.

H.title: Feeding The World's Crops
H.text: Hydrogen is essential to the Haber-Bosch process, which combines it with nitrogen to make ammonia for fertilizer. Developed by Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch in the early 1900s, this reaction supports food production for roughly half the world's population. It is also one of industry's biggest energy users, consuming a large share of global hydrogen output.

H.title: The Bond That Shapes Life
H.text: The 'hydrogen bond,' a weak attraction involving a hydrogen atom, is one of the most important forces in biology. It holds the two strands of your DNA's double helix together and gives water its unusually high boiling point and surface tension. Without hydrogen bonds, proteins could not fold into their working shapes and life as we know it could not exist.

H.title: Coldest Liquid On The Launchpad
H.text: Liquid hydrogen, used as rocket fuel, must be kept colder than minus 253 degrees Celsius, just above absolute zero. NASA's Space Shuttle and the Saturn V upper stages burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen for tremendous thrust. Hydrogen also has the highest energy content per kilogram of any common fuel, which is why rockets prize it despite the difficulty of storing it.

He.title: Found on the Sun first
He.text: Helium is the only element discovered in space before it was found on Earth. During a total solar eclipse on 18 August 1868, astronomers Jules Janssen and Norman Lockyer detected a bright yellow spectral line in the Sun's atmosphere that matched no known element. Lockyer named it after the Greek word 'helios', meaning Sun.

He.title: The reluctant noble gas
He.text: Helium has a completely filled outer electron shell with just two electrons, making it the most chemically inert element known. It forms no stable compounds under normal conditions and does not react with any other substance. This is why it is grouped with the noble gases despite having only two electrons rather than eight in its outer shell.

He.title: Never freezes on its own
He.text: Helium is the only element that cannot be frozen solid at normal atmospheric pressure, no matter how cold it gets. Even at absolute zero, it remains a liquid because its atoms have such weak attractions and large quantum motion. To make solid helium you must apply about 25 atmospheres of pressure while keeping it below roughly 1 kelvin.

He.title: A liquid that climbs walls
He.text: When cooled below 2.17 kelvin, liquid helium-4 becomes a 'superfluid' with zero viscosity. In this state it can flow through microscopic cracks, creep up and over the walls of its container as a thin film, and even form a frictionless fountain. This bizarre behavior is a rare large-scale display of quantum mechanics, and its discovery led to a Nobel Prize for Pyotr Kapitsa.

He.title: Born inside the Big Bang
He.text: About a quarter of all ordinary matter in the universe by mass is helium, making it the second most abundant element after hydrogen. Most of it was created in the first few minutes after the Big Bang, before any stars existed. Stars like our Sun also produce helium continuously by fusing hydrogen in their cores.

He.title: Why your voice goes squeaky
He.text: Breathing helium temporarily raises the pitch of your voice because sound travels nearly three times faster through helium than through ordinary air. The faster speed changes which frequencies your vocal tract amplifies, producing that famous cartoon-like sound. It is not entirely harmless, though, since inhaling pure helium displaces oxygen and can cause suffocation.

He.title: It cools the MRI machines
He.text: The powerful superconducting magnets inside hospital MRI scanners are kept working by liquid helium at around 4 kelvin, close to absolute zero. Helium is the only practical coolant cold enough for this job, and a single scanner can hold over a thousand litres of it. This makes medical imaging one of the largest industrial uses of the element.

He.title: It escapes into space forever
He.text: Helium is so light that once released into the atmosphere it drifts to the top and gradually leaks into outer space, never to return. Because of this, Earth's helium is a genuinely finite resource that comes mainly from the slow radioactive decay of uranium and thorium deep underground. It is extracted from natural gas wells, with the United States, Qatar, and Algeria among the leading producers.

He.title: Alpha particles are helium
He.text: An alpha particle emitted during radioactive decay is simply a helium nucleus, made of two protons and two neutrons with no electrons. As these particles slow down and capture electrons, they become ordinary helium atoms. This is the main natural source of the helium trapped in Earth's crust over billions of years.

He.title: Deep divers breathe it
He.text: Professional and deep-sea divers often breathe special mixtures such as heliox, which replaces some or most of the nitrogen in their air with helium. Helium does not cause the dangerous 'nitrogen narcosis' that impairs judgement at depth, and it makes the breathing gas less dense and easier to inhale under high pressure. Similar oxygen-helium blends are also used medically to help patients with severe airway obstructions breathe more easily.

Li.title: Named After Stone
Li.text: Lithium was discovered in 1817 by Swedish chemist Johan August Arfwedson while analyzing the mineral petalite. Its name comes from the Greek word 'lithos', meaning stone, because it was first found in minerals rather than in plant tissue or animal blood like the other alkali metals sodium and potassium known at the time. The pure metal was not isolated until 1821, when William Thomas Brande and Humphry Davy obtained it by electrolysis of lithium oxide.

Li.title: The Lightest Metal
Li.text: Lithium is the lightest of all metals and the least dense solid element at room temperature, with a density of about 0.534 grams per cubic centimetre. That is only about half the density of water, so a chunk of lithium would float, if it did not react violently with the water at the same time. It is soft enough to be cut with a kitchen knife and reveals a bright silvery surface that quickly tarnishes in air.

Li.title: Born In The Big Bang
Li.text: Lithium is one of only three elements, along with hydrogen and helium, created in the first few minutes after the Big Bang through Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Curiously, astronomers observe far less lithium in old stars than the theory predicts, a long-standing puzzle known as the 'cosmological lithium problem'. Stars also tend to destroy lithium in their hot interiors, which is why finding it in a star's atmosphere tells astronomers something about that star's age and structure.

Li.title: Medicine For The Mind
Li.text: Lithium salts, especially lithium carbonate, are a frontline treatment for bipolar disorder and were pioneered by Australian psychiatrist John Cade in 1949. It is one of the simplest drugs in all of medicine, just a single charged atom, yet it remains one of the most effective mood stabilizers known and can reduce the risk of suicide in patients. Exactly how it works in the brain is still not fully understood, which makes it a fascinating subject of ongoing research.

Li.title: Powering The Modern World
Li.text: Lithium-ion batteries store energy in smartphones, laptops, and electric cars because lithium's tiny, light ions move easily and pack a lot of energy for their weight. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino for developing these batteries. John Goodenough was 97 when he received it, making him the oldest Nobel laureate in history at the time.

Li.title: Crimson Fingerprint In Flame
Li.text: When a lithium compound is held in a flame, it burns a vivid crimson-red, a signature used in chemistry classrooms for the 'flame test' to identify elements. This same effect gives certain red fireworks and signal flares their deep scarlet colour. The colour arises because heated lithium atoms emit light at very specific wavelengths, a quantum fingerprint unique to the element.

Li.title: Locked In Brine And Rock
Li.text: Most of the world's lithium is extracted either from hard-rock spodumene mines, notably in Australia, or by evaporating salty groundwater from desert basins. The 'Lithium Triangle' spanning Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile holds a huge share of global reserves in high-altitude salt flats like Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni. There, brine is pumped into vast ponds and left to evaporate in the sun for many months before the lithium is purified.

Li.title: Fuel For Fusion
Li.text: The lithium isotope lithium-6 is critical to thermonuclear weapons and to future fusion reactors because it can be bombarded with neutrons to breed tritium, a heavy form of hydrogen used as fusion fuel. Experimental fusion projects like ITER plan to line their reactor walls with lithium-containing 'blankets' to generate their own tritium supply. This makes a soft, lightweight metal a surprising key to the energy of the stars.

Li.title: A Greasy Second Job
Li.text: Beyond batteries and medicine, lithium has long been used to make lithium grease, a thick lubricant that stays stable across a wide range of temperatures and resists water. This is why many car wheel bearings and industrial machines rely on it. Lithium compounds are also added to glass and ceramics to make them more heat-resistant, and to special glass-ceramic cooktops and telescope mirrors that barely expand when heated.

Li.title: Reactive But Restrained
Li.text: As an alkali metal, lithium reacts with water to release hydrogen gas, but it does so far more gently than its cousins sodium and potassium, fizzing rather than exploding. It is so chemically eager that it must be stored under oil or in an inert atmosphere to keep it from reacting with moisture and nitrogen in the air. Remarkably, lithium is one of the very few elements that reacts directly with nitrogen gas at room temperature to form lithium nitride.

Be.title: Named After a Gemstone
Be.text: Beryllium was first isolated as an oxide in 1798 by the French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin, who found it while studying the minerals beryl and emerald. The name comes from beryl (via the Greek 'beryllos'), the mineral family that includes emerald and aquamarine. The pure metal wasn't produced until 1828, when Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy independently reduced beryllium chloride with potassium.

Be.title: It Once Had a Sweet Name
Be.text: For much of the 1800s the element was called 'glucinium' (symbol Gl), from the Greek 'glykys' meaning sweet, because many of its salts taste sweet. The name beryllium eventually won out and was made official by IUPAC in 1949. Despite the sweet taste, beryllium compounds are highly toxic and should never be tasted.

Be.title: Astonishingly Stiff and Light
Be.text: Beryllium is remarkably rigid: its stiffness-to-weight ratio (specific stiffness) is roughly six times greater than that of steel. It has a very high melting point of about 1287 degrees Celsius yet a low density of only 1.85 grams per cubic centimetre, lighter than aluminium. These properties make it prized for precision parts that must not flex or expand under stress.

Be.title: Almost Transparent to X-Rays
Be.text: Because beryllium atoms have only four electrons, the metal barely absorbs X-rays, letting them pass through far more easily than glass or aluminium. This makes beryllium the standard material for the thin 'windows' in X-ray tubes and detectors. The same low atomic number makes it an excellent neutron reflector and moderator in nuclear reactors.

Be.title: Born in the Big Bang and Dying Stars
Be.text: Beryllium is one of the few elements with a cosmic supply problem: stars destroy it almost as fast as they make it, because beryllium-7 and beryllium-8 are extremely unstable in stellar cores. Most natural beryllium-9, the only stable isotope, is actually forged in interstellar space when high-energy cosmic rays smash into heavier atoms like carbon and oxygen, a process called spallation. This makes it one of the rarest of the light elements in the universe.

Be.title: The Particle That Revealed the Neutron
Be.text: In 1932 James Chadwick bombarded a beryllium target with alpha particles and detected a mysterious, electrically neutral radiation, which he identified as the neutron, earning him the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics. Beryllium is still used today as a neutron source when combined with an alpha-emitter such as americium or polonium. This experiment fundamentally reshaped our model of the atomic nucleus.

Be.title: A Berylliosis Warning
Be.text: Inhaling beryllium dust or fumes can trigger chronic beryllium disease (berylliosis), a serious lung condition caused by an immune reaction to the metal. Even tiny exposures can sensitise susceptible people, which is why machining beryllium requires strict ventilation and protective measures. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration tightly regulates workplace beryllium exposure limits as a result.

Be.title: Sparkless Tools for Explosive Places
Be.text: Alloyed with copper, beryllium forms beryllium-copper, a material that is strong, conducts electricity well, and crucially does not throw sparks when struck. This makes beryllium-copper tools the choice for working around flammable gases in oil rigs, refineries, and gas pipelines. The alloy is also used for springs, electrical connectors, and non-magnetic precision instruments.

Be.title: Eye on the Universe
Be.text: NASA chose beryllium for the 18 hexagonal mirror segments of the James Webb Space Telescope because it stays dimensionally stable at the extreme cold of deep space, around minus 230 degrees Celsius. Its lightness also meant the giant 6.5-metre mirror could be launched without excessive weight. Each segment was then coated in a microscopically thin layer of gold to reflect infrared light.

Be.title: The Element With No Stable Neighbour Below
Be.text: Beryllium occupies a unique spot on the periodic table: it is the lightest alkaline-earth metal and sits in a region where nuclear stability is fragile. Beryllium-8, which would form when two helium nuclei fuse, falls apart in about a tenth of a quadrillionth of a second, a quirk that nearly blocks the path for stars to build carbon. Only the rare 'triple-alpha' process lets stars leap past this bottleneck to make the carbon life depends on.

B.title: A three-way photo finish
B.text: Boron was first isolated in 1808, almost simultaneously by the French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thenard in Paris and the Englishman Humphry Davy in London. None of them obtained it very pure, getting samples only around 50% boron. The element was not produced in high purity until 1909, when the American chemist Ezekiel Weintraub made it about 99% pure.

B.title: Named after a desert mineral
B.text: The name boron comes from borax, a mineral known for centuries and used as a flux and cleaning agent, blended with the ending of carbon because boron resembled it. Borax itself traces to the Arabic word buraq and the Persian burah. So the element is essentially named after the salty white powder it was first extracted from.

B.title: The cosmic outsider
B.text: Boron is one of the rarest light elements in the universe because it is not made inside stars the way carbon or oxygen are. Instead it forms mostly through cosmic ray spallation, when high-energy particles racing through space smash heavier nuclei like carbon and oxygen apart. This explains why boron is roughly a million times rarer in the cosmos than carbon despite sitting right beside it.

B.title: Harder than you would guess
B.text: Boron is a metalloid that behaves much more like a hard, brittle nonmetal than a metal. Crystalline boron is one of the hardest known elements, scoring around 9.3 on the Mohs scale, placing it just below diamond. Its compound boron nitride can be arranged into a cubic form that rivals diamond as a cutting and grinding abrasive.

B.title: The neutron sponge
B.text: The isotope boron-10, which makes up about 20 percent of natural boron, is exceptionally good at absorbing neutrons. This makes boron essential in nuclear reactors, where boron control rods and boric acid dissolved in the coolant soak up excess neutrons to control or shut down the chain reaction. The same property is used in radiation shielding and emergency reactor safety systems.

B.title: It makes glass tough
B.text: Adding boron oxide to glass produces borosilicate glass, which expands very little when heated and therefore resists cracking from sudden temperature changes. This is the science behind Pyrex cookware and most laboratory glassware that can go straight from a flame into cold water. Borosilicate glass is also used for the mirrors of large telescopes because it barely changes shape with temperature.

B.title: A flash of brilliant green
B.text: When boron compounds are heated in a flame, they burn with a vivid bright green color. Chemists use this green flame test as a quick way to detect the presence of boron in a sample. The same effect gives many green fireworks their color, often using compounds such as boric acid or borax.

B.title: Quietly essential to plants
B.text: Boron is a genuine micronutrient that plants cannot live without, even though they need only tiny amounts of it. It helps build and stabilize cell walls and is vital for flowering, pollination, and seed and fruit development. Boron-deficient soils cause real crop problems worldwide, so farmers often add boron-containing fertilizers to fields.

B.title: Targeted cancer therapy
B.text: A medical technique called boron neutron capture therapy uses boron-10 to attack tumors. Doctors deliver a boron compound that accumulates in cancer cells, then irradiate the area with low-energy neutrons. Each boron-10 nucleus that captures a neutron splits and releases tiny high-energy particles that destroy the nearby cancer cell while largely sparing healthy tissue around it.

B.title: Mined from dry lakebeds
B.text: Most of the world's boron is mined as borate minerals from ancient dried-up lakes in arid regions. The single richest source is the open-pit mine at Boron, California, in the Mojave Desert, while Turkey holds the largest reserves on Earth. These deposits formed when boron-rich waters from volcanic activity slowly evaporated over geological time.

C.title: Named From Charcoal
C.text: The word carbon comes from the Latin "carbo," meaning charcoal or ember. Humans have used carbon in the form of soot and charcoal for tens of thousands of years, making it one of the few elements known since prehistoric times. It was first recognized as a true chemical element by Antoine Lavoisier in the 1770s, who proved that diamond is made of pure carbon by burning it.

C.title: Same Atom, Many Faces
C.text: Carbon exists as several allotropes built from identical atoms but with wildly different properties. Diamond is the hardest natural material because each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid 3D lattice, while graphite is soft and slippery because it stacks in flat sheets. Other forms include buckyballs (C60), nanotubes, and graphene, a one-atom-thick sheet 200 times stronger than steel.

C.title: The Backbone Of Life
C.text: Every known living thing is built on carbon, which is why biology is called "carbon-based." A single carbon atom can form four stable bonds, letting it link into long chains, rings, and branched structures that store information and energy. This versatility creates the proteins, fats, sugars, and DNA that make life possible.

C.title: It Won't Melt Easily
C.text: Carbon does not melt under normal pressure; instead it sublimes, turning straight from solid to gas at around 3,650 degrees Celsius. This gives it one of the highest sublimation points of any element. Because of this extreme heat tolerance, carbon is used in rocket nozzles, brake discs, and the heat shields that protect spacecraft during re-entry.

C.title: A Nuclear Clock
C.text: A rare radioactive form, carbon-14, forms when cosmic rays strike nitrogen in the upper atmosphere. Living things absorb it constantly, but after death it decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years. By measuring how much carbon-14 remains, scientists can date wood, bone, and cloth up to roughly 50,000 years old, a technique Willard Libby won the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing.

C.title: Forged Inside Stars
C.text: Almost all carbon in the universe is made deep inside dying stars through the triple-alpha process, where three helium nuclei fuse together. When those stars shed their outer layers or explode, they scatter carbon across space to form planets and, eventually, people. As astronomer Carl Sagan put it, we are quite literally made of stardust.

C.title: The Fourth Most Abundant
C.text: By mass, carbon is the fourth most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen, helium, and oxygen. On Earth it cycles constantly between the atmosphere, oceans, rocks, and living things through the carbon cycle. Vast amounts are locked in limestone and chalk, which are largely the calcium carbonate skeletons of ancient sea creatures.

C.title: Master Of Compounds
C.text: Carbon forms more compounds than all other elements combined, with well over ten million known and counting. This entire field is called organic chemistry, even though many of these molecules are made in labs and have nothing to do with living things. From plastics and medicines to fuels and dyes, carbon chemistry underpins much of the modern world.

C.title: Diamonds Are Forever Old
C.text: Natural diamonds form roughly 150 to 200 kilometers below the surface, where intense heat and pressure squeeze carbon into its hardest crystal form. Many are over a billion years old and are carried upward by rare volcanic eruptions through rock called kimberlite. Despite their value, diamond and humble pencil graphite are chemically the very same element.

C.title: Carbon In Steel And Air
C.text: Adding just a fraction of a percent of carbon to iron creates steel, the alloy that built skyscrapers, bridges, and railways. In the air, carbon travels as carbon dioxide, the gas plants breathe in for photosynthesis and the one driving modern climate change. Activated carbon, riddled with microscopic pores, is also used to purify water and filter air because of its enormous surface area.

N.title: Discovered by a student
N.text: Nitrogen was isolated in 1772 by Daniel Rutherford, a Scottish physician and student of Joseph Black at the University of Edinburgh. He removed oxygen and carbon dioxide from air and found a residual gas that could not support a flame or animal life. He called it "noxious air," because mice placed in it quickly suffocated.

N.title: The name means 'lifeless'
N.text: The name "nitrogen" comes from the French azote, coined by Lavoisier from Greek roots meaning "without life," reflecting that the gas does not sustain breathing or combustion. The modern name was later built from "niter" (potassium nitrate) plus the suffix -gen, meaning "niter-forming." Several languages, including French and Russian (azot), still use the older name today.

N.title: It rules the air you breathe
N.text: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume, making it by far the most abundant gas in the air. Despite being all around us, the N2 molecule is so unreactive that most living things cannot use it directly. Every breath you take is mostly nitrogen that passes in and out of your lungs untouched.

N.title: One of the strongest bonds in nature
N.text: In N2 the two nitrogen atoms are held together by a triple bond, one of the strongest chemical bonds known, requiring about 945 kilojoules per mole to break. This extreme stability is why atmospheric nitrogen is so chemically inert at ordinary temperatures. Breaking that bond to make useful compounds takes enormous energy, which is the central challenge of nitrogen chemistry.

N.title: The reaction that feeds billions
N.text: In the early 1900s, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a process to combine nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia (NH3) at high temperature and pressure with an iron catalyst. This Haber-Bosch process produces the fertilizers that now sustain roughly half of the world's food supply. It is often called one of the most important inventions of the 20th century, and Haber received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

N.title: A building block of life
N.text: Nitrogen is an essential component of amino acids, which form proteins, and of the bases that make up DNA and RNA. Without nitrogen there would be no enzymes, muscle, or genetic code. Although plants and animals cannot use N2 directly, specialized bacteria in soil and in the roots of legumes "fix" it into usable forms, anchoring the entire food web.

N.title: It boils at minus 196 degrees
N.text: Liquid nitrogen boils at about -196 degrees Celsius (77 kelvin) and is produced industrially by distilling liquefied air. Cheap and intensely cold, it is used to flash-freeze food, preserve biological samples and reproductive cells, and create dramatic fog effects. A spilled drop skitters across a warm floor on a cushion of its own vapor, an example of the Leidenfrost effect.

N.title: The gas that makes you laugh
N.text: Nitrous oxide (N2O), a compound of nitrogen and oxygen, was discovered to have anesthetic and giddy effects by Humphry Davy around 1800, earning it the nickname "laughing gas." It is still used today in dentistry and medicine for mild sedation and pain relief. The same gas is also a potent greenhouse compound and is used as a propellant in whipped cream cans.

N.title: Lightning makes fertilizer
N.text: The intense energy of a lightning bolt can rip apart the triple bond in N2, allowing nitrogen to combine with oxygen and form nitrogen oxides. Rain then washes these compounds into the soil as natural nitrates that plants can absorb. In this way thunderstorms quietly fertilize the land, a process that supplied usable nitrogen long before factories existed.

N.title: It paints the polar skies
N.text: Nitrogen atoms and molecules high in the atmosphere contribute to the aurora, glowing when struck by charged particles from the Sun. Nitrogen emissions add blue and deep red hues to the curtains of light, complementing the green and red produced by oxygen. Beyond Earth, nitrogen ice covers parts of Pluto and Neptune's moon Triton, where geysers have been seen erupting nitrogen gas.

O.title: Discovered Three Times Over
O.text: Oxygen was isolated independently by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Sweden around 1771-1772 and by Joseph Priestley in England in 1774, but Priestley published first. It was Antoine Lavoisier in France who recognized it as a true element and explained its role in combustion, demolishing the old phlogiston theory. His insight reshaped chemistry into a quantitative science.

O.title: A Name That Means Acid-Maker
O.text: Lavoisier coined the name 'oxygène' in 1777 from the Greek words 'oxys' (sharp or acid) and 'genes' (producer), because he wrongly believed oxygen was an essential ingredient of all acids. We now know hydrogen, not oxygen, is the defining element of acids. The mistaken name stuck and is still used worldwide today.

O.title: The Most Abundant Element on Earth
O.text: By mass, oxygen makes up about 46% of Earth's crust, making it the most abundant element in the rocks beneath our feet. It is locked into silicate minerals, oxides, and water rather than floating free as gas. Oxygen is also the third most abundant element in the entire universe, forged inside massive stars.

O.title: It Turns Liquids Pale Blue
O.text: When cooled to about -183 degrees Celsius, oxygen condenses into a pale sky-blue liquid, and it freezes into a bluish solid near -219 degrees. This faint color comes from the way oxygen molecules absorb red light. Liquid oxygen is also magnetic and will visibly cling to the poles of a strong magnet.

O.title: The Air We Cannot Live Without
O.text: Oxygen makes up roughly 21% of the air by volume, the precise level our bodies are tuned to. In our cells, it serves as the final electron acceptor in respiration, allowing mitochondria to extract energy from food efficiently. Without it, complex animal life as we know it could not exist.

O.title: Photosynthesis Filled the Sky
O.text: Earth's early atmosphere had almost no free oxygen until cyanobacteria began producing it through photosynthesis billions of years ago. This triggered the Great Oxidation Event around 2.4 billion years ago, transforming the planet's chemistry and rusting the oceans' dissolved iron. Nearly all the oxygen we breathe today is a byproduct of living organisms.

O.title: Ozone, Oxygen's Protective Cousin
O.text: Three oxygen atoms can bond into ozone (O3), a pale blue gas with a sharp smell you may notice after a thunderstorm. High in the stratosphere, the ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, shielding life below. At ground level, however, ozone is a pollutant that can damage lungs and crops.

O.title: The Engine of Combustion and Rust
O.text: Oxygen does not burn itself, but it powerfully supports burning by reacting with fuels to release heat and light. The same chemistry, running slowly, causes iron to rust and apples to brown. Industries exploit this by blasting pure oxygen into steel furnaces, where it rapidly removes carbon impurities from molten iron.

O.title: A Lifesaver in Medicine
O.text: Medical oxygen is one of the most widely used treatments in hospitals, given to patients with pneumonia, severe asthma, or low blood oxygen. Liquid oxygen also fuels rockets, including the engines that powered the Saturn V and the Space Shuttle. Most industrial oxygen is produced by chilling and distilling ordinary air into its components.

O.title: Three Isotopes Tell Earth's Story
O.text: Natural oxygen comes mostly as oxygen-16, with tiny amounts of oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. Scientists measure the ratio of these isotopes trapped in ancient ice cores and seashells to reconstruct past climates. Because heavier oxygen-18 evaporates less easily, its abundance acts as a natural thermometer reaching back hundreds of thousands of years.

F.title: Named From Latin for Flow
F.text: Fluorine takes its name from the mineral fluorite (calcium fluoride), whose own name comes from the Latin verb fluere, meaning 'to flow.' The mineral was used as a flux in metal smelting because it lowers the melting point of ores and helps them flow more easily. The element's connection to the word 'fluorescence' is no coincidence: glowing fluorite specimens gave that phenomenon its name in 1852.

F.title: A Prize Won at a Deadly Cost
F.text: Isolating pure fluorine was so dangerous that several 19th-century chemists were poisoned or killed trying, earning them the grim nickname 'fluorine martyrs.' Frenchman Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 by electrolyzing potassium fluoride dissolved in liquid hydrogen fluoride at about -50 degrees Celsius. The achievement earned him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

F.title: The Most Reactive Element
F.text: Fluorine is the most electronegative and most chemically reactive of all elements, attacking almost everything it touches. It can ignite materials like glass, water, asbestos, and even bricks, and it reacts explosively with hydrogen in the dark. It is one of the very few substances that can pry oxygen out of water, releasing oxygen gas and sometimes ozone.

F.title: A Pale Yellow Gas
F.text: At room temperature fluorine is a pale yellow-green gas with a sharp, penetrating odor, condensing to a bright yellow liquid at -188 degrees Celsius. Despite its ferocious reactivity, the pure element is rare in nature precisely because it bonds so eagerly with other atoms. Almost all fluorine on Earth exists locked safely inside minerals as fluoride compounds.

F.title: Teflon's Slippery Secret
F.text: The famous non-stick coating Teflon is polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a long chain of carbon atoms wrapped in fluorine. The carbon-fluorine bond is one of the strongest single bonds in organic chemistry, which makes PTFE remarkably resistant to heat and chemical attack. It was discovered by accident in 1938 by Roy Plunkett at DuPont when a tank of gas unexpectedly polymerized into a waxy white solid.

F.title: Strengthening Your Teeth
F.text: Tiny amounts of fluoride ions strengthen tooth enamel by converting its mineral hydroxyapatite into a tougher, more acid-resistant form called fluorapatite. Grand Rapids, Michigan became the first city in the world to add fluoride to its public water supply in 1945, and dental cavities in children there dropped dramatically. Today fluoride toothpaste is one of the most widespread preventive health measures on the planet.

F.title: Splitting the Atom With Fluorine
F.text: Because fluorine has only one stable isotope and forms gaseous compounds, it is vital to the nuclear industry. Uranium is converted into uranium hexafluoride (UF6), a gas used to separate the fissile isotope uranium-235 from uranium-238 by centrifuge or diffusion. Without fluorine chemistry, enriching uranium for reactors would be far more difficult.

F.title: Born in Dying Stars
F.text: Astronomers long puzzled over where the universe makes fluorine, since the element is easily destroyed inside stars. Evidence now points to aging red giant stars and possibly powerful Wolf-Rayet stars and supernovae as the cosmic fluorine factories. In 2021 scientists even detected fluorine in a galaxy seen as it was over 12 billion years ago, showing the element was being forged in the early universe.

F.title: Medicine's Imaging Workhorse
F.text: A radioactive form of fluorine, fluorine-18, is the most widely used tracer in PET (positron emission tomography) scans. Attached to a sugar molecule called FDG, it accumulates in active tissues like tumors and lights them up for doctors. Fluorine also appears in roughly a fifth to a quarter of all modern pharmaceuticals, including the antidepressant Prozac, because adding fluorine can make drugs last longer in the body.

F.title: A Greenhouse Gas Champion
F.text: Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), a dense and harmless-seeming gas used as an electrical insulator in high-voltage switchgear, is the most potent greenhouse gas known. Molecule for molecule it traps thousands of times more heat than carbon dioxide and can persist in the atmosphere for over a thousand years. This fluorine compound shows how the element's super-strong bonds can be both extraordinarily useful and an environmental concern.

Ne.title: Discovered in 15 days
Ne.text: Neon was discovered in London in June 1898 by Scottish chemist William Ramsay and his assistant Morris Travers. They found it by chilling air into a liquid and slowly boiling it off, capturing a leftover gas after argon, krypton, and xenon. Travers later wrote that the brilliant crimson glow it gave off in a discharge tube 'told its own story and was a sight to dwell upon and never to forget.'

Ne.title: Named by a curious child
Ne.text: The name comes from the Greek word 'neos,' meaning 'new.' According to Travers, it was Ramsay's 13-year-old son Willie who suggested calling the new element 'novum,' which his father adapted into the Greek-rooted 'neon.' The choice fit, since it was the freshest addition to the newly minted family of noble gases.

Ne.title: The signature red glow
Ne.text: The familiar red-orange light of 'neon signs' is true neon's natural color when an electric current excites its atoms. Pure neon in a glass tube emits a distinctive reddish-orange light at wavelengths near 640 nanometers. Other colors seen in commercial signs actually come from different gases or coated tubes, so a genuinely red sign is the only one truly powered by neon.

Ne.title: Almost impossible to react
Ne.text: Neon is the most inert of all the elements, with chemists never having made a single stable, ordinary chemical compound of it. Its outer electron shell is completely full, and it holds its electrons so tightly that it resists bonding even with the most aggressive reactants like fluorine. This extreme reluctance makes neon, in practical terms, the most chemically unreactive substance known.

Ne.title: Brighter than its noble cousins
Ne.text: For a given electrical input, a neon discharge produces far more intense light than the other noble gases, which is why it became the workhorse of luminous tube lighting. French engineer Georges Claude exploited this, displaying the first neon lamp in Paris in December 1910 and the first neon advertising sign by 1912. His company Claude Neon went on to sell the technology worldwide.

Ne.title: Rare on Earth, abundant in stars
Ne.text: Neon is the fifth most abundant element in the entire universe, yet it makes up only about 18 parts per million of Earth's atmosphere. The mismatch exists because neon is so light and unreactive that early Earth's gravity could not hold onto it, letting most of it escape to space. In stars, neon is forged during the late 'neon-burning' stage of massive stellar evolution shortly before they explode.

Ne.title: A super-cold refrigerant
Ne.text: Liquid neon is a remarkably powerful coolant, with more than 40 times the refrigerating capacity per unit volume of liquid helium and over three times that of liquid hydrogen. It boils at about minus 246 degrees Celsius, just 27 degrees above absolute zero. This makes it valuable for cryogenics where engineers need intense cooling without the extreme expense and handling difficulty of liquid helium.

Ne.title: Three stable isotopes
Ne.text: Natural neon is a mix of three stable isotopes: neon-20 makes up about 90.5 percent, neon-22 about 9.3 percent, and neon-21 a tiny 0.27 percent. Studying the precise ratios of these isotopes in volcanic rocks and meteorites lets geologists trace material that came from deep within the Earth's mantle. Such 'neon fingerprints' are key evidence in understanding how our planet first acquired its gases.

Ne.title: No role in life
Ne.text: Despite being all around us in the air we breathe, neon plays no known biological role in any living organism. It is completely non-toxic and chemically harmless, simply passing in and out of the lungs without taking part in any process. The only real danger it poses is as a simple asphyxiant, since a room flooded with neon would displace the oxygen needed to breathe.

Ne.title: A discharge-tube workhorse
Ne.text: Beyond advertising, neon's reliable glow made it useful in voltage testers, high-voltage indicators, and the little orange pilot lamps once common in electronics. Because neon ionizes at a predictable voltage, tiny neon bulbs were used as simple indicators and even as components in early electronic logic and timing circuits. Neon is also mixed into helium-neon lasers, which produced the steady red beams used for decades in supermarket barcode scanners.

Na.title: Born From Electricity
Na.text: Sodium was first isolated in 1807 by the English chemist Humphry Davy, who passed an electric current through molten sodium hydroxide (caustic soda). He watched tiny silvery globules of pure metal form at the negative electrode. This made sodium one of the first elements ever obtained by electrolysis, a technique still used to produce it industrially today.

Na.title: Why The Symbol Is Na
Na.text: The English name 'sodium' comes from 'soda', the old word for sodium carbonate compounds. Its two-letter symbol Na, however, comes from the Latin 'natrium', which traces back to the ancient Egyptian 'natron', a naturally occurring salt mixture used to dry and preserve mummies. So the symbol on the periodic table is a direct echo of ancient embalming practice.

Na.title: A Metal You Can Cut
Na.text: Pure sodium is so soft that you can slice it with an ordinary knife, revealing a bright silvery surface that instantly dulls to gray as it reacts with air. It is also remarkably light, with a density of about 0.97 grams per cubic centimetre, which is less than water, so a piece of sodium would float, if it didn't react so violently with the water first.

Na.title: It Bursts Into Flame On Water
Na.text: Drop sodium into water and it reacts immediately, producing sodium hydroxide and hydrogen gas while releasing so much heat that the hydrogen often ignites. The reaction can fizz, dart across the surface, and even explode. This is why sodium is stored under kerosene or mineral oil, sealed away from both air and moisture.

Na.title: The Color Of Street Lights
Na.text: When sodium is heated or electrified, it glows with an intense yellow-orange light at two close wavelengths near 589 nanometres, known as the sodium D-lines. This is why classic low-pressure sodium street lamps cast that distinctive amber glow. Astronomers prize these lamps because their single color is easy to filter out, reducing light pollution in telescope images.

Na.title: Half Of Every Salt Crystal
Na.text: The salt on your dinner table is sodium chloride, and roughly 39 percent of its mass is sodium. In each crystal, sodium and chloride ions lock together in a perfectly repeating cubic lattice, each sodium surrounded by six chlorides and vice versa. This orderly arrangement is why salt grains naturally form tiny cube shapes.

Na.title: Your Nerves Run On Sodium
Na.text: Sodium is an essential electrolyte, and your body uses gradients of sodium ions to fire every nerve impulse and heartbeat. Cells spend enormous energy running 'sodium-potassium pumps' that push sodium out and pull potassium in. When a nerve fires, sodium ions rush back inward, creating the electrical signal that lets you think, feel, and move.

Na.title: Sixth Most Abundant On Earth
Na.text: Sodium is the sixth most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up about 2.3 percent of it by mass. It is also the most abundant dissolved metal ion in seawater, which is why the oceans taste salty. Because sodium reacts so readily, it is never found as a free metal in nature, only locked into compounds.

Na.title: Coolant Inside Nuclear Reactors
Na.text: Liquid sodium is used as a coolant in some advanced 'fast' nuclear reactors because it conducts heat extremely well and stays liquid over a wide temperature range, from about 98 to 883 degrees Celsius. Unlike water, it doesn't slow down neutrons much, which suits these reactor designs. The catch is that it must be handled with great care, since it reacts fiercely with air and water.

Na.title: A Tail On A Comet And The Moon
Na.text: Spacecraft and telescopes have detected sodium atoms forming a faint, glowing tail streaming off comets, pushed away by sunlight. The Moon, too, has an ultra-thin atmosphere containing sodium, knocked loose from its surface by sunlight and meteorite impacts. This sodium glow is so distinctive that scientists use it to study these airless worlds from afar.

Mg.title: Named After a Greek Region
Mg.text: Magnesium takes its name from Magnesia, a district in Thessaly, Greece, where mineral-rich ores were found in antiquity. The same root also gave us the words manganese and magnet. The element was first isolated in 1808 by the English chemist Humphry Davy, who used electrolysis to separate it from magnesium oxide.

Mg.title: It Burns With Blinding Light
Mg.text: When ignited, magnesium burns with an intensely bright white flame that can reach roughly 3,100 degrees Celsius. This is why it was used in early photographic flash powder and in incendiary devices and flares. The light is so rich in ultraviolet that staring at it directly can damage your eyes.

Mg.title: The Lightest Structural Metal
Mg.text: With a density of about 1.74 grams per cubic centimeter, magnesium is the lightest metal used for everyday structural purposes, around 35 percent lighter than aluminum. Alloyed with elements like aluminum and zinc, it makes parts for cars, aircraft, laptops, and cameras where saving weight matters. The trade-off is that pure magnesium is relatively soft and flammable in finely divided form.

Mg.title: Green Blood of Plants
Mg.text: Every chlorophyll molecule has a single magnesium atom at its center, held within a ring structure that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. Without magnesium, plants cannot make the green pigment that converts carbon dioxide and water into sugars. In a real sense, almost all life on Earth depends on this metal sitting at the heart of leaves.

Mg.title: Essential Inside Your Body
Mg.text: An adult human body contains roughly 25 grams of magnesium, most of it stored in bones and muscles. It is required as a cofactor for more than 300 enzyme reactions, including those that make and use ATP, the cell's energy currency. It also helps regulate nerve signals, muscle contraction, and a steady heartbeat.

Mg.title: The Eighth Most Common Element
Mg.text: Magnesium is the eighth most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass and the fourth most common element in the planet as a whole. It is never found free in nature because it reacts readily, but it is locked into minerals such as dolomite, magnesite, and carnallite. The mineral olivine, rich in magnesium, makes up much of the Earth's mantle.

Mg.title: A Sea Full of Magnesium
Mg.text: Seawater is one of the largest practical sources of magnesium, containing about 1.3 grams of magnesium per liter. During World War II, factories extracted the metal directly from ocean water to build lightweight aircraft. Because the ocean is so vast, this supply is effectively inexhaustible.

Mg.title: Medicine Cabinet Staple
Mg.text: Magnesium compounds are common remedies: milk of magnesia is magnesium hydroxide used as an antacid and laxative, while Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate used in soaking baths. In hospitals, intravenous magnesium sulfate is a frontline treatment for eclampsia in pregnancy and for certain dangerous heart rhythms. These uses rely on magnesium's gentle, well-understood chemistry.

Mg.title: Forged Inside Dying Stars
Mg.text: Magnesium is created deep inside massive stars through nuclear fusion, particularly during carbon and neon burning late in a star's life. When such stars explode as supernovae, they scatter magnesium across space, where it later becomes part of new planets. The magnesium in your bones was literally cooked in a star billions of years ago.

Mg.title: Fires You Cannot Put Out With Water
Mg.text: A burning magnesium fire is notoriously dangerous because pouring water on it makes things worse. The hot metal splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, feeding the flames and risking an explosion. For this reason, magnesium fires must be smothered with dry sand or special Class D extinguishers rather than water or standard foam.

Al.title: Once Pricier Than Gold
Al.text: In the mid-19th century aluminium was so hard to isolate that it was considered a precious metal. Napoleon III reportedly reserved aluminium cutlery for his most honored guests while lesser visitors made do with gold. At the 1855 Paris Exposition, bars of aluminium were displayed beside the French crown jewels.

Al.title: Named for Alum
Al.text: The name comes from 'alumen', the Latin word for alum, a compound used by Greeks and Romans for dyeing and as a styptic. Humphry Davy proposed the name 'alumium' in 1808, then revised it to 'aluminum'; British editors later standardized 'aluminium' to match elements like sodium and potassium. Both spellings remain in use today, with 'aluminum' favored in North America.

Al.title: Most Abundant Metal in the Crust
Al.text: Aluminium makes up about 8.2% of Earth's crust by mass, making it the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element overall after oxygen and silicon. Despite this, it is never found as a pure metal in nature because it bonds so eagerly with oxygen. It occurs locked inside minerals such as feldspars, micas, and the ore bauxite.

Al.title: The Hall-Heroult Breakthrough
Al.text: In 1886, 22-year-old American Charles Martin Hall and Frenchman Paul Heroult independently discovered the same way to extract aluminium using electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite. This process slashed the price of aluminium from a luxury metal to an everyday material within a few years. The Hall-Heroult process still produces essentially all the world's primary aluminium today.

Al.title: It Wears Invisible Armor
Al.text: Although aluminium is highly reactive, a freshly exposed surface instantly forms a thin, transparent layer of aluminium oxide only a few nanometers thick. This self-healing film is tough and tightly bonded, protecting the metal underneath from further corrosion. This is why aluminium pans, foil, and aircraft skins resist rust so well even though the metal itself is chemically eager to react.

Al.title: Recycling Saves 95% of the Energy
Al.text: Smelting aluminium from ore is enormously energy-intensive, but recycling used aluminium requires only about 5% of that energy. A discarded drink can be melted down, reformed, refilled, and back on a shelf in as little as 60 days. Roughly 75% of all aluminium ever produced is estimated to still be in use thanks to this near-infinite recyclability.

Al.title: Light Enough to Fly
Al.text: With a density of about 2.7 grams per cubic centimeter, aluminium is roughly one-third the weight of steel, which is why it became the backbone of aviation and spaceflight. Alloyed with copper, magnesium, or zinc, it gains the strength needed for aircraft fuselages, rockets, and satellites. The Wright brothers used an aluminium engine block in 1903 because no other strong, light metal was available.

Al.title: A Gemstone in Disguise
Al.text: Pure aluminium oxide is the mineral corundum, and tiny traces of other elements turn it into famous gemstones. A pinch of chromium makes it a red ruby, while iron and titanium produce blue sapphire. Synthetic corundum is also one of the hardest materials made, ranking 9 on the Mohs scale just below diamond.

Al.title: Forged in Dying Stars
Al.text: The aluminium in your soda can was created inside massive stars through nuclear fusion, particularly during the carbon and neon burning stages near the end of a star's life. A radioactive form, aluminium-26, glows in gamma rays across our galaxy and helped heat the earliest rocky bodies in the young Solar System. Detecting this isotope lets astronomers map where new stars are currently forming in the Milky Way.

Al.title: No Job in the Human Body
Al.text: Unlike iron, calcium, or zinc, aluminium has no known biological function in humans and is not needed by any living cell. The body absorbs very little of what we eat, and healthy kidneys efficiently filter out the rest. Plants, however, can suffer from aluminium toxicity in acidic soils, where the dissolved metal stunts root growth and limits crop yields worldwide.

Si.title: Named for flint and stone
Si.text: The name silicon comes from the Latin words silex and silicis, meaning flint or hard stone, reflecting how common the element is in rocks. The English chemist Thomas Thomson coined the modern name in 1817, adding the -on ending to group it with the nonmetals carbon and boron. Earlier names like silicium are still used in many languages today, including French and German.

Si.title: First isolated in 1824
Si.text: Swedish chemist Jons Jacob Berzelius is credited with first isolating reasonably pure silicon in 1824 by heating potassium with silicon tetrafluoride and then washing away the byproducts. Humphry Davy and others had tried earlier and failed to get the pure element. Berzelius produced amorphous brown silicon; crystalline silicon was not made until Henri Sainte-Claire Deville did so in 1854.

Si.title: Earth's second most abundant element
Si.text: Silicon makes up about 28 percent of the Earth's crust by mass, making it the second most abundant element after oxygen. It is almost never found free in nature because it bonds so eagerly with oxygen to form silica and silicates. Quartz, sand, granite, clay, and mica are all built around silicon-oxygen frameworks.

Si.title: The brain of every computer
Si.text: Ultrapure silicon, refined to 99.9999999 percent purity (nine nines), is the foundation of nearly all modern electronics. As a semiconductor it can be precisely doped with traces of boron or phosphorus to control how it conducts electricity, which is the basis of the transistor. A single modern microchip can pack tens of billions of these silicon transistors into an area smaller than a fingernail.

Si.title: Why Silicon Valley got its name
Si.text: The nickname Silicon Valley was popularized by journalist Don Hoefler in a 1971 newspaper series about the chip industry south of San Francisco. The region became the heart of semiconductor manufacturing because companies there built integrated circuits from silicon wafers. The name has since become shorthand for the global technology industry itself.

Si.title: A diamond-like crystal
Si.text: Crystalline silicon shares the same tetrahedral diamond cubic structure as carbon diamond, with each atom bonded to four neighbors. It is a hard, brittle, blue-grey solid that shatters rather than bends, behaving like a ceramic. Unlike most metalloids it has a relatively high melting point of about 1,414 degrees Celsius.

Si.title: It expands when it freezes
Si.text: Like water, silicon is one of the few substances that is denser as a liquid than as a solid, so it expands when it solidifies. This unusual property comes from its open tetrahedral crystal structure, which takes up more room than the closely packed liquid. The same behavior is shared by germanium and gallium.

Si.title: Glass is mostly silicon dioxide
Si.text: Ordinary window glass is made primarily from silicon dioxide, the same compound found in quartz sand, melted with soda and lime. Pure fused silica can transmit ultraviolet light and withstand huge temperature swings, which is why it is used for laboratory glassware and telescope optics. The optical fibers carrying internet data across oceans are also drawn from ultrapure silica.

Si.title: Stardust forged silicate planets
Si.text: Silicon is produced inside massive stars through oxygen burning, and dying stars scatter it into space where it forms tiny silicate dust grains. These grains are the building blocks of rocky planets, which is why Earth, Mars, and the Moon are largely made of silicate minerals. Astronomers can detect this dust by the characteristic infrared light that silicate grains emit around young stars.

Si.title: Essential to life, but quietly
Si.text: Trace amounts of silicon play a structural role in living things, helping form connective tissue, bone, and skin in animals. Diatoms, a vast group of ocean microalgae, build intricate glass-like shells from dissolved silica and produce a large share of Earth's oxygen. In plants like rice and horsetail, silicon stiffens stems and helps defend against pests and disease.

P.title: Born from boiled urine
P.text: Phosphorus was the first element discovered with a known discoverer: the German alchemist Hennig Brand isolated it in Hamburg around 1669 while boiling down vast quantities of urine in search of gold. The glowing white substance he produced was the first new element found since antiquity. Brand kept his method secret for years, but the recipe eventually spread across Europe.

P.title: Named for the morning star
P.text: The name phosphorus comes from the Ancient Greek 'phosphoros', meaning 'light-bearer' or 'bringer of light'. It was originally a name for the planet Venus when it appears as the morning star. The element earned it because white phosphorus glows faintly in the dark, a property that fascinated early scientists.

P.title: It glows by slow burning
P.text: The eerie green glow of white phosphorus in air is not heat or radioactivity but chemiluminescence: the phosphorus slowly reacts with oxygen, emitting light without much warmth. Ironically, the word 'phosphorescence' was coined from this element, even though the glow is technically chemiluminescence, not true phosphorescence. The effect gave rise to the broader scientific term still used today.

P.title: Many faces, one element
P.text: Phosphorus exists in strikingly different allotropes that behave like different substances entirely. White phosphorus is waxy, toxic and ignites in air near 30 degrees Celsius, while red phosphorus is far more stable and is the material struck on the side of a matchbox. Black phosphorus, the most stable form, conducts electricity and forms layered sheets similar to graphite, making it a candidate for future electronics.

P.title: Half your DNA backbone
P.text: Phosphorus is one of the six essential elements of life, and it forms the literal backbone of DNA and RNA through phosphate groups linking the sugar molecules. It is also central to ATP, the energy currency that powers nearly every process in your cells. Without phosphorus, there would be no genetic code and no way for living things to store and spend energy.

P.title: Stored in your bones
P.text: About 85 percent of the phosphorus in your body is locked into your bones and teeth, combined with calcium as a mineral called hydroxyapatite. An adult human body contains roughly 700 grams of phosphorus in total. This mineral gives skeletons their hardness while also acting as a reserve the body can draw on when blood phosphate runs low.

P.title: It feeds the world
P.text: Phosphorus is irreplaceable in agriculture because plants cannot grow without it, and most of the world's supply is mined as phosphate rock for fertilizer. Morocco and Western Sahara together hold the majority of known reserves, giving the region enormous influence over global food production. Because there is no substitute for phosphorus in fertilizer, scientists warn of a future 'peak phosphorus' supply challenge.

P.title: From matches to safer matches
P.text: Early friction matches used toxic white phosphorus, and factory workers who inhaled its fumes suffered a horrific bone disease called 'phossy jaw'. The 1906 Bern Convention banned white phosphorus in matches, pushing manufacturers to switch to safer red phosphorus. Today's safety matches keep the red phosphorus on the striking strip, separate from the match head.

P.title: Forged in dying stars
P.text: The phosphorus in your body was created inside massive stars and scattered through space when they exploded as supernovae. Astronomers have found that phosphorus is relatively rare in the cosmos compared to other life-essential elements, which raises intriguing questions about where life's phosphorus came from. In 2020 researchers traced phosphorus-bearing molecules from a star-forming region to a comet, hinting that comets may have delivered it to early Earth.

P.title: A weapon and a medicine
P.text: Phosphorus chemistry spans extremes: nerve agents and many pesticides are organophosphorus compounds that disrupt the nervous system, while other phosphorus compounds save lives. Bisphosphonate drugs treat osteoporosis by strengthening bone, and radioactive phosphorus-32 has been used to treat certain blood disorders. The same element that can poison can also heal, depending entirely on how its atoms are arranged.

S.title: Known Since Antiquity
S.text: Sulfur is one of a handful of elements known since prehistoric times, with no single discoverer. The Bible refers to it as "brimstone" (literally "burning stone"), and Egyptians used it for bleaching cloth thousands of years ago. In 1777 Antoine Lavoisier finally proved it was a true chemical element rather than a compound.

S.title: Why It Is Spelled "Sulfur"
S.text: The name derives from the Latin "sulphur," itself possibly rooted in a Sanskrit word for fire. In 1990 the IUPAC officially adopted "sulfur" with an f as the international standard spelling, and the British Royal Society of Chemistry followed in 1992. The older "sulphur" spelling is now considered traditional rather than correct in scientific writing.

S.title: It Powers Global Industry
S.text: More sulfuric acid (H2SO4) is produced than any other industrial chemical on Earth, with hundreds of millions of tonnes made each year. A nation's sulfuric acid output is often used as a rough index of its industrial strength. The bulk of it goes into making phosphate fertilizers that feed much of the world's agriculture.

S.title: A Champion of Allotropes
S.text: Sulfur forms more allotropes (different structural forms) than almost any other element, with more than 30 known. Its most stable form at room temperature is orthorhombic alpha-sulfur, built from crown-shaped rings of eight atoms (S8). When you melt and heat these rings further they break and tangle, which is why molten sulfur strangely gets more viscous as it gets hotter before thinning out again.

S.title: Essential to Your Body
S.text: Sulfur is the eighth most abundant element in the human body and is vital to life. It sits inside the amino acids cysteine and methionine, and the disulfide bonds it forms hold proteins like keratin in your hair and nails into their shapes. This same chemistry is why burning hair smells so distinctly of sulfur.

S.title: Volcanoes and Yellow Lakes
S.text: Sulfur often occurs in pure native form around volcanoes and hot springs, where it crystallizes into vivid yellow deposits. At Indonesia's Kawah Ijen volcano, miners famously carry heavy baskets of solid sulfur out of a crater that also glows with eerie blue flames of burning sulfur gas at night. Underground deposits were historically mined by the Frasch process, which melts sulfur with superheated water and pumps it to the surface.

S.title: It Built the Sky of Venus
S.text: Sulfur is widespread in the cosmos and dramatically shapes other worlds. The thick clouds of Venus are made largely of sulfuric acid droplets, and Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, painted yellow, orange, and red by sulfur compounds erupting from its surface. Sulfur is forged in massive stars and scattered by supernova explosions.

S.title: The Spark in Gunpowder
S.text: Sulfur is one of the three classic ingredients of black powder, alongside charcoal and potassium nitrate (saltpeter). It lowers the temperature needed to ignite the mixture and helps the reaction spread quickly, which is why this combination revolutionized warfare and later powered fireworks. The same readiness to burn is why ancient writers called it brimstone.

S.title: Vulcanizing Rubber Changed the World
S.text: In 1839 Charles Goodyear discovered that heating natural rubber with sulfur transformed it from a sticky, temperature-sensitive material into the tough, springy substance we use today. The sulfur atoms form cross-links between the rubber's polymer chains, a process now called vulcanization. Without it there would be no durable car tires, and the Goodyear tire company is named in his honor.

S.title: Medicine, Old and New
S.text: Sulfur has a long medical history, from ancient skin treatments to the sulfonamides ("sulfa drugs") of the 1930s, the first widely effective antibacterial medicines that saved countless lives before penicillin. Sulfur-containing compounds remain important in many modern drugs and in fungicides for crops. It also occurs naturally in garlic and onions, where sulfur compounds create their pungent flavors and make your eyes water.

Cl.title: Named For Its Green Color
Cl.text: Chlorine takes its name from the Greek word "chloros," meaning pale green or yellow-green, the exact color of the gas. At room temperature pure chlorine is a dense, choking yellow-green gas, which made it one of the few elements named directly for its appearance. The name was coined by Sir Humphry Davy in 1810.

Cl.title: Davy Proved It An Element
Cl.text: Carl Wilhelm Scheele first isolated the gas in 1774, but he believed it was a compound containing oxygen. It was Humphry Davy who, in 1810, demonstrated that the substance was a brand-new chemical element that could not be broken down further. His careful experiments overturned the prevailing chemistry of the time.

Cl.title: The First Chemical Weapon
Cl.text: On 22 April 1915 at Ypres, Belgium, German forces released around 168 tons of chlorine gas from cylinders, marking the first large-scale use of a chemical weapon in war. Because chlorine is denser than air, it sank into the trenches and forced soldiers out into the open. The horror of that day directly shaped the later Geneva Protocol banning chemical warfare.

Cl.title: It Helped Defeat Cholera
Cl.text: Adding tiny amounts of chlorine to drinking water kills bacteria, viruses, and parasites, and the practice dramatically reduced deadly diseases like cholera and typhoid in the early 1900s. Jersey City, New Jersey, became one of the first U.S. cities to continuously chlorinate its public water supply in 1908. Water chlorination is considered one of the most important public-health advances in history.

Cl.title: You Are Eating It Daily
Cl.text: Common table salt is sodium chloride, so every grain you sprinkle is roughly 60 percent chlorine by mass, locked safely as the chloride ion. In this form chlorine is not a poison gas at all but an essential nutrient. Chloride ions help your stomach make hydrochloric acid for digestion and keep the body's fluids in proper balance.

Cl.title: Hidden Inside Most Plastics
Cl.text: The "vinyl" in PVC stands for polyvinyl chloride, a tough plastic built around chlorine atoms that makes up pipes, window frames, flooring, and medical tubing. PVC is one of the world's most-produced plastics, and chlorine chemistry is essential to manufacturing it. Roughly a third of all chlorine produced industrially ends up in plastics like PVC.

Cl.title: A Gas Made From Salt
Cl.text: Industry produces chlorine by passing electricity through salty water (brine) in a process called the chlor-alkali process, splitting it into chlorine gas, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide. This single reaction supplies almost all the chlorine humanity uses. It is one of the largest-scale electrochemical processes on Earth, consuming enormous amounts of electricity worldwide.

Cl.title: Two Twins In Every Sample
Cl.text: Natural chlorine is a mix of two stable isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, in a roughly 3-to-1 ratio. Averaging them gives chlorine its distinctive atomic weight of about 35.45, one of the few that sits far from a whole number. Mass spectrometers see this 3:1 "chlorine pattern" as a tell-tale fingerprint when identifying molecules that contain it.

Cl.title: A Thirsty Electron Grabber
Cl.text: With seven electrons in its outer shell, chlorine is desperate to gain just one more to complete its set, making it fiercely reactive. This hunger gives it one of the highest electron affinities of any element and explains why it readily attacks metals and other substances. It is this reactivity that makes chlorine such a powerful disinfectant and bleaching agent.

Cl.title: It Punched The Ozone Hole
Cl.text: When chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) drift into the stratosphere, ultraviolet light frees their chlorine atoms, and a single chlorine atom can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules in a chain reaction. This discovery, honored with the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, revealed how CFCs were thinning Earth's protective ozone layer. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs, and the ozone layer is now slowly healing.

Ar.title: The Lazy Gas
Ar.text: Argon's name comes from the Greek word "argos," meaning "lazy" or "idle," a nod to its extreme chemical unreactivity. Like the other noble gases, its outer electron shell is completely full (electron configuration [Ne]3s²3p⁶), so it has almost no drive to bond with other atoms. For over a century chemists believed it formed no compounds at all.

Ar.title: Discovered by Subtraction
Ar.text: In 1894, Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay noticed that nitrogen extracted from air was about 0.5% denser than nitrogen made chemically. By removing the oxygen, nitrogen, and other known gases from air, they isolated a mysterious leftover gas — argon. The discovery earned Rayleigh the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physics and Ramsay the 1904 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Ar.title: The Third Most Common Air
Ar.text: Argon makes up about 0.93% of Earth's atmosphere by volume, making it the third most abundant atmospheric gas after nitrogen and oxygen. That means there is far more argon in the air you breathe than carbon dioxide. It is also the most abundant noble gas on Earth by a wide margin.

Ar.title: Born From Radioactive Decay
Ar.text: Most of Earth's argon is argon-40, and almost all of it formed underground from the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in rocks over billions of years. This is why argon is so common in our atmosphere compared to the cosmos at large. Geologists exploit this in potassium-argon dating to measure the age of volcanic rocks and ancient minerals.

Ar.title: A Different Argon in Space
Ar.text: In the universe as a whole, the dominant isotope is argon-36, produced by nuclear fusion in massive stars, not the argon-40 that dominates on Earth. Argon is actually one of the more common elements in the cosmos. In 2013 the Herschel Space Observatory detected argon hydride (ArH⁺) in the Crab Nebula — the first noble-gas molecule ever found in space.

Ar.title: It Can Form Compounds After All
Ar.text: For decades argon was thought to be completely inert, but in 2000 a team at the University of Helsinki created argon fluorohydride (HArF). The molecule is only stable at temperatures below about 27 kelvin (−246 °C), but its existence proved argon chemistry is possible. It remains the only neutral argon compound ever synthesized.

Ar.title: Shielding the Welder's Arc
Ar.text: Argon's reluctance to react makes it a perfect protective blanket. In TIG and MIG welding it is blown over the molten metal to shield it from oxygen and nitrogen, which would otherwise weaken the weld. The same inert quality lets it fill the space inside double-glazed windows, where it insulates better than ordinary air.

Ar.title: Glowing Lilac in a Tube
Ar.text: When electricity is passed through low-pressure argon, it glows a distinctive lilac or pale violet-blue. This makes it a workhorse in lighting and neon-style signs, and it was once used to fill incandescent bulbs to stop the tungsten filament from burning up. Argon is also the buffer gas in many fluorescent lamps and plasma displays.

Ar.title: Preserving the Past
Ar.text: Because it crowds out reactive oxygen without harming materials, argon is used to protect priceless artifacts and documents. The original U.S. Declaration of Independence and Constitution are sealed in argon-filled cases at the National Archives. Vintners and chemists likewise use argon to blanket wine and air-sensitive substances from spoilage.

Ar.title: Heavier Than Air, and Silent Danger
Ar.text: At about 1.78 grams per liter, argon is denser than air, so it can pool in low or enclosed spaces and silently displace breathable oxygen. It is colorless, odorless, and tasteless, giving no warning before causing asphyxiation — a real industrial hazard. Argon plays no biological role in the body and is completely non-toxic; the only danger is the lack of oxygen it leaves behind.

K.title: Named From Wood Ash
K.text: The English name potassium comes from "potash" — the residue left when you soak wood ash in a pot and boil away the water. Sir Humphry Davy coined the name in 1807 after isolating the metal. The chemical symbol K, however, comes from the Latin "kalium," which itself traces back to the Arabic "al-qali," meaning the calcined ashes of plants.

K.title: Born From Electricity
K.text: Potassium was the first metal ever isolated by electrolysis. In October 1807 Humphry Davy passed an electric current from a powerful battery through molten potash and watched tiny shiny globules of a brand-new metal burst into lilac flame. It was one of the very first elements discovered using electrical power rather than chemical reactions alone.

K.title: A Metal You Can Cut
K.text: Potassium is astonishingly soft — you can slice it with a butter knife, and a freshly cut surface gleams silvery-white before tarnishing in seconds. It is also lighter than water, with a density of about 0.86 grams per cubic centimetre, so a lump of it actually floats. It is one of only a handful of metals less dense than water.

K.title: It Sets Water On Fire
K.text: Drop potassium into water and it reacts violently, fizzing across the surface and igniting the hydrogen gas it releases with a distinctive lilac-purple flame. The reaction is far more vigorous than sodium's and can detonate. This is why potassium metal is stored submerged in mineral oil or kerosene, sealed away from air and moisture.

K.title: The Purple Flame Test
K.text: When heated, potassium ions glow a characteristic pale violet or lilac colour, a signature chemists use to identify the element in flame tests. The colour comes from electrons dropping back to lower energy levels and emitting light at specific wavelengths around 766 nanometres. Because sodium's intense yellow can mask it, analysts often view potassium's flame through blue cobalt glass.

K.title: Essential To Every Heartbeat
K.text: Potassium is the most abundant positive ion inside your cells, and the flow of potassium across cell membranes generates the electrical signals that fire nerves and contract muscles — including your heart. An adult body holds roughly 120 to 140 grams of it. Both too little and too much in the blood can cause dangerous, even fatal, irregular heartbeats.

K.title: You Are Slightly Radioactive
K.text: About 0.012 percent of all natural potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40, which decays with a half-life of around 1.25 billion years. Because potassium is in every cell, your own body emits roughly 4,000 to 5,000 radioactive decays per second from it. Geologists use potassium-40's decay into argon-40 to date rocks millions to billions of years old.

K.title: Feeding The World
K.text: Potassium is one of the three primary plant nutrients — the "K" in N-P-K fertilizer labels — and roughly 95 percent of mined potash goes into agriculture. Plants need it to regulate water, build proteins, and resist disease. Canada, Russia, and Belarus dominate global potash mining, much of it dug from ancient buried seabeds laid down hundreds of millions of years ago.

K.title: The Element That Built Banana Myths
K.text: Bananas are famous for potassium, packing about 358 milligrams per 100 grams, but they are far from the richest source — dried apricots, beans, spinach, and potatoes all contain more. The persistent idea that a banana makes you measurably radioactive is technically true but trivially so. The dose is so tiny it has become a tongue-in-cheek unit called the "banana equivalent dose."

K.title: Gunpowder's Secret Ingredient
K.text: Potassium nitrate, also known as saltpetre, makes up about 75 percent of traditional black gunpowder and was prized for centuries as the oxidizer that lets the mixture burn explosively without outside air. The same compound is used today to cure meats, in some fertilizers, and in heat-treating glass. Other potassium salts give fireworks and matches their colour and their spark.

Ca.title: Named For Lime Itself
Ca.text: Calcium takes its name from the Latin word calx, meaning lime or limestone, the chalky material burned by builders for thousands of years. The element was first isolated in 1808 by the English chemist Humphry Davy, who used electrolysis on a moistened mixture of lime and mercuric oxide. Although ancient civilizations used calcium compounds in mortar and plaster, no one had ever seen the pure metal until Davy's experiments.

Ca.title: A Metal You Can Cut
Ca.text: Pure calcium is a soft, silvery-white metal that is hard enough to dent but soft enough to cut with a knife. It is surprisingly light for a metal, with a density of about 1.55 grams per cubic centimeter, only a little denser than water. When freshly cut its bright surface quickly dulls as it reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air, forming a grey-white coating of oxide and nitride.

Ca.title: The Bone Builder
Ca.text: About 99 percent of the calcium in your body is locked inside your bones and teeth as a crystalline mineral called hydroxyapatite. An adult human body contains roughly one kilogram of calcium, making it the most abundant metal in the body by mass. The remaining one percent circulates in blood and cells, where it is so vital that the body will dissolve bone to keep blood levels stable.

Ca.title: Sparks Every Heartbeat
Ca.text: Calcium ions act as a universal signaling switch inside living cells, triggering muscle contraction, nerve impulses, and the release of hormones. Every single heartbeat depends on a precisely timed surge of calcium ions flooding into heart muscle cells.
