This is why the concentration of calcium in your blood is kept within an extremely narrow range, controlled by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D.

Ca.title: Fifth Most Abundant Element
Ca.text: Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the Earth's crust by mass, at about 4.1 percent, and the third most abundant metal after aluminium and iron. It is far too reactive to exist as a free metal in nature, so it is always found locked in compounds. Vast deposits appear as limestone, marble, chalk, and gypsum, much of it built from the shells and skeletons of ancient sea creatures.

Ca.title: Forged In Dying Stars
Ca.text: The calcium in your bones was created inside massive stars through nuclear fusion and scattered across space when those stars exploded as supernovae. Calcium is one of the elements astronomers detect most easily in starlight, because its ions produce strong dark lines in stellar spectra known as the Fraunhofer H and K lines. In a real sense, every skeleton on Earth is made of stardust.

Ca.title: Burns Brick-Red
Ca.text: When a calcium compound is heated in a flame, it glows a distinctive orange-red to brick-red color. Chemists use this flame test to identify the element, and the same effect helps give some red fireworks and emergency flares their warm color. The glow comes from electrons in calcium atoms absorbing heat energy and then releasing it as specific wavelengths of light.

Ca.title: It Sweats In Water
Ca.text: Drop calcium metal into water and it reacts steadily, fizzing as it releases hydrogen gas and forming calcium hydroxide. The reaction is brisk but gentler than the violent explosions of sodium or potassium, partly because the calcium hydroxide produced is only slightly soluble and coats the metal. This controlled reactivity is one reason calcium sits in the alkaline-earth group rather than the wildly reactive alkali metals.

Ca.title: Caves And Cathedrals
Ca.text: The stalactites and stalagmites in caves are sculpted over thousands of years by calcium carbonate slowly precipitating from dripping mineral-rich water. The same compound, as limestone and marble, built the Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, and countless cathedrals. Quicklime made by roasting limestone has been the key ingredient in mortar and cement since antiquity, literally holding civilization together.

Ca.title: Steel's Hidden Cleaner
Ca.text: Industry uses calcium metal as a powerful reducing agent to extract other metals such as uranium, thorium, and zirconium from their compounds. It is also added to molten steel and aluminium alloys, where it scavenges dissolved oxygen and sulfur to remove impurities and improve quality. This deoxidizing role makes calcium quietly essential to modern metallurgy, even though most of it never appears in the final product.

Sc.title: Predicted Before It Was Found
Sc.text: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for a missing element he called "eka-boron," predicting its atomic mass and that it would form an oxide of the type X2O3. When scandium was isolated a decade later, its properties matched Mendeleev's forecast almost exactly, becoming one of the triumphs that convinced chemists the periodic table really worked.

Sc.title: Named for Scandinavia
Sc.text: Swedish chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered scandium in 1879 while analyzing the rare minerals euxenite and gadolinite at Uppsala University. He named it after Scandinavia (Latin "Scandia"), and the element's symbol Sc and atomic number 21 still anchor it at the top of the transition-metal block.

Sc.title: A Surprisingly Lightweight Metal
Sc.text: Although it sits among the transition metals, scandium is remarkably light, with a density of about 2.99 grams per cubic centimeter — closer to aluminum than to iron. Combined with a high melting point near 1541 degrees Celsius, this low density is exactly what makes it so prized for high-performance aluminum alloys.

Sc.title: The Secret in MiG Jets
Sc.text: Adding less than half a percent of scandium to aluminum dramatically refines the metal's grain structure, boosting strength and resistance to cracking during welding. Soviet engineers exploited this in the airframes and welded fuel tanks of MiG-21 and MiG-29 fighter jets, and today the same alloys appear in premium bicycle frames, baseball bats, and lacrosse sticks.

Sc.title: It Lights Up Stadiums
Sc.text: Scandium iodide is added to high-intensity metal-halide lamps because, when vaporized in the arc, it emits a broad spectrum of light very close to natural daylight. These bright, efficient lamps illuminate sports stadiums, film sets, and large arenas, giving cameras the white balance they need.

Sc.title: Rare in Rock, Not in the Cosmos
Sc.text: Scandium makes up only about 22 parts per million of Earth's crust, and it is so thinly scattered that it rarely forms concentrated ores of its own. Yet it is comparatively abundant in the Sun and many stars, where spectral lines of scandium are routinely detected — a reminder that crustal scarcity and cosmic abundance are very different things.

Sc.title: Forged in Dying Stars
Sc.text: The scandium in existence was built inside stars, partly through explosive nucleosynthesis in supernovae where extreme temperatures fuse lighter nuclei. Its single stable isotope, scandium-45, carries 21 protons and 24 neutrons, and is the only naturally occurring form, making scandium one of just a handful of mononuclidic elements.

Sc.title: Pulled From Uranium Waste
Sc.text: Because scandium so rarely concentrates on its own, most of the world's supply is recovered as a byproduct of processing other ores — including the tailings from uranium mining, and residues from titanium, nickel, and rare-earth extraction. The remote Norwegian mine at Ytterby and deposits in places like Bayan Obo, China, have historically been important sources.

Sc.title: No Job in Your Body
Sc.text: Unlike iron, zinc, or copper, scandium has no known biological role in humans, animals, or plants, and living cells get along perfectly well without it. It also shows low toxicity and is not readily absorbed, so it poses little hazard in everyday amounts — though, as with any fine metal powder, its dust can be flammable.

Sc.title: A Radioactive Tracer in Medicine
Sc.text: While stable scandium-45 is biologically inert, artificially made radioactive isotopes such as scandium-44 and scandium-47 are being developed for nuclear medicine. Scandium-44 emits positrons useful for PET imaging, while scandium-47 releases particles that can destroy tumor cells, making the pair attractive for "theranostics" that diagnose and treat cancer with chemically identical tracers.

Ti.title: Named for the Titans
Ti.text: Titanium was first recognized in 1791 by English clergyman and amateur mineralogist William Gregor, who found it in black sand near Manaccan, Cornwall. A few years later, German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth independently identified it and named it after the Titans of Greek mythology, the powerful children of Gaia and Uranus. The name nodded to its anticipated strength, even though pure metal would not be isolated for over a century.

Ti.title: A century to purify
Ti.text: Although discovered in the 1790s, reasonably pure titanium metal was not produced until 1910, when Matthew Hunter at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute reduced titanium tetrachloride with sodium. The metal stayed a laboratory curiosity until Luxembourg-born scientist William Kroll developed the magnesium-reduction Kroll process in 1940. That process is still the industrial standard today, which is one reason titanium remains relatively expensive.

Ti.title: Strong as steel, far lighter
Ti.text: Titanium has one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios of any structural metal. It is about as strong as many steels but roughly 45 percent lighter, with a density of about 4.5 grams per cubic centimeter versus around 7.9 for steel. This combination is why it is prized for jet engines, airframes, and high-performance bicycle frames.

Ti.title: It heals its own armor
Ti.text: Titanium resists corrosion because it instantly forms a thin, tough oxide layer when exposed to air or water. If this passive film is scratched, it re-forms in milliseconds wherever oxygen is present, protecting the metal underneath. This self-repairing shield lets titanium survive seawater and harsh chemicals that would rapidly eat away ordinary steel.

Ti.title: The body accepts it
Ti.text: Titanium is remarkably biocompatible, meaning the human body rarely rejects it. It can bond directly with living bone in a process called osseointegration, discovered by Swedish researcher Per-Ingvar Branemark in the 1950s. This makes it the material of choice for dental implants, hip and knee replacements, and surgical plates and screws.

Ti.title: Hidden in your sunscreen
Ti.text: The compound titanium dioxide is one of the whitest and most opaque substances known, so it is used as a pigment in paint, paper, plastics, and even toothpaste. It also absorbs and scatters ultraviolet light, which is why it is a common active ingredient in mineral sunscreens. Most titanium that is mined ends up as this dioxide rather than as the pure metal.

Ti.title: Ninth most abundant element
Ti.text: Titanium is the ninth most abundant element in Earth's crust, making up about 0.6 percent of it by mass. It is more common than familiar metals such as copper, nickel, and zinc, but it is never found as a free metal in nature. Instead it is locked inside minerals like rutile and ilmenite, and its difficult extraction keeps it costly despite its abundance.

Ti.title: Moon rocks were rich in it
Ti.text: Titanium is widespread in the cosmos and was found in surprising quantities in lunar samples returned by the Apollo missions. Some Moon basalts contain more than 10 percent titanium dioxide, far richer than typical Earth rocks of the same type. Astronomers also detect titanium oxide in the atmospheres of cool red stars, where it strongly shapes their spectra.

Ti.title: Burns with a brilliant white
Ti.text: While bulk titanium is hard to ignite, finely divided titanium powder or shavings burn fiercely with an intense white flame. It is one of the few elements that will keep burning in pure nitrogen gas, forming titanium nitride, and it also reacts directly with oxygen and even carbon at high temperatures. Because of this, titanium is used in fireworks and military flares to produce bright sparks.

Ti.title: It turns rainbow colors
Ti.text: When titanium is anodized, an electric current thickens its oxide layer to a precisely controlled depth. Light reflecting off this transparent film interferes with itself, producing vivid blues, purples, and golds with no dyes or paints involved. Jewelers and artists exploit this effect, and the colors are determined purely by the oxide thickness, which depends on the voltage used.

V.title: Discovered Twice, Named Once
V.text: Vanadium was first spotted in 1801 by Spanish-Mexican mineralogist Andrés Manuel del Río, who called it 'erythronium' because its salts turned red on heating. He was wrongly convinced he had merely found impure chromium and withdrew his claim. The element was rediscovered in 1830 by Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefström, who got the lasting credit.

V.title: Named For A Norse Goddess
V.text: Sefström named the element after Vanadís, another name for Freyja, the Norse goddess of beauty and fertility. The choice honors vanadium's strikingly beautiful, multicolored compounds. It is one of the few elements named after a figure from Norse mythology rather than Greek or Roman.

V.title: A Rainbow In A Test Tube
V.text: Vanadium is famous for forming ions in four common oxidation states, each with its own vivid color: +2 is violet, +3 is green, +4 is blue, and +5 is yellow. Chemistry teachers reduce a yellow vanadium(V) solution with zinc to watch it cascade through blue, green, and violet. This makes vanadium a classic classroom demonstration of redox chemistry.

V.title: The Secret In Strong Steel
V.text: Roughly 85 percent of all vanadium produced goes into steel alloys, where adding less than one percent dramatically increases strength, toughness, and resistance to fatigue. Henry Ford famously used vanadium steel in the chassis of the Model T to make it lighter yet more durable. Vanadium steel is also prized for surgical instruments, springs, and high-speed tools.

V.title: It Made Pure Aluminum Possible
V.text: In 1908, American metallurgist John Wesley Marden produced metallic vanadium that was 99.7 percent pure by reducing vanadium oxide with calcium. High-purity vanadium is ductile and workable. Today vanadium is added in tiny amounts to refine the grain structure of aluminum and titanium alloys used in aerospace.

V.title: Sea Creatures Hoard It
V.text: Marine animals called tunicates, or sea squirts, concentrate vanadium in special blood cells called vanadocytes at levels up to a million times higher than the surrounding seawater. Scientists still debate exactly why, with theories ranging from predator defense to a role in oxygen transport. Certain mushrooms, like Amanita muscaria, also accumulate surprising amounts of vanadium.

V.title: A Battery The Size Of A House
V.text: Vanadium redox flow batteries store energy by dissolving vanadium ions in tanks of liquid electrolyte, exploiting the metal's multiple oxidation states. Because you can scale storage simply by using bigger tanks, these batteries are ideal for grid-scale storage of solar and wind power. The largest, in Dalian, China, can deliver hundreds of megawatt-hours.

V.title: Possibly An Essential Nutrient
V.text: Trace amounts of vanadium are present in the human body, and some marine and bacterial enzymes, such as vanadium-dependent nitrogenase and bromoperoxidase, rely on it to function. Studies suggest vanadium compounds can mimic insulin and lower blood sugar in animals, though they are not yet an approved human treatment. Whether vanadium is truly essential for people remains an open scientific question.

V.title: Forged Inside Dying Stars
V.text: Vanadium is created in the cosmos largely during supernova explosions and explosive silicon burning in massive stars. Its single stable isotope, vanadium-51, makes up about 99.75 percent of natural vanadium. The remaining trace is vanadium-50, which is faintly radioactive with a half-life of around 271 quadrillion years, far longer than the current age of the universe.

V.title: A Catalyst For Modern Industry
V.text: Vanadium pentoxide is the workhorse catalyst in the contact process, which manufactures sulfuric acid, one of the most produced industrial chemicals on Earth. It speeds the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide without being consumed. The same compound also catalyzes the production of maleic anhydride, used in making plastics and resins.

Cr.title: Named For Its Colors
Cr.text: Chromium gets its name from the Greek word "chroma," meaning color, because so many of its compounds are vividly pigmented. French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin isolated the metal in 1797-1798 from a bright orange-red Siberian mineral called crocoite (lead chromate). He was struck by the rainbow of greens, yellows, reds, and oranges its salts could produce.

Cr.title: The Hardest Common Metal
Cr.text: Chromium is the hardest pure metal known, scoring about 8.5 on the Mohs scale, harder than hardened steel and nearly as hard as topaz. This extreme hardness, combined with a high melting point of 1907 degrees Celsius, is why it is used to harden alloys and create wear-resistant coatings. Despite being so hard, pure chromium is also quite brittle at room temperature.

Cr.title: The Reason Steel Doesn't Rust
Cr.text: Stainless steel is defined as steel containing at least 10.5 percent chromium, and the chromium is what makes it "stainless." The metal reacts with oxygen to form an ultra-thin, invisible, self-repairing passive layer of chromium oxide just a few nanometers thick. If the surface is scratched, this protective film instantly reforms, sealing the metal against corrosion.

Cr.title: Rubies And Emeralds Owe It Their Color
Cr.text: The deep red of a ruby and the lush green of an emerald both come from trace amounts of chromium ions replacing aluminum in the crystal. The same chromium impurity produces red in one gem and green in the other because the surrounding crystal structure changes how the ion absorbs light. Chromium-doped synthetic ruby also powered the very first working laser, built by Theodore Maiman in 1960.

Cr.title: A Metal Magnetic Only When Cold
Cr.text: Pure chromium is the only elemental solid that is antiferromagnetic at room temperature, meaning its atomic magnetic moments line up in alternating opposite directions and cancel out. It loses this ordered magnetism above its Neel temperature of about 38 degrees Celsius, becoming an ordinary paramagnet. This unusual behavior makes chromium a favorite subject for physicists studying magnetism.

Cr.title: Glittering Shop-Window Chrome
Cr.text: The shiny "chrome" finish on car bumpers, motorcycle parts, and bathroom fixtures is a thin layer of chromium applied by electroplating. The coating is prized because it stays bright, resists tarnish and scratches, and reflects light almost like a mirror. Decorative chrome plating boomed in the 1920s and 1930s and became an icon of the automotive age.

Cr.title: An Essential Trace Nutrient
Cr.text: Your body contains only a few milligrams of chromium, yet the trivalent form, chromium(III), is generally considered a trace nutrient that helps the hormone insulin work efficiently. It is found in foods such as broccoli, whole grains, nuts, and brewer's yeast. The amounts needed are tiny, and chromium(III) should not be confused with its toxic cousin.

Cr.title: A Tale Of Two Charges
Cr.text: Chromium's most famous oxidation states behave like opposites: chromium(III) is essential and relatively harmless, while chromium(VI), or hexavalent chromium, is a recognized carcinogen. Hexavalent chromium contamination of drinking water is the pollutant made famous by the legal case dramatized in the film Erin Brockovich. Industries that once used it for plating and pigments now face strict regulation worldwide.

Cr.title: Forged Inside Dying Stars
Cr.text: Chromium is created deep inside massive stars and during supernova explosions through nuclear fusion of lighter elements. Its most abundant isotope, chromium-52, is built up in the same processes that forge iron, one of the most stable nuclei in the universe. Astronomers detect chromium's spectral fingerprints in the Sun and in distant stars, tracing how galaxies enrich themselves with metals.

Cr.title: Tanning Leather And Protecting Wood
Cr.text: Roughly 90 percent of the world's leather is tanned using chromium(III) salts, a process that takes hours instead of the weeks needed by older vegetable methods. Chromium compounds also serve as wood preservatives, green and yellow pigments, and catalysts in the chemical industry. Most chromium ore is mined as chromite, with South Africa and Kazakhstan holding the largest reserves.

Mn.title: Named From Magnetic Confusion
Mn.text: Manganese was first isolated in 1774 by Swedish chemist Johan Gottlieb Gahn, who reduced the mineral pyrolusite with charcoal. Its name traces back to 'magnesia nigra' (black magnesia), a term once muddled with the minerals that gave us both magnesium and the magnet, since these dark ores were long confused with one another.

Mn.title: Four Brittle Crystal Forms
Mn.text: Pure manganese is hard yet extremely brittle, so brittle that it cannot be machined or worked like ordinary metals. At room temperature it adopts a bizarre crystal structure called alpha-manganese with 58 atoms packed into a single unit cell, and it shifts through four different solid forms (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) as it is heated toward its melting point of about 1246 degrees Celsius.

Mn.title: The Rainbow Of Oxidation States
Mn.text: Manganese is a chemical chameleon that can exist in oxidation states from minus three all the way up to plus seven. Each state has a signature color in solution: the plus two ion is pale pink, plus six gives a deep green manganate, and plus seven yields the intense purple of permanganate, making manganese chemistry a vivid playground for the periodic table.

Mn.title: Steel's Secret Ingredient
Mn.text: More than 90 percent of all manganese produced goes into making steel, where it removes unwanted oxygen and sulfur and dramatically improves strength. Hadfield steel, invented by Robert Hadfield in 1882 with about 12 to 14 percent manganese, becomes harder the more it is hammered, which is why it is used for railway crossings, rock crushers, and prison bars.

Mn.title: Purple Crystals That Clean Water
Mn.text: Potassium permanganate, KMnO4, forms striking dark purple crystals and is a powerful oxidizing agent used worldwide to purify drinking water, treat skin infections, and remove iron and odors from well water. In the chemistry lab it serves as a self-indicating titration reagent, since it turns colorless the instant it is fully reduced, signaling the endpoint without any added dye.

Mn.title: Essential For Every Breath You Take
Mn.text: Manganese is a trace element vital to life, sitting at the heart of enzymes like manganese superoxide dismutase that protects your mitochondria from damaging free radicals. Most strikingly, the oxygen-evolving complex in plant photosynthesis uses a cluster of four manganese atoms to split water molecules, meaning nearly all the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere is released with manganese's help.

Mn.title: Treasure Nodules On The Seabed
Mn.text: Vast fields of potato-sized lumps called manganese nodules carpet parts of the deep ocean floor, especially the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific. These nodules grow agonizingly slowly, sometimes only a few millimeters every million years, yet collectively they hold billions of tons of manganese along with nickel, cobalt, and copper, making them a tempting and controversial mining target.

Mn.title: Painted In The Ice Age
Mn.text: Long before it was a metal, manganese was a pigment: prehistoric artists used black manganese dioxide to paint animals on cave walls at sites like Lascaux in France around 17,000 years ago. The same compound also colors glass, and historically glassmakers added it as 'glassmaker's soap' to cancel out the green tint caused by iron impurities.

Mn.title: A Metal You Can See In Space
Mn.text: Manganese is forged in the explosive deaths of massive stars and in thermonuclear supernovae, then scattered across the galaxy to become part of new worlds. Astronomers measure manganese abundances in distant stars to trace the chemical history of the Milky Way, and the element ranks among the dozen most abundant metals in Earth's crust at roughly 0.1 percent by mass.

Mn.title: Too Much Causes Manganism
Mn.text: Although the body needs only tiny amounts, chronic overexposure to manganese dust, common among miners and welders, can cause a serious neurological disorder called manganism with symptoms resembling Parkinson's disease. This happens because excess manganese accumulates in the basal ganglia of the brain, a sobering reminder that an element essential for life can become a hazard at high doses.

Fe.title: A Symbol From Latin
Fe.text: Iron's chemical symbol Fe comes from its Latin name, ferrum. The English word 'iron' descends from Old English isern and Proto-Germanic isarnan, words that predate written records. This split between a Germanic common name and a Latin scientific symbol is why the abbreviation looks nothing like the spoken word.

Fe.title: Older Than Smelting
Fe.text: Long before humans learned to smelt ore around 1200 BCE, ancient Egyptians crafted iron beads from meteorites. Beads found at Gerzeh and dated to about 3200 BCE were hammered from nickel-rich meteoric iron, which is why the Egyptians sometimes called iron 'metal of heaven.' These are among the oldest known iron artifacts on Earth.

Fe.title: The Cosmic Dead End
Fe.text: Iron sits at a special peak in nuclear binding energy: its isotope iron-56 is among the most tightly bound nuclei that exist. This means a massive star cannot release energy by fusing iron, so when its core turns to iron, fusion stops and the star collapses, triggering a supernova. Iron is effectively the ash of stellar fusion.

Fe.title: The Reason Blood Is Red
Fe.text: Each molecule of hemoglobin in your red blood cells contains four iron atoms, and each can grab one oxygen molecule for transport around the body. An average adult carries roughly 3 to 4 grams of iron, most of it locked inside this protein. The interaction of light with the iron-bearing heme group is what gives oxygen-rich blood its bright red color.

Fe.title: Earth's Molten Heart
Fe.text: Iron is the most abundant element on Earth by mass, largely because the planet's core is mostly iron mixed with some nickel. The solid inner core and liquid outer core are made of this metal, and churning currents in the molten outer core generate Earth's magnetic field. That field deflects harmful solar radiation and lets compasses point north.

Fe.title: Rust Never Sleeps
Fe.text: When iron meets oxygen and water, it forms hydrated iron oxides we call rust. Unlike the protective oxide layer on aluminum, rust is flaky and porous, so it keeps exposing fresh metal and eats steadily into the metal. Corrosion of iron and steel costs the global economy hundreds of billions of dollars every year.

Fe.title: Curie's Magnetic Limit
Fe.text: Iron is one of only a few elements that are ferromagnetic, meaning it can become a permanent magnet at room temperature. But heat destroys this property: above its Curie temperature of 770 degrees Celsius, iron loses its magnetism entirely. Cool it back down and the magnetic ordering returns.

Fe.title: From Iron To Steel
Fe.text: Pure iron is actually fairly soft; its strength as a building material comes from alloying it with carbon to make steel. Adding less than 2 percent carbon dramatically increases hardness, and steel is now produced at well over a billion tonnes per year. This alloy underpins skyscrapers, ships, cars, and railways worldwide.

Fe.title: The Red Planet's Coat
Fe.text: Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron oxide dust, essentially the same rust that forms on Earth. Iron is also common in asteroids and meteorites, and iron-nickel meteorites provided some of humanity's earliest usable metal. The element is one of the most abundant in the universe, forged inside stars.

Fe.title: Shape-Shifting Crystals
Fe.text: Solid iron does not keep one fixed atomic arrangement; it changes its crystal structure as it heats. Below 912 degrees Celsius it is body-centered cubic (called ferrite), then it switches to a face-centered cubic form (austenite) at higher temperatures. Metallurgists exploit these transformations, along with rapid cooling, to control the hardness and toughness of steel.

Co.title: Named After Goblins
Co.text: The name cobalt comes from the German word "Kobold," meaning goblin or evil spirit. Medieval Saxon miners blamed these mischievous sprites when a bluish ore poisoned them and yielded no useful metal despite looking like valuable silver or copper ore. The toxic fumes were actually arsenic released when the cobalt-arsenic minerals were smelted.

Co.title: A Swedish First
Co.text: In 1735 the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt isolated cobalt, proving the blue color in glass and ceramics came from a new metal, not from bismuth as many believed. This made cobalt the first new metal discovered since antiquity, when only seven metals like gold, silver, and iron were known. Brandt's work helped open the door to modern systematic chemistry.

Co.title: Blue That Lasts Millennia
Co.text: Cobalt compounds have colored glass and pottery a vivid blue for over 4,000 years, appearing in ancient Egyptian and Chinese artifacts long before anyone knew cobalt was an element. The pigment cobalt blue (cobalt aluminate) was perfected in 1802 and prized by painters like Maxfield Parrish and Vincent van Gogh. Just a tiny amount of cobalt oxide tints a large batch of glass deep blue.

Co.title: One Of Three Magnetic Metals
Co.text: Cobalt is one of only three elements that are ferromagnetic at room temperature, alongside iron and nickel. It has the highest Curie temperature of any metal at about 1,121 degrees Celsius, meaning it keeps its magnetism at extreme heat better than iron or nickel. This makes cobalt essential in powerful permanent magnets such as alnico and samarium-cobalt alloys used in motors and sensors.

Co.title: The Vitamin B12 Core
Co.text: Cobalt sits at the very center of vitamin B12 (cobalamin), making it the only metal known to be required inside a vitamin. This nutrient is essential for forming red blood cells, building DNA, and keeping the nervous system healthy, and a deficiency causes pernicious anemia. Humans cannot make B12 themselves, so we rely on bacteria that build it atom by atom around a single cobalt ion.

Co.title: A Cancer-Fighting Isotope
Co.text: The artificial isotope cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and has a half-life of about 5.27 years. Since the 1950s, cobalt-60 "bombs" have delivered radiation therapy to shrink tumors, and the same rays sterilize medical equipment and preserve food. It is produced by bombarding ordinary cobalt-59 with neutrons inside a nuclear reactor.

Co.title: Powering Your Phone
Co.text: Cobalt is a key ingredient in the lithium-ion batteries that run smartphones, laptops, and electric cars, where it stabilizes the cathode and boosts energy density. More than 70 percent of the world's mined cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, often as a byproduct of copper and nickel mining. The surging demand for electric vehicles has made cobalt one of the most strategically important metals of the 21st century.

Co.title: Built To Take The Heat
Co.text: Superalloys based on cobalt keep their strength at temperatures that would weaken most metals, so they line the hottest parts of jet engines and gas turbines. Cobalt-chromium alloys are also hard, corrosion-resistant, and biocompatible, which is why they are used for artificial hip and knee joints and dental implants. The trade name Stellite describes wear-resistant cobalt alloys used for cutting tools and engine valves.

Co.title: Forged In Dying Stars
Co.text: Cobalt is created deep inside massive stars and is flung across space when those stars explode as supernovae. Much of the cobalt in the universe actually begins as radioactive nickel-56, which decays into cobalt-56 and then into stable iron-56, powering the fading light of a supernova for months. Earth's cobalt is concentrated in the planet's core and scattered through its crust at only about 25 parts per million.

Co.title: The Color-Changing Trick
Co.text: Cobalt chloride is famous for changing color with humidity, turning pink when wet and blue when dry, which is why it once coated "weather" novelty cards and silica-gel drying packets. This reversible shift happens because water molecules attach to and detach from the cobalt ion, rearranging how it absorbs light. Chemistry teachers still use the effect as a vivid, hands-on way to demonstrate hydration and equilibrium.

Ni.title: Named After a Devil
Ni.text: Nickel's name comes from the German "Kupfernickel," meaning "copper-devil" or "Old Nick's copper." Medieval Saxon miners cursed a reddish ore that looked like copper but yielded none, blaming a mischievous goblin (Nickel). The Swedish chemist Axel Fredrik Cronstedt isolated the metal from this very ore in 1751.

Ni.title: It Used to Be Magnetic
Ni.text: Nickel is one of only four elements that are ferromagnetic at room temperature, alongside iron, cobalt, and gadolinium. This means it can be permanently magnetized and is strongly attracted to magnets. However, if you heat nickel above its Curie temperature of about 354 degrees Celsius, it abruptly loses its magnetism.

Ni.title: The Coin With Almost No Nickel
Ni.text: The American five-cent coin is called a "nickel," but it is actually only 25 percent nickel and 75 percent copper. Ironically, the U.S. one-cent penny and even the silvery dime contain copper as their main metal too. Pure nickel coins were once common in countries like Canada and Switzerland.

Ni.title: Stainless Steel's Secret Ingredient
Ni.text: Roughly two-thirds of all nickel produced goes into making stainless steel. Adding about 8 to 10 percent nickel to chromium steel creates the most common type, called 18/8 or 304 stainless, used in kitchen sinks and cutlery. The nickel stabilizes the steel's crystal structure and dramatically boosts its resistance to corrosion.

Ni.title: A Planet's Iron Heart
Ni.text: Earth's core is composed mainly of an iron-nickel alloy, with nickel making up an estimated 5 to 10 percent of it. The swirling motion of this molten metal generates Earth's magnetic field, which shields us from solar radiation. Many iron meteorites are also iron-nickel alloys, and their nickel content is how scientists tell them apart from ordinary rocks.

Ni.title: The Memory Metal
Ni.text: Nitinol, an alloy of nickel and titanium, is a remarkable "shape-memory" material. Bend it out of shape, then warm it up, and it springs back to its original form as if it remembered. This property makes Nitinol invaluable for medical stents that expand inside arteries and for bendable, hard-to-break eyeglass frames.

Ni.title: Powering Your Devices
Ni.text: Nickel is a key component of rechargeable batteries, including nickel-cadmium (NiCd) and nickel-metal-hydride (NiMH) cells. It is also vital in the lithium-ion batteries that power electric cars, where high-nickel cathodes pack in more energy. This battery demand is now one of the fastest-growing reasons the world mines nickel.

Ni.title: A Common Allergy Culprit
Ni.text: Nickel is the single most common cause of allergic contact dermatitis, affecting an estimated 10 to 20 percent of people. The reaction often appears as an itchy rash where jewelry, watch backs, or belt buckles touch the skin. To protect consumers, the European Union strictly limits how much nickel can leach from items worn against the body.

Ni.title: Essential Element of Life
Ni.text: Many bacteria, archaea, plants, and fungi depend on nickel as a trace nutrient. It sits at the heart of at least nine known enzymes, including urease, which breaks down urea, and the hydrogenases that handle hydrogen gas. Plants like soybeans need tiny amounts of nickel to grow properly, making it a genuine micronutrient.

Ni.title: The Mond Purification Trick
Ni.text: In 1890, chemist Ludwig Mond discovered that nickel reacts with carbon monoxide gas at around 50 degrees Celsius to form a volatile compound called nickel tetracarbonyl. Heated further, this gas decomposes and deposits pure nickel back out. This elegant "Mond process" is still used industrially to refine nickel to extreme purity, though the gas is dangerously toxic.

Cu.title: One Of Civilization's First Metals
Cu.text: Copper was among the very first metals humans worked, with copper artifacts from around 9000 BCE found in the Middle East. Because nuggets of native copper occur naturally in metallic form, early people could hammer it cold into beads and tools long before they learned to smelt ores. Its use was so transformative that it gave its name to the Copper Age (Chalcolithic), the bridge between the Stone Age and the Bronze Age.

Cu.title: Named After An Island
Cu.text: The symbol Cu comes from the Latin word cuprum, which itself derives from 'aes cyprium' meaning 'metal of Cyprus.' The Mediterranean island of Cyprus was the Roman Empire's main source of copper, so the metal was literally named after the place it was mined. The English word 'copper' evolved from the same Latin root through Old English 'coper.'

Cu.title: Bronze And Brass Builders
Cu.text: Copper rarely works alone in history: alloyed with tin it makes bronze, and with zinc it makes brass. The invention of bronze around 3300 BCE was so important it defined an entire era, the Bronze Age, because bronze tools and weapons were far harder than pure copper. These two alloys remain workhorses today in everything from musical instruments to ship propellers and plumbing fittings.

Cu.title: Second-Best Conductor Of Electricity
Cu.text: Copper conducts electricity better than every metal except silver, which is why roughly two-thirds of all copper produced goes into electrical wiring. Silver is only marginally better but far too expensive for mass use, so copper became the practical champion of the electrical age. This single property is why power grids, motors, and the device you are reading this on all depend on copper.

Cu.title: It Turns Green On Purpose
Cu.text: Copper does not rust like iron; instead it slowly forms a green coating called a patina, made of copper carbonate and sulfate compounds. This patina actually protects the metal underneath from further corrosion, which is why copper roofs and statues can last for centuries. The Statue of Liberty, sheathed in about 80 tonnes of copper, owes its famous green color to this very process over more than a century.

Cu.title: Essential Inside Your Body
Cu.text: Copper is a trace nutrient your body genuinely needs, with adults containing only about 50 to 120 milligrams of it total. It is a key part of enzymes that help form red blood cells, build connective tissue, and run your nervous system. Too little causes anemia and bone problems, which is why foods like shellfish, nuts, seeds, and dark chocolate are valued copper sources.

Cu.title: Blue Blood Of The Sea
Cu.text: While humans use iron-based hemoglobin to carry oxygen, animals like octopuses, squid, lobsters, and many snails use a copper-based protein called hemocyanin instead. Because copper turns blue when it binds oxygen, the blood of these creatures is literally blue rather than red. This adaptation works especially well in the cold, low-oxygen waters of the deep ocean.

Cu.title: A Natural Germ Killer
Cu.text: Copper surfaces are antimicrobial, killing bacteria, viruses, and fungi that land on them through a process scientists call the oligodynamic effect. The metal releases ions that puncture microbial cell membranes and disrupt their DNA, often clearing germs within hours. For this reason hospitals increasingly use copper-alloy doorknobs, bed rails, and handles to help reduce the spread of infections.

Cu.title: Forged In Dying Stars
Cu.text: Copper is not made in ordinary stellar burning but is forged in the violent deaths of massive stars, particularly during supernova explosions. Processes that rapidly add neutrons to lighter nuclei build up elements like copper, which are then scattered across space to seed new worlds. Every copper atom in a wire or coin was created in such a cosmic cataclysm billions of years ago.

Cu.title: Endlessly Recyclable Money Metal
Cu.text: Copper can be recycled over and over without any loss of quality, and a large share of the copper ever mined is still in use today. It has also long been a coinage metal: many 'silver' coins and most modern small change are actually copper or copper alloys, and the US penny is copper-plated zinc. With Chile alone producing roughly a quarter of the world's supply, copper remains one of the most economically vital metals on Earth.

Zn.title: Named From The German
Zn.text: The name "zinc" comes from the German word Zink, popularized by the alchemist and physician Paracelsus in the 16th century. It likely refers to the pointed, tooth-like (Zinke means "prong" or "tine") shape of the crystals that form when the molten metal solidifies. Although the pure metal was isolated relatively late in Europe, the word entered chemistry long before zinc was recognized as a distinct element.

Zn.title: India Smelted It First
Zn.text: While Europeans were still puzzling over it, metallurgists in India were already producing metallic zinc on an industrial scale by around the 12th century at Zawar in Rajasthan. They used clever downward-distillation retorts to capture zinc vapor, which boils off at only 907 C and would otherwise escape as gas. The German chemist Andreas Marggraf is usually credited with isolating zinc scientifically in 1746, centuries after these Indian smelters.

Zn.title: It Protects By Sacrificing Itself
Zn.text: Zinc is more chemically reactive than iron, so when steel is coated in zinc (galvanizing), the zinc corrodes first and shields the iron underneath. This is called sacrificial or cathodic protection, and it works even where the coating is scratched, because the surrounding zinc keeps giving up electrons. Roughly half of all the zinc mined each year goes into galvanizing to stop steel from rusting.

Zn.title: A Spark In Your Brain
Zn.text: Zinc is the second most abundant trace metal in the human body after iron, and an adult carries about 2 to 3 grams of it. It is a structural or catalytic component of hundreds of enzymes and of the "zinc finger" proteins that grip DNA to switch genes on and off. In the brain, neurons store zinc in synaptic vesicles and release it during signaling, making it essential for memory and learning.

Zn.title: The Original Battery Metal
Zn.text: When Alessandro Volta built the first true battery, the voltaic pile of 1800, he stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth. Zinc readily gives up electrons, so it still serves as the negative electrode in everyday alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries. Zinc-air cells, which pull oxygen straight from the atmosphere, power most modern hearing aids.

Zn.title: Brass Came Before Pure Zinc
Zn.text: Humans used zinc in alloys long before they could make the pure metal. Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, was produced by the Romans by heating copper with zinc ore (calamine) and charcoal, a trick that dissolved the zinc without ever isolating it. Adding zinc to copper makes brass harder, more golden, and far easier to cast and machine than copper alone.

Zn.title: The Healing Mineral
Zn.text: Zinc oxide is the white, opaque paste in sunscreens and diaper creams, where it physically blocks ultraviolet light and soothes irritated skin. Adequate zinc is critical for wound healing and a working immune system, and the World Health Organization recommends zinc supplements to treat childhood diarrhea in developing countries. Severe deficiency causes a rare disease called acrodermatitis enteropathica, marked by skin lesions and stunted growth.

Zn.title: Forged In Dying Stars
Zn.text: Zinc is built inside massive stars and scattered across the galaxy when they explode as supernovae. Astronomers actually use zinc to measure pollution of the early universe, because unlike iron it is barely absorbed onto interstellar dust grains, so it faithfully tracks how much heavy-element "metal" a distant gas cloud truly contains. The Sun and the wider cosmos contain only trace amounts, making zinc a relatively rare element compared with the iron it so often guards.

Zn.title: Cold Snap, Brittle Metal
Zn.text: Zinc has a surprising mechanical personality that depends sharply on temperature. At room temperature cast zinc is fairly brittle, but between about 100 and 150 C it becomes soft and malleable enough to roll into sheets, then turns brittle again above roughly 210 C. Because its melting point is a low 420 C, zinc is easy to die-cast into intricate shapes for car parts, hardware, and toys.

Zn.title: Pennies Are Mostly Zinc
Zn.text: Since 1982 the United States one-cent coin has been made of 97.5 percent zinc with only a thin copper plating, because copper had become too expensive to mint. So while a penny looks coppery, it is really a zinc slug wearing a copper coat. Zinc's affordability and the ease of plating it make this kind of disguise a common industrial trick.

Ga.title: Predicted Before It Was Found
Ga.text: In 1871 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for a missing element he called "eka-aluminium," predicting its atomic weight, density, and even that it would have a low melting point. Just four years later, in 1875, the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated it and confirmed the predictions almost exactly. This stunning success helped convince skeptical scientists that the periodic table was a genuine law of nature, not a coincidence.

Ga.title: A Patriotic (and Sneaky) Name
Ga.text: Boisbaudran named the element gallium after Gallia, the Latin name for France, his homeland. Some chemists have long suspected a hidden pun, because "Lecoq" means "the rooster" in French, and the Latin word for rooster is gallus. Boisbaudran denied any wordplay, but the coincidence has delighted chemistry students for nearly 150 years.

Ga.title: It Melts in Your Hand
Ga.text: Gallium has a melting point of just 29.76 degrees Celsius (about 85.6 degrees Fahrenheit), low enough that a solid chunk turns to liquid in the warmth of your palm. Yet it does not boil until around 2,400 degrees Celsius, giving it one of the largest liquid temperature ranges of any element. This odd combination makes it useful in high-temperature thermometers where mercury would boil away.

Ga.title: The Spoon That Vanishes
Ga.text: Because gallium is solid at room temperature but melts near body temperature, chemists use it to make a classic prank: a spoon that dissolves into a hot cup of tea. Gallium is also far less toxic than mercury, the other famous room-temperature-adjacent metal, which is why it is sometimes called a safer liquid metal. Despite melting easily, it is not something to eat, but handling it briefly is generally harmless.

Ga.title: It Expands When It Freezes
Ga.text: Like water, ice, and only a handful of other substances such as bismuth and silicon, gallium is denser as a liquid than as a solid, so it expands when it solidifies. This means freezing gallium can crack its container, so it is never stored in completely full sealed glass or metal vessels. This anomaly comes from the unusual way its atoms pack together in the crystal.

Ga.title: The Heart of Modern Electronics
Ga.text: Gallium's most important use is in compound semiconductors, especially gallium arsenide (GaAs) and gallium nitride (GaN). GaN is what makes the blue and white LEDs in your phone screen and modern light bulbs possible, an achievement that won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. GaAs powers high-speed chips in satellites, radar, and 5G base stations because electrons move through it faster than through ordinary silicon.

Ga.title: No Mining Required
Ga.text: There is no such thing as a gallium mine, because the element is too scattered to form its own ore deposits. Instead, it is recovered as a byproduct of refining aluminium from bauxite and processing zinc ores. The average crust contains gallium at roughly 19 parts per million, similar to lead, but it is almost always thinly diluted inside other minerals.

Ga.title: A Spy Inside Your Bones
Ga.text: Doctors use radioactive gallium-67 and gallium-68 as tracers in medical imaging. Because gallium ions behave chemically a bit like iron, the body transports them to sites of infection, inflammation, and certain tumors, where scanners can detect the faint radiation. Gallium-68 PET scans are now a powerful tool for finding prostate cancer and neuroendocrine tumors with remarkable precision.

Ga.title: Liquid Metal That Heals Itself
Ga.text: Alloys of gallium with indium and tin, such as galinstan, stay liquid well below room temperature and conduct electricity, making them candidates for flexible, stretchable, and self-healing circuits. Researchers are exploring these liquid metals for soft robotics and wearable electronics that can bend without breaking. Gallium-based coolants are also studied for chips because liquid metal carries heat far better than water.

Ga.title: It Quietly Attacks Aluminium
Ga.text: A small amount of liquid gallium can soak into aluminium along its grain boundaries and make the strong metal crumble like a cracker, a process called liquid metal embrittlement. For this reason gallium is banned from aircraft cabins and carefully kept away from aluminium structures. The same property fascinates materials scientists studying how metals fail at the atomic scale.

Ge.title: Predicted Before Discovered
Ge.text: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table and predicted an unknown element he called "eka-silicon," estimating its atomic weight, density, and oxide formula. When Clemens Winkler isolated germanium in 1886, its measured properties matched the prediction almost exactly. This stunning success became one of the strongest early confirmations that the periodic law was real.

Ge.title: Named For Germany
Ge.text: Clemens Winkler discovered the element in 1886 in Freiberg, Saxony, while analyzing a silver mineral called argyrodite. He named it after his home country, Germany (Latin Germania). For a brief moment he considered the name "neptunium," but that label was eventually given to a different element decades later.

Ge.title: A Metal That Isn't
Ge.text: Germanium is a metalloid: it looks like a shiny, silvery-white metal but behaves chemically and electrically like a semiconductor. At room temperature it is a brittle, crystalline solid that shares the same diamond cubic structure as silicon and carbon. This in-between nature is exactly why it became so important to electronics.

Ge.title: It Powered The First Transistor
Ge.text: The very first working transistor, built at Bell Labs in December 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley, was made from germanium, not silicon. Germanium dominated early electronics through the 1950s before silicon took over because it handles heat better and forms a more stable oxide. That single germanium device launched the entire age of modern computing.

Ge.title: It Expands When It Freezes
Ge.text: Like water and silicon, germanium is one of the rare substances that expands when it solidifies rather than contracting. Its liquid form is actually denser than its solid form, so solid germanium floats on its own melt. This anomaly comes from the open, tetrahedral crystal structure it forms when it freezes.

Ge.title: Eyes For Night Vision
Ge.text: Germanium is remarkably transparent to infrared light while being opaque to visible light, which makes it ideal for lenses and windows in thermal-imaging and night-vision cameras. Much of the world's germanium is used to make optics for military, firefighting, and security infrared systems. A polished germanium lens looks like dark metal to your eye but is crystal-clear to a heat camera.

Ge.title: The Backbone Of Fiber Optics
Ge.text: Adding germanium dioxide to the silica core of an optical fiber raises its refractive index, allowing light to be guided down the fiber over long distances. This doping is essential to the high-speed fiber-optic cables that carry most of the internet's data. A huge share of global germanium production goes into telecommunications glass.

Ge.title: Hiding In Coal And Zinc
Ge.text: Germanium is fairly rare, making up only about 1.6 parts per million of Earth's crust, and it has no rich ore of its own. Instead it is recovered mostly as a byproduct of zinc smelting and from the ash of certain coal deposits. China produces the majority of the world's supply, which makes germanium a strategically important critical mineral.

Ge.title: Not Needed By Life
Ge.text: Germanium has no known biological role in humans, plants, or animals, and the body does not require it. Despite this, some "organic germanium" supplements were marketed as health remedies, but inorganic germanium compounds taken over time have caused serious kidney damage and even deaths. Health agencies now warn against germanium dietary supplements.

Ge.title: Forged In Dying Stars
Ge.text: Germanium is produced in the cosmos mainly through the slow neutron-capture process (the s-process) inside aging red giant stars, and partly in the explosive r-process of supernovae and neutron-star mergers. The germanium on Earth was inherited from such stellar debris that seeded the cloud which formed our solar system. Ultra-pure germanium crystals are even used today as detectors to hunt for gamma rays and dark matter.

As.title: Named After a Color
As.text: The word arsenic traces back to the Greek 'arsenikon', which itself came from the Syriac 'zarniqa' and ultimately the Old Iranian word for gold, referring to the brilliant golden-yellow mineral orpiment (arsenic sulfide). Ancient writers used the term for the colorful sulfide minerals long before the pure element was isolated. The Greek root was sometimes mistakenly linked to 'arsenikos', meaning masculine or potent, reflecting old beliefs about the substance's strength.

As.title: Isolated by Albertus Magnus
As.text: Although arsenic compounds were known and used for thousands of years, the medieval scholar Albertus Magnus is usually credited with first isolating the element around 1250 by heating orpiment with soap. This makes arsenic one of the very first elements to be isolated in a recognizable elemental form, centuries before modern chemistry existed. Earlier alchemists in the Islamic world, including Jabir ibn Hayyan, had already studied its compounds extensively.

As.title: It Skips the Liquid Phase
As.text: At ordinary atmospheric pressure, gray arsenic does not melt into a liquid when heated; instead it sublimates, turning directly from a solid into a vapor at about 615 degrees Celsius. To get liquid arsenic you must heat it under pressure of roughly 28 atmospheres or more. This unusual behavior set it apart from most metals and made it tricky for early chemists to purify.

As.title: Three Faces of One Element
As.text: Arsenic exists in several allotropes, the most common being a brittle, metallic gray form, alongside a yellow waxy form and a black amorphous form. Gray arsenic has a layered crystal structure similar to that of black phosphorus and conducts electricity, while yellow arsenic is soft, unstable, and made of tetrahedral As4 molecules much like white phosphorus. Exposure to light or gentle heat quickly converts the unstable yellow form back into the stable gray one.

As.title: A Metalloid on the Staircase
As.text: Arsenic sits along the zig-zag dividing line of the periodic table that separates metals from nonmetals, which is why it is classified as a metalloid with properties of both. It shares group 15 with nitrogen and phosphorus above it and with antimony and bismuth below, so it shows the typical valences of plus three and plus five. This in-between character is exactly why arsenic is so valuable in making semiconductors.

As.title: The Heart of Gallium Arsenide
As.text: Combined with gallium, arsenic forms gallium arsenide, a semiconductor that moves electrons faster than silicon and converts electricity into light very efficiently. This compound powers high-frequency chips in mobile phones and radar, the red and infrared LEDs in remote controls, and high-efficiency solar cells used on satellites and Mars rovers. Without arsenic, much of modern high-speed and optoelectronic technology would look very different.

As.title: From Poison to Pharmacy
As.text: In 1910 Paul Ehrlich and his team introduced Salvarsan, an arsenic-based drug that became the first effective treatment for syphilis and a founding example of modern chemotherapy. More recently, arsenic trioxide, once feared purely as a poison, has become a highly successful medicine for acute promyelocytic leukemia, often producing remission when other treatments fail. The same element that kills can, in carefully controlled doses, save lives.

As.title: The Inheritance Powder
As.text: Arsenic trioxide earned the grim nickname 'inheritance powder' in Renaissance Europe because it is nearly tasteless, dissolves easily in food and drink, and once produced symptoms resembling natural illness. For centuries it was almost untraceable, until chemist James Marsh devised the sensitive Marsh test in 1836, which could reveal tiny amounts of arsenic in a body. That breakthrough turned forensic toxicology into a real science and made arsenic poisoning far easier to detect.

As.title: A Hidden Threat in Groundwater
As.text: Naturally occurring arsenic leaches from certain rocks and sediments into groundwater, and in regions of Bangladesh and West Bengal millions of people have been exposed by drinking from contaminated wells. The World Health Organization sets a safety limit of just 10 micrograms of arsenic per liter of drinking water. This contamination is considered one of the largest mass poisonings in human history, driving major efforts in well testing and filtration.

As.title: Life That Tolerates Arsenic
As.text: Although arsenic is toxic to most organisms because it mimics phosphorus and disrupts energy metabolism, some microbes have evolved to thrive around it. Certain bacteria can actually use arsenic compounds in their metabolism, breathing arsenate the way we breathe oxygen, in environments like California's Mono Lake. Studying these extremophiles helps scientists understand the chemical limits of life and even how life might survive on other worlds.

Se.title: Named After the Moon
Se.text: Selenium was discovered in 1817 by the Swedish chemists Jons Jacob Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn, who found it as a red residue in the lead chambers of a sulfuric acid plant. Because it closely resembled the recently discovered element tellurium (named for the Earth, from Latin 'tellus'), Berzelius named it after the Moon using the Greek word 'selene'. The two elements remain chemical cousins, sitting next to each other in group 16.

Se.title: It Sees the Light
Se.text: Selenium is a photoconductor: its electrical resistance drops dramatically when light shines on it, conducting electricity far better when illuminated than in the dark. This light-sensitive behavior, noticed in the 1870s, made selenium the heart of early light meters, photocells, and the first experiments in transmitting images. It even played a role in Alexander Graham Bell's 'photophone', which sent sound over a beam of light.

Se.title: The Father of Photocopying
Se.text: Selenium's photoconductivity is what made the photocopier and the laser printer possible. In Chester Carlson's xerography process, a thin selenium coating on a drum holds an electric charge in the dark, then loses that charge wherever light strikes it, forming a hidden electrostatic image that toner powder clings to. For decades, amorphous selenium drums were the standard imaging surface inside Xerox machines worldwide.

Se.title: An Essential Trace Nutrient
Se.text: Selenium is vital to human life in tiny amounts, forming the core of the unusual amino acid selenocysteine, sometimes called the 21st amino acid. It sits in the active site of enzymes like glutathione peroxidase, which protect cells from oxidative damage, and the deiodinases that activate thyroid hormone. The recommended daily intake for adults is only about 55 micrograms, yet a deficiency can cause real disease.

Se.title: A Heart Disease in China
Se.text: In selenium-poor regions of China, a deficiency was linked to Keshan disease, a serious heart muscle disorder named after Keshan County in Heilongjiang province where it was studied. Large public health programs distributing selenium supplements in the 1970s dramatically reduced its incidence. The discovery helped prove that selenium is genuinely essential rather than merely a curious trace element.

Se.title: Beneficial but Easily Toxic
Se.text: Selenium has one of the narrowest safe ranges of any nutrient: helpful around 55 micrograms a day, but toxic when intake climbs into the milligram range. Chronic overexposure causes selenosis, whose signs include brittle hair and nails, skin rashes, and a distinctive garlic odor on the breath from exhaled dimethyl selenide. Livestock grazing on selenium-accumulating plants like locoweed can suffer 'alkali disease', a warning known to ranchers in parts of the American West.

Se.title: It Changes Its Form
Se.text: Selenium is famously polymorphic, existing in several distinct forms called allotropes. Glassy black selenium and bright red forms can be coaxed by heat into a stable grey 'metallic' crystalline form built from long spiral chains of atoms. Only this grey form shows the strong photoconductivity, so the element's most useful property depends entirely on which arrangement its atoms take.

Se.title: Glassmaker's Secret Weapon
Se.text: Iron impurities give ordinary glass an unwanted greenish tint, and a pinch of selenium acts as a decolorizer because its pink-red color is complementary to that green, cancelling it out to yield clear glass. In larger amounts, selenium and cadmium selenide are deliberately added to produce vivid 'selenium ruby' red glass, long prized for railway signal lenses and decorative ware. The same red pigments color some traffic lights and artistic glasswork.

Se.title: Forged in Dying Stars
Se.text: Selenium is not made in ordinary stellar burning but is built up in the cosmos mainly by neutron capture, the slow s-process inside aging stars and the rapid r-process in violent events like supernovae and neutron-star mergers. On Earth it is relatively rare in the crust, rarely forming its own ores and instead riding along with copper sulfide minerals. Almost all commercial selenium is recovered as a byproduct of refining copper, collected from the anode sludge left behind.

Se.title: A Surprisingly Smelly Glow Detector
Se.text: Selenium has a strong appetite for capturing electrons and X-rays, which is why amorphous selenium is used today in flat-panel detectors for digital mammography, converting X-ray energy directly into electrical signals for sharp medical images. The same element also flavors everyday life through its compounds in dandruff shampoos, where selenium sulfide slows the skin cells of the scalp. From the moon-named lab residue of 1817 to modern hospitals, selenium quietly bridges chemistry, biology, and technology.

Br.title: Named for its stench
Br.text: Bromine's name comes from the Greek word brômos, meaning stench. The pure element is a dense, dark reddish-brown liquid whose vapors have a sharp, choking, chlorine-like smell, which is exactly the property that inspired chemists to name it.

Br.title: A teenager's discovery
Br.text: Bromine was isolated in 1825-1826 by the young French chemist Antoine-Jérôme Balard, who was only in his early twenties at the time, while studying salty marsh water near Montpellier. The German chemist Carl Löwig independently prepared it around the same time, but Balard published first and is usually credited with the discovery.

Br.title: One of only two liquid elements
Br.text: At room temperature and standard pressure, bromine is one of only two elements that exist as a liquid; the other is the metal mercury. Bromine melts at about -7 degrees Celsius and boils at roughly 59 degrees Celsius, so it is liquid across normal indoor temperatures.

Br.title: It lives in the sea
Br.text: Bromine occurs in nature mainly as bromide ions dissolved in seawater, salt lakes, and underground brines rather than as the free element. The Dead Sea is exceptionally rich in it, and Israel, Jordan, the United States, and China are among the leading producers extracting bromine from such brines.

Br.title: The royal purple dye
Br.text: Long before bromine was identified as an element, its compounds colored the ancient world. Tyrian purple, the fabulously expensive dye worn by Roman emperors, is an organobromine compound (6,6'-dibromoindigo) produced by Murex sea snails, making bromine chemistry literally a mark of royalty.

Br.title: Flame retardant workhorse
Br.text: For decades, brominated compounds were among the most widely used flame retardants, added to plastics, electronics casings, and textiles to slow ignition. When heated, they release bromine radicals that interrupt the chemical chain reactions of combustion, although concerns about persistence and toxicity have since phased out several of these compounds.

Br.title: Once in every gas tank
Br.text: In the era of leaded gasoline, 1,2-dibromoethane was added as a 'lead scavenger' to keep engines clean by carrying lead away as volatile lead bromide. This was once a huge industrial use of bromine, but it largely vanished as leaded fuel was banned worldwide for health and environmental reasons.

Br.title: A guardian of the ozone layer's foe
Br.text: Atom for atom, bromine is far more destructive to stratospheric ozone than chlorine, by a factor often estimated near 45 to 60 times. Because of this, ozone-depleting bromine compounds such as halons (once used in fire extinguishers) and methyl bromide (a soil fumigant) have been heavily restricted under the Montreal Protocol.

Br.title: Maybe essential for life
Br.text: In 2014 researchers reported that bromine appears to be a genuinely essential trace element for animals, the 28th element known to be required. It plays a role in assembling collagen IV, a protein scaffold needed to build basement membranes, the thin tissue layers that support cells, suggesting bromide is not just an inert passenger in our bodies.

Br.title: The element that exposed photos
Br.text: Silver bromide was the light-sensitive heart of traditional photographic film and paper for over a century. When struck by light, tiny crystals of silver bromide form clusters of metallic silver that can be chemically developed into an image, a process that powered photography from the 1800s until the rise of digital cameras.

Kr.title: Hidden in the Air
Kr.text: Krypton was discovered in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers in London while studying the residue left after evaporating nearly all of a sample of liquid air. They named it from the Greek word 'kryptos', meaning 'hidden', because it had stayed concealed in the atmosphere. In the same remarkable few weeks the pair also isolated neon and xenon from the same air residues.

Kr.title: A Rare Breath of Air
Kr.text: Despite being all around us, krypton makes up only about 1.1 parts per million of Earth's atmosphere by volume, roughly one atom in every 900,000. The only practical way to obtain it is by fractional distillation of liquefied air, which is why it remains relatively expensive. The entire atmosphere holds krypton, yet you would inhale only trace amounts with every breath.

Kr.title: It Once Defined the Meter
Kr.text: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was officially defined using krypton-86: exactly 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red light it emits in an electric discharge. This replaced an aging platinum-iridium metal bar as the world standard for length. Krypton lost the honor only when the meter was redefined in terms of the speed of light.

Kr.title: Noble, But Not Inert
Kr.text: For decades chemists believed the noble gases formed no compounds at all, but krypton proved them slightly wrong. Krypton difluoride (KrF2) can be made by exposing a mixture of krypton and fluorine to electrical discharge or ultraviolet light at very low temperatures. It is a powerful oxidizing and fluorinating agent, so reactive that it slowly attacks the containers it is stored in.

Kr.title: Light for Airport Runways
Kr.text: Krypton gas glows a bright whitish color when electricity passes through it, making it useful in high-intensity lighting. It is used in some airport runway approach lights and in high-speed photographic flash lamps because it can produce brief, brilliant bursts of light. Mixing krypton with argon also improves the efficiency and lifespan of certain fluorescent and incandescent lamps.

Kr.title: The Window Gas
Kr.text: Krypton's low thermal conductivity makes it an excellent insulator, so it is pumped into the space between panes of high-performance double- and triple-glazed windows. The dense, sluggish gas slows the flow of heat far better than ordinary air, helping buildings stay warm in winter and cool in summer. Krypton-filled windows are thinner than argon-filled ones for the same insulating effect, saving space and weight.

Kr.title: A Powerful Eye Surgery Laser
Kr.text: The krypton fluoride excimer laser produces deep ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 248 nanometers. This precise, cool-cutting beam is used in laser eye surgery and in photolithography, the process that etches microscopic circuit patterns onto computer chips. The same excimer technology has been explored for driving experimental nuclear fusion research.

Kr.title: A Fingerprint of Nuclear Activity
Kr.text: Krypton-85 is a radioactive isotope produced by nuclear fission, and it leaks into the atmosphere from nuclear reactors and fuel-reprocessing plants. Because it is chemically unreactive and easy to detect, scientists monitor atmospheric krypton-85 to help estimate global nuclear activity. Its presence is also used by hydrologists to date underground water that fell as rain within roughly the last 50 years.

Kr.title: Forged in Exploding Stars
Kr.text: Krypton is created in the cosmos through nucleosynthesis inside stars, including the slow neutron-capture process in aging giant stars and the explosive conditions of supernovae. These stellar furnaces build heavier elements that are later scattered into space and recycled into new stars and planets. The krypton in Earth's air is therefore a genuine sample of ancient stellar chemistry.

Kr.title: Harmless to Breathe, But Beware
Kr.text: Krypton is chemically non-toxic and plays no role in human biology, passing through the body without taking part in any reactions. However, because it is denser than air and inert, a high concentration can displace oxygen and cause suffocation, a real hazard in poorly ventilated spaces. Under high pressure krypton also becomes mildly narcotic, an effect related to the dangers of nitrogen narcosis faced by deep-sea divers.

Rb.title: Born From a Rainbow
Rb.text: Rubidium was discovered in 1861 by German scientists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff, the pioneers of flame spectroscopy. They spotted two brilliant deep-red spectral lines in mineral water from Bad Dürkheim that matched no known element. The name comes from the Latin 'rubidus', meaning 'deepest red', after those signature lines.

Rb.title: Melts in Your Hand (Almost)
Rb.text: Rubidium is so soft and low-melting that it would turn liquid at about 39.3 degrees Celsius (102.7 F), just a few degrees above body temperature. It is a silvery metal soft enough to cut with a knife. Because of this, it is one of only a handful of metals that can be molten on a warm summer day.

Rb.title: Violently Allergic to Water
Rb.text: As an alkali metal, rubidium reacts explosively with water, producing hydrogen gas and enough heat to ignite it instantly. It also bursts into flame on contact with air, so it must be stored under dry mineral oil or in sealed glass ampoules under inert gas. This extreme reactivity is why pure rubidium is never found free in nature.

Rb.title: Hiding in Plain Sight
Rb.text: Rubidium is actually the 23rd most abundant element in Earth's crust, more common than copper or zinc. Yet it has no ores of its own and is always scattered as a minor companion inside potassium minerals like lepidolite, pollucite, and carnallite. Most commercial rubidium is recovered as a byproduct of refining lithium and cesium.

Rb.title: A Built-In Atomic Clock
Rb.text: About 28 percent of natural rubidium is the radioactive isotope rubidium-87, which decays into strontium-87 with a half-life of roughly 49 billion years, far longer than the age of the universe. Geologists exploit this rubidium-strontium decay to date rocks and meteorites that are billions of years old. The same isotope made rubidium a key tool in measuring the age of the Solar System.

Rb.title: Heart of the Atomic Clock
Rb.text: Rubidium is the working element in compact, affordable atomic clocks used to keep time with extraordinary precision. Rubidium clocks ride aboard GPS satellites and anchor cellular networks, drifting by only a fraction of a second over thousands of years. Their small size and low cost make them the workhorse atomic clock of modern telecommunications.

Rb.title: The Coldest Stuff Ever Made
Rb.text: In 1995, physicists Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman used a cloud of about 2,000 rubidium-87 atoms to create the first Bose-Einstein condensate, a bizarre state of matter predicted by Einstein 70 years earlier. They cooled the atoms to within billionths of a degree of absolute zero, the coldest temperatures ever achieved. This breakthrough earned a share of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Rb.title: Cousin to Potassium
Rb.text: Because rubidium ions behave chemically much like potassium, your body actually absorbs small amounts of it from food, and an average adult carries roughly half a gram of it. It is not a required nutrient and has no known biological function, but the body treats it as a harmless potassium stand-in. Concentrations are highest in muscle tissue.

Rb.title: Tracing the Beating Heart
Rb.text: Doctors use radioactive rubidium-82 as a tracer in PET scans to image blood flow through the heart muscle. Injected into a vein, it follows the same paths as potassium and lights up healthy versus damaged heart tissue. With a half-life of just 75 seconds, it delivers its picture and then vanishes almost immediately, keeping radiation exposure very low.

Rb.title: Painting the Flame Purple
Rb.text: When rubidium compounds are heated in a flame, they glow a striking reddish-violet, a direct visual echo of the red spectral lines that revealed the element. This property is sometimes used in specialty fireworks and signal flares to produce purple hues. The same effect lets chemists identify rubidium with a simple flame test.

Sr.title: Named After a Scottish Village
Sr.text: Strontium is the only element named after a place in the United Kingdom: the village of Strontian (Sròn an t-Sìthein) in the Scottish Highlands. The mineral strontianite was first noticed in lead mines there in the 1790s. The pure metal was finally isolated in 1808 by Humphry Davy using electrolysis, the same technique he used to win several other elements that year.

Sr.title: The Color of Red Fireworks
Sr.text: Strontium salts such as strontium nitrate and strontium carbonate are the classic source of brilliant crimson-red in fireworks, flares, and emergency road signals. When heated, strontium atoms emit light strongly at wavelengths around 650-680 nanometers, producing one of the purest reds available to pyrotechnicians. This same red flame test is a quick laboratory way to confirm the presence of strontium.

Sr.title: Twin of Calcium
Sr.text: Strontium sits directly below calcium in Group 2 of the periodic table, so it behaves chemically very much like it. Because of this similarity, the body treats strontium like calcium and deposits roughly 99% of any absorbed strontium into bones and teeth. This biological mimicry is the key to both its medical uses and its dangers.

Sr.title: The Fallout Isotope
Sr.text: Strontium-90 is a radioactive isotope produced in nuclear fission, and it became infamous during 1950s atmospheric bomb testing. Because it mimics calcium, it lodges in growing bones, where its half-life of about 28.8 years means it can irradiate tissue for decades. Detecting Sr-90 in children's baby teeth helped build public pressure that led to the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.

Sr.title: A Battery for Spacecraft
Sr.text: That same strontium-90 is actually useful as a power source, because its radioactive decay releases a steady stream of heat. Radioisotope thermoelectric generators fueled by Sr-90 once powered remote lighthouses, weather stations, and navigation beacons in the former Soviet Union. The heat is converted directly into electricity with no moving parts, allowing decades of unattended operation.

Sr.title: Fighting Bone Cancer Pain
Sr.text: The radioactive isotope strontium-89, sold as a chloride solution, is injected to ease the severe pain of cancer that has spread to the bones. Because strontium concentrates in bone, the isotope's beta radiation targets the tumor sites directly while sparing much of the body. It offers relief to patients whose pain no longer responds well to standard medication.

Sr.title: Stronger Teeth and Bones
Sr.text: In a non-radioactive form, strontium ranelate was prescribed in Europe to treat osteoporosis, because it both slows bone breakdown and modestly encourages new bone formation. Strontium chloride is also the active ingredient in some toothpastes marketed for sensitive teeth, where it helps block exposed nerve channels in dentine. These uses again exploit strontium's natural affinity for hard tissues.

Sr.title: It Glows Through Old TVs
Sr.text: For much of the 20th century, one of the largest industrial uses of strontium was in the glass faceplates of cathode-ray-tube televisions and monitors. Strontium oxide added to the glass absorbed harmful X-rays generated by the electron beam, protecting viewers. As flat-screen displays replaced bulky CRTs, this once-dominant market for strontium largely disappeared.

Sr.title: Forged in Dying Stars
Sr.text: Strontium is created in the cosmos mainly inside aging stars through slow neutron capture, the so-called s-process. In 2019, astronomers detected newly made strontium in the glowing debris of a neutron-star collision observed in 2017, the first clear identification of a specific heavy element from such a merger. This confirmed that violent stellar smashups help seed the universe with elements like strontium.

Sr.title: A Clock Accurate to the Cosmos
Sr.text: Atoms of strontium are at the heart of some of the most precise clocks ever built. Optical lattice clocks trap strontium atoms in a grid of laser light and measure an electron transition that ticks hundreds of trillions of times per second. The best strontium clocks are so stable they would neither gain nor lose a single second over many billions of years, longer than the current age of the universe.

Y.title: Born from a Swedish village
Y.text: Yttrium owes its name to Ytterby, a tiny quarry village near Stockholm, Sweden. In 1787 the chemist Carl Axel Arrhenius found a heavy black mineral there that he called ytterbite, later renamed gadolinite. From this single rock, Johan Gadolin isolated a new "earth" in 1794 — the first identification of yttrium's oxide.

Y.title: One village, four elements
Y.text: Ytterby is the most element-honored place on Earth, lending its name to four elements: yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium. Three more elements found in the same ore — scandium, holmium, and thulium — were named for Scandinavia and nearby regions. No other location has inspired so many entries on the periodic table.

Y.title: A metal that resists fire
Y.text: Yttrium metal forms a protective oxide film that makes it surprisingly stable in air, even though finely divided shavings can ignite above about 400 degrees Celsius. Bulk yttrium melts at 1526 degrees Celsius and stays solid in air far better than most reactive metals. This durability is why small amounts are added to alloys to improve their resistance to oxidation at high temperature.

Y.title: The red glow in old TVs
Y.text: For decades, yttrium compounds produced the vivid red phosphors in color television tubes and computer monitors. Yttrium oxysulfide and yttrium oxide doped with europium emit a pure, bright red when struck by electrons or ultraviolet light.
