Ir.text: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter found a worldwide layer of clay, dated to 66 million years ago, that was unusually rich in iridium. Because iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, they argued a giant impact caused the mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs. The crater was later found at Chicxulub in Mexico, supporting their bold idea.

Ir.title: Rarer Than Gold In The Crust
Ir.text: Iridium is one of the least abundant elements in Earth's crust, present at only about 0.001 parts per million. Most of the planet's iridium sank into the molten iron core during Earth's formation because it bonds readily with iron. The iridium we mine today is recovered mainly as a byproduct of nickel and platinum refining in South Africa and Russia.

Ir.title: Guardian Of The Old Kilogram
Ir.text: From 1889 to 2019, the world's standard kilogram was a cylinder made of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, kept in a vault near Paris. Iridium was added for hardness and stability so the mass would barely change over a century. The standard meter bar of the same era used the identical platinum-iridium alloy.

Ir.title: Tipping Fountain Pens And Spark Plugs
Ir.text: Because it is so hard and wear-resistant, iridium has long been used to tip premium fountain pen nibs so they glide for decades without wearing down. The same toughness makes iridium ideal for the firing tips of high-performance spark plugs in cars. Its sky-high melting point of around 2,446 degrees Celsius lets it survive intense heat without deforming.

Ir.title: A Catalyst For Modern Drugs
Ir.text: Iridium complexes are powerful catalysts in the chemical industry, famously used in the Cativa process to make acetic acid efficiently from methanol. Chemists also prize iridium catalysts for adding hydrogen to molecules with precise control, helping build pharmaceuticals. These reactions often need only tiny amounts of the metal to transform huge quantities of material.

Ir.title: Light For Screens And Medicine
Ir.text: Iridium sits at the heart of many efficient OLED display materials, where iridium-based compounds emit bright, saturated light in phones and televisions. In hospitals, the radioactive isotope iridium-192 is a key source for brachytherapy, delivering targeted radiation to treat cancers from inside the body. The same isotope is widely used in industry to X-ray welds and pipelines for hidden flaws.

Pt.title: Frustrating the conquistadors
Pt.text: When 16th-century Spanish colonists panned for gold in the rivers of the Choco region of Colombia, they kept finding a stubborn white metal mixed in with their nuggets. They dismissively named it 'platina', meaning 'little silver', and some even threw it back into the water believing it was an unripe form of gold. It would be centuries before this 'nuisance' metal was recognized as one of the most valuable elements on Earth.

Pt.title: Heavier than it looks
Pt.text: Platinum is extraordinarily dense, packing about 21.45 grams into every cubic centimeter. A cube of platinum just 30 centimeters on a side would weigh roughly 580 kilograms, more than a grand piano. This density is why a small platinum ring feels noticeably heavier in the hand than a gold one of the same size.

Pt.title: The metal that refuses to rust
Pt.text: Platinum is one of the least reactive metals known, resisting attack from oxygen, water, and most acids even when heated. It will not dissolve in either nitric or hydrochloric acid alone, but only in a freshly mixed 3-to-1 blend of the two called aqua regia ('royal water'). This near-total corrosion resistance is why platinum survives buried in riverbeds for millions of years looking as bright as the day it formed.

Pt.title: The clean-air catalyst
Pt.text: The single largest use of platinum is inside the catalytic converters of cars, where a thin coating of the metal speeds up reactions that turn toxic exhaust gases into harmless ones. Platinum helps convert carbon monoxide and unburned fuel into carbon dioxide and water without being consumed itself, the hallmark of a true catalyst. A modern converter contains only a few grams of platinum-group metals, yet it cleans the exhaust of a vehicle for its entire life.

Pt.title: Once the world's master ruler
Pt.text: From 1889 to 2019, the kilogram itself was defined by a single cylinder made of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, kept under three glass bell jars near Paris. Platinum was chosen because it is dense, stable, and almost immune to corrosion, so the artifact would not gain or lose mass over time. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined using the Planck constant, finally retiring this gleaming metal standard.

Pt.title: A weapon against cancer
Pt.text: Platinum sits at the heart of some of the most important chemotherapy drugs ever made, including cisplatin, discovered to fight tumors by physicist Barnett Rosenberg in the 1960s. These drugs work by binding to the DNA inside cancer cells, kinking the double helix so the cells can no longer divide and multiply. Cisplatin and its relatives are still used today to treat testicular, ovarian, bladder, and other cancers, saving countless lives.

Pt.title: Born in cosmic cataclysms
Pt.text: Platinum is not made in ordinary stars; the leading explanation is that heavy elements like it are forged when neutron stars collide or in rare violent supernovae. In 2017 astronomers watched two neutron stars merge and detected the chemical signatures of newly created heavy metals in the debris. The platinum in a piece of jewelry was likely created in such a catastrophe billions of years before our Sun was born.

Pt.title: Rarer than gold
Pt.text: Platinum is far scarcer in the Earth's crust than gold, and roughly three-quarters of the world's supply comes from a single geological formation, the Bushveld Igneous Complex in South Africa. Extracting it is brutally inefficient: producing a single ounce of pure platinum requires mining and processing several tons of ore. This scarcity, combined with deep mining and intensive refining, is a major reason the metal commands such high prices.

Pt.title: It drinks hydrogen gas
Pt.text: Finely divided platinum, known as platinum black or platinum sponge, can absorb enormous volumes of hydrogen gas relative to its own size and hold it loosely on its surface. This property makes platinum a superb catalyst for reactions involving hydrogen and a key electrode material in hydrogen fuel cells. By splitting hydrogen and oxygen reactions, platinum helps fuel cells generate electricity with water as the only byproduct.

Pt.title: Hypoallergenic and eternal
Pt.text: Because platinum is so chemically inert, it almost never triggers the skin allergies that nickel-containing alloys can cause, making it a favorite for piercings and fine jewelry. It is also remarkably ductile and strong, so jewelers can hold gemstones securely with thin, durable prongs that resist wear for generations. A gram of platinum can be drawn into a wire over two kilometers long without breaking.

Au.title: A Name From the Dawn
Au.text: The symbol Au comes from the Latin word 'aurum', meaning 'shining dawn' or 'glow of sunrise'. Gold is one of the very few metals known to humanity since prehistoric times, with worked gold artifacts from the Varna necropolis in Bulgaria dating back about 6,500 years. Because it was never 'discovered' by a single person, no individual is credited with finding it.

Au.title: Born in Cosmic Collisions
Au.text: Most of the gold in the universe was forged not in ordinary stars but in violent events like neutron-star mergers and certain supernovae, where extreme neutron flux builds heavy nuclei. Astronomers confirmed this in 2017 when the GW170817 neutron-star collision, detected by LIGO, produced a glowing 'kilonova' rich in heavy elements. The gold in your jewelry literally predates the Earth and arrived in the cloud of dust that formed our planet.

Au.title: Almost Impossibly Unreactive
Au.text: Gold is famously a 'noble' metal: it does not rust, tarnish, or react with oxygen or most acids, which is why ancient gold coins emerge from shipwrecks still gleaming. It dissolves only in special mixtures such as aqua regia, a 3:1 blend of hydrochloric and nitric acid named 'royal water' because it could dissolve the king of metals. This chemical stability is the main reason gold has held value across thousands of years.

Au.title: Hammered Thinner Than Light
Au.text: Gold is the most malleable of all metals: a single gram can be beaten into a sheet covering about one square meter. Gold leaf can be made so thin, around 100 nanometers, that it becomes partly transparent and transmits a greenish-blue light. A single ounce of gold can be drawn into a wire roughly 80 kilometers long without breaking.

Au.title: Why Gold Looks Golden
Au.text: Almost all pure metals are silvery, but gold has a warm yellow color because of Einstein's relativity. Its electrons move so fast around the heavy nucleus that relativistic effects shift the light it absorbs into the blue range, so the reflected light appears golden. The same relativistic physics helps explain why neighboring mercury is a liquid at room temperature.

Au.title: Medicine Made of Metal
Au.text: Gold compounds called chrysotherapy, such as auranofin and sodium aurothiomalate, were used for decades to treat rheumatoid arthritis by calming inflammation. Today, tiny gold nanoparticles are being developed to carry cancer drugs and to heat and destroy tumors when struck by infrared light. Radioactive gold-198 has even been used directly in some cancer treatments.

Au.title: The Metal Inside Your Phone
Au.text: Gold is an outstanding electrical conductor that never corrodes, so it is plated onto connectors, circuit boards, and SIM cards in nearly every smartphone and computer. Roughly 7 to 50 milligrams of gold sit inside a typical mobile phone, which is why 'urban mining' of electronic waste can be richer than digging real ore. A tonne of discarded phones can yield more gold than a tonne of mined rock.

Au.title: Dissolved Across the Oceans
Au.text: Earth's seawater contains an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 tonnes of dissolved gold, but it is spread so thinly, only parts per trillion, that no one has found a profitable way to extract it. In the 1920s the German chemist Fritz Haber, a Nobel laureate, spent years trying to harvest sea gold to pay World War I reparations, and ultimately failed. The vast majority of usable gold instead sits locked in rock deep underground.

Au.title: Edible and Officially Safe
Au.text: Because gold is so unreactive, pure gold leaf is biologically inert and approved as a food additive in Europe under the code E175. It passes through the body without being absorbed, so the flakes on luxury desserts and the gold in some liqueurs add sparkle but no flavor or nutrition. It has no known biological role in humans, which is exactly why it can be eaten safely.

Au.title: Guarding Spacecraft and Astronauts
Au.text: Gold reflects infrared radiation extremely well, so a thin gold coating shields satellites and astronauts' helmet visors from intense solar heat and glare. The visors on Apollo lunar helmets and the sunshield on the James Webb Space Telescope both rely on gold films just micrometers thick. The same reflective property makes gold valuable for protecting sensitive electronics in the harsh environment of space.

Hg.title: The Only Liquid Metal
Hg.text: Mercury is the only metallic element that is liquid at ordinary room temperature, staying fluid from its freezing point of -38.83 degrees Celsius all the way up to 356.73 degrees Celsius. This happens because mercury's outer electrons are held so tightly by relativistic effects that the atoms barely share them, leaving the metallic bonds unusually weak. Only the nonmetal bromine joins it as a liquid element under normal conditions.

Hg.title: Named for a Planet and a God
Hg.text: Mercury's chemical symbol Hg comes from the Latin word hydrargyrum, meaning water-silver, a translation of the Greek term for the shiny, flowing metal. Its English name honors the Roman messenger god Mercury, famed for his speed, just as the planet Mercury was named for racing quickly around the Sun. The element has been known since at least 1500 BCE and was found in Egyptian tombs.

Hg.title: Relativity You Can Pour
Hg.text: The reason mercury is a liquid is a striking everyday example of Einstein's relativity. Electrons in mercury's inner shells move at a large fraction of the speed of light, gaining effective mass and pulling the 6s electrons close to the nucleus. These contracted electrons resist bonding with neighboring atoms, so mercury cannot lock into a solid lattice at room temperature the way other metals do.

Hg.title: It Climbed Into Thermometers
Hg.text: Because mercury expands very evenly as it warms and does not stick to glass, Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit used it to build the first reliable mercury thermometer in 1714. The same uniform expansion made mercury the heart of barometers, blood-pressure cuffs, and thermostats for centuries. Many of these instruments are now being phased out worldwide to reduce toxic mercury pollution.

Hg.title: A Poison That Maddened Hatters
Hg.text: Mercury is a potent neurotoxin, and chronic exposure to mercury compounds in 19th-century felt-hat making caused tremors, slurred speech, and personality changes, the origin of the phrase mad as a hatter. The element accumulates in the brain and kidneys and can cross the placenta. In 1956, an industrial dump of methylmercury into Japan's Minamata Bay poisoned thousands and gave its name to Minamata disease.

Hg.title: Cinnabar, Its Fiery Ore
Hg.text: Mercury rarely appears as a free metal in nature; most of it is locked in a brilliant red ore called cinnabar, which is mercury sulfide. Roasting cinnabar in air releases mercury vapor that is then condensed back into liquid metal. Ground cinnabar was prized as the pigment vermilion and colored everything from ancient Roman frescoes to Chinese lacquerware.

Hg.title: Gold's Liquid Magnet
Hg.text: Mercury readily dissolves many metals, including gold and silver, forming soft alloys called amalgams. Gold miners have long exploited this by mixing mercury with crushed ore to capture tiny gold flecks, then boiling the mercury away. Dentists used silver-mercury amalgam fillings for over 150 years because the paste is soft enough to shape yet hardens into a durable, long-lasting solid.

Hg.title: Glowing in Every Streetlight
Hg.text: When an electric current passes through mercury vapor, it emits ultraviolet and blue-green light, the principle behind fluorescent tubes and the old bluish mercury-vapor street lamps. In fluorescent bulbs the UV strikes a phosphor coating that re-emits visible light, making them far more efficient than incandescent bulbs. This is why even modern compact fluorescent lamps contain a few milligrams of mercury.

Hg.title: Heavier Than Iron Cannonballs
Hg.text: Mercury is astonishingly dense at about 13.5 grams per cubic centimeter, roughly 13.5 times denser than water and heavier than lead by volume's feel. An iron cannonball or a lump of lead will actually float on a pool of liquid mercury rather than sink. This great density is what let a short column of mercury in a barometer balance the entire weight of the atmosphere.

Hg.title: A Frozen World Shares Its Name
Hg.text: The planet Mercury, the solar system's smallest and innermost planet, was named for the same swift god, but it is not made of the metal. Curiously, NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft confirmed in 2012 that the planet hides large deposits of frozen water ice in permanently shadowed craters near its poles, despite daytime temperatures exceeding 400 degrees Celsius. The metal mercury, meanwhile, is forged in stars and scattered by supernova explosions.

Tl.title: Born From a Green Flame
Tl.text: Thallium was discovered in 1861 by the British chemist William Crookes, who spotted a brilliant, unexpected green line while examining residues from a sulfuric acid plant with a spectroscope. He named the element after the Greek word 'thallos', meaning a green shoot or twig, in honor of that vivid emerald spectral line. It was one of the first elements ever identified by spectroscopy rather than by classical chemical separation.

Tl.title: A Discovery Claimed Twice
Tl.text: Although Crookes detected thallium's spectral signature first, it was the French chemist Claude-Auguste Lamy who, in 1862, isolated a sizeable metallic ingot and characterized its properties. The two men disputed credit for years, and Lamy even exhibited his thallium metal at the 1862 London International Exhibition. Today both are usually credited, with Crookes recognized for the discovery and Lamy for the isolation.

Tl.title: Soft Enough to Cut
Tl.text: Pure thallium is a bluish-grey, remarkably soft metal that can be cut with a knife and marks paper much like lead. Freshly exposed surfaces are shiny but quickly tarnish to a dull grey oxide layer in moist air. With a melting point of about 304 degrees Celsius and a density around 11.85 grams per cubic centimeter, it is both heavy and easily worked.

Tl.title: The Poisoner's Poison
Tl.text: Thallium salts are colorless, odorless, tasteless, and highly toxic, earning the element a grim reputation in the history of crime. Thallium sulfate was once widely sold as a rat poison and ant killer until many countries banned it for household use in the mid-20th century because of accidental deaths. A lethal dose for an adult can be roughly one gram, and poisoning famously causes dramatic hair loss alongside nerve damage.

Tl.title: A Detective's Lifesaver
Tl.text: In 1977 the writer Agatha Christie's novel 'The Pale Horse' helped save a real life: a nurse recognized the symptoms of thallium poisoning she had read about in the book in a sick infant in London. Doctors confirmed the diagnosis and treated the child, who recovered. Thallium poisoning is now treated with Prussian blue, a pigment that binds the metal in the gut so it can be excreted.

Tl.title: Two Faces, One Element
Tl.text: Thallium shows an unusual chemistry because it forms stable compounds in two oxidation states: +1 (thallous) and +3 (thallic). The +1 state is exceptionally stable thanks to the 'inert pair effect', where its two outer 6s electrons resist bonding. In the +1 form, thallium chemically mimics potassium and is taken up by the body through the same channels, which is precisely why it is so insidiously toxic.

Tl.title: Imaging the Living Heart
Tl.text: A radioactive isotope, thallium-201, became a cornerstone of nuclear cardiology because the body treats it like potassium and concentrates it in healthy, well-perfused heart muscle. In a thallium stress test, doctors track its gamma emissions to map blood flow and reveal areas damaged by a heart attack or starved by blocked arteries. Thallium-201 has a half-life of about 73 hours, convenient for medical imaging.

Tl.title: Seeing in the Dark
Tl.text: Thallium dramatically extends how far into the infrared we can see. Crystals of thallium bromide-iodide, sold under the trade name KRS-5, transmit long-wavelength infrared light and are used in spectroscopy and thermal optics. Thallium-doped sodium iodide crystals are also workhorse scintillation detectors, flashing with light when struck by gamma rays in everything from medical scanners to airport security.

Tl.title: Hidden in Sulfide Ores
Tl.text: Thallium is not especially rare in the crust, at roughly 0.7 parts per million, but it almost never forms its own ore deposits. Instead it hides as a trace impurity inside the sulfide minerals of copper, lead, zinc, and iron, and it is recovered chiefly as a byproduct of smelting those metals and from flue dusts. Rare thallium minerals such as crookesite and lorandite do exist but are collector's curiosities.

Tl.title: A Superconducting Surprise
Tl.text: Thallium-based copper-oxide ceramics are among the higher-temperature superconductors known, with some thallium-barium-calcium-copper-oxide compounds losing all electrical resistance above 120 kelvin. That is well above the boiling point of cheap liquid nitrogen at 77 kelvin, which makes such materials attractive for research. In a very different role, thallium-mercury alloys stay liquid down to about minus 60 degrees Celsius, useful in extreme-cold thermometers.

Pb.title: A Symbol From Latin
Pb.text: Lead's chemical symbol Pb comes from its Latin name plumbum, the same root that gives us the words plumber and plumbing because the Romans built their water pipes from it. Plumbum itself may trace back to an even older Mediterranean word for the metal. This is one of seven metals known since antiquity, alongside gold, silver, copper, iron, tin and mercury.

Pb.title: Soft Enough To Scratch
Pb.text: Lead is remarkably soft for a metal, with a Mohs hardness of only about 1.5, so you can scratch it with a fingernail and dent it with your thumb. It is also highly malleable and ductile, which let ancient craftsmen hammer it into sheets and pipes by hand. Despite this softness it is dense and heavy, which made it ideal for weights and seals.

Pb.title: Surprisingly Heavy
Pb.text: With a density of about 11.34 grams per cubic centimetre, lead is roughly 1.5 times denser than iron, so a small block feels startlingly heavy in the hand. This is why it has long been used for fishing sinkers, diving weights and the keels of sailboats. Its density also makes it an excellent absorber of X-rays and gamma rays.

Pb.title: The End Of The Decay Line
Pb.text: Lead is the final, stable resting place for three great radioactive decay chains: uranium-238 ends as lead-206, uranium-235 ends as lead-207, and thorium-232 ends as lead-208. Because of this, measuring the ratio of these lead isotopes in rocks is a cornerstone of uranium-lead dating, used to determine the age of the Earth. Lead-208 is also the heaviest completely stable atomic nucleus known.

Pb.title: Shielding Against Radiation
Pb.text: Its high density and many electrons make lead one of the best everyday materials for blocking ionizing radiation. That is why the heavy aprons worn during dental and medical X-rays contain lead, and why radioactive sources are stored in lead-lined containers called pigs. The same property protects technicians in nuclear facilities and hospitals.

Pb.title: A Quiet Poison
Pb.text: Lead has no known biological role and is toxic to humans, especially children, because it mimics calcium and disrupts the nervous system and the production of haemoglobin. Concern over this toxicity led many countries to phase out leaded gasoline, with the United States completing its road-fuel ban in 1996 and the very last nation, Algeria, ending sales in 2021. Old lead-based paint and plumbing remain important sources of exposure today.

Pb.title: Sweet But Dangerous
Pb.text: Lead compounds such as lead(II) acetate have a sweet taste, which earned the compound the historical nickname sugar of lead. The Romans boiled grape juice in lead pots to make a sweet syrup called sapa or defrutum used to preserve and sweeten wine. Historians debate how much this contributed to chronic lead poisoning among the Roman elite, but it shows how the metal's chemistry was exploited long before its dangers were understood.

Pb.title: Powering Your Car
Pb.text: The lead-acid battery, invented by French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859, was the first rechargeable battery and still starts the engine of almost every petrol and diesel car on the road. It uses lead and lead dioxide plates in sulfuric acid, and despite being old technology it is prized for delivering a large burst of current cheaply. Lead-acid batteries are also among the most recycled products in the world, with recovery rates above 95 percent in many countries.

Pb.title: It Glides Under Pressure
Pb.text: Lead exhibits creep, meaning it slowly flows and deforms under its own weight over years even at room temperature, which is why old lead roofing and church organ pipes can sag noticeably. It also becomes a superconductor when cooled below about 7.2 kelvin, conducting electricity with zero resistance. These two extremes show how differently the same metal behaves depending on temperature and time.

Pb.title: Forged In Dying Stars
Pb.text: Most of the lead in the universe was created inside stars through the slow neutron-capture process, the s-process, in aging red giant stars, with additional amounts made in explosive events. Because so many radioactive isotopes ultimately decay into it, lead is more abundant in the cosmos than its high atomic number of 82 would otherwise suggest. On Earth it is mined mainly as the mineral galena, which is lead sulfide and often glitters with a metallic shine.

Bi.title: The Last Stable Myth
Bi.text: For two centuries bismuth-209 was considered the heaviest stable isotope in nature. In 2003 French physicists at the Institut d'Astrophysique Spatiale in Orsay measured it actually undergoing alpha decay with a half-life of about 20 billion billion years (2.01 x 10^19 years). That is more than a billion times the current age of the universe, so a chunk of bismuth is, for any practical purpose, eternal.

Bi.title: A White Metal With a Misleading Name
Bi.text: The name likely comes from the German Weisse Masse or Wismut, meaning white mass, later Latinized to bisemutum. Although early miners often confused it with lead and tin, Claude Geoffroy the Younger demonstrated in 1753 that bismuth is a distinct element. It remains one of the few elements known since antiquity yet only formally identified in the modern chemical era.

Bi.title: It Expands When It Freezes
Bi.text: Like water, gallium, and antimony, bismuth is one of the rare substances that expands as it solidifies, growing about 3.3 percent in volume. This makes solid bismuth less dense than its own liquid, so a chunk will float on the molten metal. The property historically made it valuable in type-metal alloys, because the expansion forced the metal sharply into every detail of a printing mould.

Bi.title: The Most Diamagnetic Metal
Bi.text: Bismuth is the most strongly diamagnetic of all metals, meaning it is repelled by magnetic fields rather than attracted. A small bismuth slab can help levitate a tiny magnet by passively pushing back against it. This same electronic structure also gives bismuth an unusually large Hall effect and very low thermal conductivity for a metal.

Bi.title: Rainbow Crystals From the Lab
Bi.text: When molten bismuth cools slowly it forms striking hopper crystals: stair-stepped, geometric structures with a brilliant oil-slick iridescence. The colors are not the metal itself but a thin oxide layer that forms on the surface and creates thin-film interference, splitting white light into pinks, blues, golds, and purples. These crystals are a favorite of chemistry demonstrations and mineral collectors precisely because they are easy to grow at home.

Bi.title: The Pink Stuff in Your Medicine Cabinet
Bi.text: Bismuth subsalicylate is the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol and similar stomach remedies. It coats the digestive lining, has a mild antibacterial action, and is even used as part of combination therapy against Helicobacter pylori, the bacterium behind many stomach ulcers. Bismuth compounds have soothed upset stomachs since the 18th century, making this heavy metal a surprisingly gentle medicine.

Bi.title: A Green Replacement for Lead
Bi.text: Because bismuth sits just next to lead on the periodic table but is far less toxic, industry increasingly uses it as a non-toxic substitute. It appears in lead-free solders, free-machining brasses, fishing sinkers, and even some shotgun pellets. This shift matters for environmental and worker safety, letting manufacturers keep useful density and low melting points without lead's well-known health hazards.

Bi.title: Metal That Melts in Hot Water
Bi.text: Alloyed with lead, tin, cadmium, or indium, bismuth forms fusible alloys with astonishingly low melting points. Field's metal melts at about 62 degrees Celsius and Wood's metal at around 70 degrees, both below the boiling point of water. These alloys are used in fire-sprinkler triggers and electrical fuses, where a small temperature rise melts the metal and sets off a safety response.

Bi.title: Forged in Dying Stars
Bi.text: Bismuth is created in the cosmos mainly through the slow neutron-capture process, the s-process, inside aging red giant stars. Lighter nuclei capture neutrons one at a time over thousands of years, climbing the chart of isotopes until they reach bismuth. Because the next steps lead to unstable, rapidly decaying elements, bismuth marks a natural endpoint of this stellar nucleosynthesis pathway.

Bi.title: Rare and Quietly Useful
Bi.text: Bismuth makes up only about 8.5 parts per billion of Earth's crust, making it roughly as scarce as silver. It is mostly recovered as a byproduct of refining lead, copper, and tin ores rather than mined on its own. Despite its rarity, it finds work in cosmetics as pearlescent bismuth oxychloride, in pigments, and as a catalyst, proving that even an uncommon element can be remarkably versatile.

Po.title: Named for a Homeland
Po.text: Polonium was discovered in 1898 by Marie Curie and her husband Pierre while sifting through tons of uranium ore called pitchblende from Bohemia. Marie named it after Poland, her native country, which at the time did not exist as an independent state but was partitioned among Russia, Prussia, and Austria. It was the very first element she discovered, several months before radium.

Po.title: A Sliver in a Mountain of Ore
Po.text: Polonium is staggeringly rare: uranium ores contain only about 0.1 milligram of polonium per metric tonne of uranium. The Curies had to process several tonnes of pitchblende just to isolate trace amounts, doing the back-breaking chemistry by hand in a leaky shed. Today almost all usable polonium is made artificially in nuclear reactors rather than mined.

Po.title: It Glows and Heats Itself
Po.text: Polonium-210 is so intensely radioactive that a single gram releases about 140 watts of heat, enough to glow with a faint blue light caused by the surrounding air being ionized. A capsule of it stays noticeably warm to the touch entirely on its own. This self-heating once made it a candidate fuel for compact thermoelectric power sources.

Po.title: Powering Spacecraft and Rovers
Po.text: Because polonium-210 produces tremendous heat as it decays, it was used as a radioisotope heater unit to keep equipment from freezing in space. The Soviet Lunokhod 1 and Lunokhod 2 moon rovers in the early 1970s carried polonium heat sources to survive the bitterly cold lunar nights. Its short half-life, however, limits such uses to short missions.

Po.title: The Eight-Alpha Decay Origin
Po.text: Naturally occurring polonium is a fleeting member of the uranium-238 decay chain, formed when uranium slowly transforms through a long series of radioactive steps. Polonium-210 itself is the granddaughter of lead-210 and emerges far down that chain. This means tiny traces of polonium exist anywhere uranium is found, including ordinary soil and rocks.

Po.title: Half-Life of 138 Days
Po.text: Polonium-210, the most common isotope, has a half-life of about 138 days, meaning half of any sample decays away in roughly four and a half months. It emits almost pure alpha particles, with very little penetrating gamma radiation. This makes it relatively harmless outside the body but extremely dangerous if inhaled or swallowed.

Po.title: Hiding in Tobacco Smoke
Po.text: Polonium-210 is a real, measurable component of cigarette smoke, having been absorbed by tobacco plants from soil and phosphate fertilizers. When the leaves are burned and inhaled, the polonium lodges in lung tissue and delivers a tiny but persistent dose of alpha radiation. Researchers consider it one of the contributors to smoking-related lung cancer risk.

Po.title: A Tool Against Static
Po.text: In industry, polonium's flood of alpha particles is harnessed to ionize the air and neutralize static electricity. Anti-static brushes and devices using sealed polonium sources are used to clean dust from camera lenses, photographic film, and sensitive electronics. The same alpha emission that makes it dangerous internally is safely blocked by the device's casing.

Po.title: Igniting the First Bombs
Po.text: During the Manhattan Project, polonium was paired with beryllium to build neutron initiators, the tiny triggers that started the chain reaction in early atomic bombs. When polonium's alpha particles strike beryllium, they knock loose a burst of neutrons at exactly the right instant. This urchin-like initiator sat at the heart of the first nuclear weapons.

Po.title: A Metal That Self-Destructs
Po.text: Solid polonium is a genuine metal with two crystalline forms, and it conducts electricity, yet its own radioactivity is so fierce that it can damage and disrupt its own crystal structure over time. The constant alpha decay generates heat that can melt small samples and slowly degrades any container holding it. Studying it requires sealed apparatus because even handling a visible amount is profoundly hazardous.

At.title: Predicted Before It Was Found
At.text: Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap below iodine in his periodic table and called the missing element 'eka-iodine,' predicting a heavy halogen would eventually fill it. For decades chemists hunted for this element in nature, but every claimed discovery turned out to be a mistake. The real element finally arrived in 1940 by creating it artificially rather than finding it in a mineral.

At.title: Born in a Berkeley Cyclotron
At.text: Astatine was first synthesized in 1940 by Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, and Emilio Segre at the University of California, Berkeley. They bombarded bismuth-209 with alpha particles in a cyclotron, producing astatine-211 through a nuclear reaction. This made it one of the first elements created by humans rather than discovered in rocks or minerals.

At.title: A Name Meaning 'Unstable'
At.text: The element's name comes from the Greek word 'astatos,' meaning unstable, a fitting label for one of the most radioactive elements known. Every single isotope of astatine is radioactive, with none being stable. The name was officially adopted in 1947, capturing the defining feature that no atom of it lasts very long.

At.title: The Rarest Natural Element on Earth
At.text: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element in Earth's crust, with estimates suggesting less than 30 grams exist worldwide at any moment. It forms continuously as a fleeting product in the decay chains of uranium and thorium, only to vanish almost immediately. If you could gather every natural astatine atom on the planet, it would not fill a teaspoon.

At.title: A Few-Hour Lifetime at Best
At.text: The longest-lived isotope, astatine-210, has a half-life of only about 8.1 hours, while the medically useful astatine-211 lasts roughly 7.2 hours. Many other isotopes survive for mere seconds or fractions of a second. This extreme instability means astatine cannot be stockpiled and must be produced fresh and used quickly.

At.title: Nobody Has Ever Seen It
At.text: Astatine is so radioactive that a visible, weighable sample can never be assembled, because its own intense radiation would instantly vaporize any lump through the heat it generates. Scientists study it only in vanishingly tiny, invisible quantities containing far fewer than a billionth of a gram. As a result, no human has ever actually seen pure astatine with their own eyes, and its exact appearance is unknown.

At.title: The Metallic Halogen
At.text: Although astatine sits among the halogens with fluorine, chlorine, and iodine, it behaves in surprisingly metallic ways as the heaviest member of the group. Chemists predict it would look dark or even shiny like a metalloid rather than a colorful gas or solid. Some of its chemistry resembles a metal, showing how elements can shift character as they grow heavier down a column.

At.title: A Cancer-Targeting Bullet
At.text: Astatine-211 is studied for targeted alpha-particle therapy, a promising cancer treatment that attaches the isotope to molecules which seek out tumor cells. When astatine-211 decays it releases alpha particles that travel only a few cell-widths, destroying cancer cells while largely sparing healthy tissue nearby. This short range makes it a precise tool against small tumors and scattered cancer cells.

At.title: Made One Atom at a Time
At.text: Producing astatine-211 for research requires a particle accelerator to bombard bismuth targets with high-energy alpha particles, a process only a handful of facilities worldwide can perform. The yields are so small that scientists often work with quantities measured in billionths of a gram. This scarcity and difficulty of production remain major hurdles to using astatine in widespread medicine.

At.title: Thyroid Cousin of Iodine
At.text: Because astatine is a halogen like iodine, the human thyroid gland tends to absorb it, just as it collects iodine from food. This behavior interests medical researchers, since it could allow astatine-211 to be delivered to the thyroid for treating certain cancers. The same chemical family relationship that defines its place on the periodic table also shapes how it interacts with the body.

Rn.title: Born From Radium's Breath
Rn.text: Radon was discovered in 1899-1900 by Ernest Rutherford and Robert B. Owens, who noticed a radioactive 'emanation' coming off thorium, while Friedrich Ernst Dorn independently observed the same gas escaping from radium. Because it seeped out of radium it was first called 'radium emanation' or 'niton,' and only in 1923 did it receive the official name radon. Its name literally points to its parent: it is the gaseous offspring of decaying radium.

Rn.title: The Heaviest Gas You'll Meet
Rn.text: Radon is the densest noble gas and one of the densest gases known, roughly 7.5 times heavier than air, which is why it tends to pool in basements, mines, and low-lying enclosed spaces. A single liter weighs about 9.7 grams at standard conditions. This heaviness, combined with being colorless and odorless, makes it impossible to detect by human senses alone.

Rn.title: A Noble Gas That Reacts
Rn.text: Although noble gases are famous for being chemically aloof, radon is reactive enough to form compounds, most notably radon difluoride (RnF2), which forms readily when radon meets fluorine. This happens because radon's outer electrons are so far from the nucleus that they are loosely held and easier to coax into bonding. Studying these fragile compounds is extremely hard, since the radon decays away even as chemists try to work with it.

Rn.title: It Literally Glows
Rn.text: In high enough concentrations radon and the air around it can emit a faint luminescence, and when chilled the gas glows yellow, deepening to an orange-red as it approaches its very low temperatures. This glow comes from the intense radiation it emits exciting the surrounding atoms. Early researchers described frozen radon shining like a tiny radioactive lantern.

Rn.title: The Four-Day Half-Life
Rn.text: The most common isotope, radon-222, has a half-life of just 3.82 days, meaning half of any sample vanishes through radioactive decay in under four days. This makes radon a fleeting element: it is constantly being created by decaying radium and constantly disappearing. Because it is so short-lived, there is no stable form of radon anywhere in nature.

Rn.title: Seeping Up From Granite
Rn.text: Radon forms naturally underground as uranium and radium in rocks and soil decay, and it is especially abundant where there is granite, shale, or phosphate-rich bedrock. The gas escapes through cracks and pores and can accumulate inside buildings, particularly in poorly ventilated basements. This is why some regions, such as parts of the Appalachian mountains and Cornwall in England, have notably high indoor radon levels.

Rn.title: A Leading Cause of Lung Cancer
Rn.text: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking, and the leading cause among people who have never smoked, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the World Health Organization. The danger comes not from radon itself but from its solid radioactive decay products, which lodge in the lungs and bombard tissue with radiation. Millions of homes are tested and ventilated each year specifically to keep radon exposure low.

Rn.title: Once Used to Fight Cancer
Rn.text: Before modern radiotherapy, hospitals sealed radon gas into tiny gold capsules called 'radon seeds' and implanted them in tumors to kill cancer cells with radiation. This was a direct extension of radium therapy, using the more convenient gas form. The practice has largely been abandoned in favor of safer, more controllable radiation sources, but it represents a striking early chapter in nuclear medicine.

Rn.title: An Earthquake Early Warning
Rn.text: Scientists monitor radon levels in soil gas, groundwater, and wells because surges in radon are sometimes detected before earthquakes, as shifting rock opens new pathways for the gas to escape. Researchers in countries including Japan and Italy have studied these anomalies as a possible piece of an earthquake prediction puzzle. While not yet a reliable standalone forecast, radon remains a fascinating natural tracer of what is happening deep underground.

Rn.title: A Tracer For Air And Water
Rn.text: Because radon is chemically inert and decays at a precisely known rate, scientists use it as a natural tracer to study how air moves through soil, how water flows underground, and how gases mix in the atmosphere. By measuring radon, geologists can map fault lines and hydrologists can track where groundwater connects to rivers and oceans. Its steady radioactive clock turns an invisible gas into a powerful scientific measuring tool.

Fr.title: Last Natural Element Found
Fr.text: Francium was the last element discovered in nature, identified in 1939 by Marguerite Perey at the Curie Institute in Paris. She spotted it while purifying a sample of actinium and noticed an unexpected radioactive decay product. It was the final element on the periodic table to be found in a natural source rather than created artificially in a lab.

Fr.title: Named For France
Fr.text: Marguerite Perey named the element after her home country, France, giving it the symbol Fr. She originally proposed the name 'catium' for its strongly cation-forming nature, but colleagues worried it sounded too much like 'cat' in English. Perey later became the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences in 1962.

Fr.title: Vanishingly Rare On Earth
Fr.text: Francium is the second-rarest naturally occurring element, after astatine. Scientists estimate that at any given moment the entire Earth's crust contains only about 20 to 30 grams of it, scattered as fleeting atoms inside uranium and thorium minerals. It forms continuously as a decay product but vanishes almost as fast as it appears.

Fr.title: A Fleeting Half-Life
Fr.text: Francium's most stable isotope, francium-223, has a half-life of only about 22 minutes, and every other isotope decays even faster. This extreme instability means no one has ever assembled a visible, weighable lump of the metal. Any sample large enough to see would generate so much heat from its own radioactivity that it would instantly vaporize itself.

Fr.title: The Heaviest Alkali Metal
Fr.text: Francium sits at the bottom of Group 1, making it the heaviest of the alkali metals below lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium. Based on periodic trends, it should be the most reactive of them all and would react violently with water. Because so few atoms have ever existed at once, this dramatic reaction has never actually been observed directly.

Fr.title: Trapped By Lasers
Fr.text: In 1995, physicists at Stony Brook University used magneto-optical traps and laser cooling to hold clouds of about 10,000 francium atoms suspended in a vacuum. This let them study francium's light spectrum without ever needing a solid sample. The glowing trapped atoms were even photographed, producing some of the only real images of francium's behavior.

Fr.title: A Probe For Fundamental Physics
Fr.text: Francium's heavy nucleus and single outer electron make it a prized testing ground for studying the weak nuclear force and parity violation. Researchers at facilities like TRIUMF in Canada produce francium atoms specifically to hunt for tiny deviations from the Standard Model of particle physics. Its simple structure plus large size amplifies subtle effects that are nearly impossible to measure in lighter atoms.

Fr.title: Made To Order In Accelerators
Fr.text: Because natural francium is so scarce, scientists manufacture it by bombarding gold or thorium targets with beams of oxygen or proton ions in particle accelerators. This approach can produce up to roughly a million francium atoms per second for experiments. Even at that rate, the atoms decay continuously, so they must be studied the instant they are created.

Fr.title: No Biological Role
Fr.text: Francium has no known function in any living organism, and because it is both incredibly rare and intensely radioactive, it plays no part in biology or nutrition. Living things never encounter meaningful amounts of it. Any practical danger comes purely from its radioactivity rather than chemical toxicity, but no realistic exposure scenario exists outside a research lab.

Fr.title: Once Mistaken For New Elements
Fr.text: Before Perey's confirmation, francium was the subject of several false claims and placeholder names, including 'eka-caesium,' 'virginium' and 'moldavium.' Dmitri Mendeleev had predicted the missing element decades earlier, foreseeing a heavy alkali metal beneath caesium. It took until 1939 for genuine, reproducible evidence to settle the long search for element 87.

Ra.title: Discovered in radioactive dregs
Ra.text: Radium was discovered in December 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie, working in a leaky shed in Paris with leftover uranium ore called pitchblende from Joachimsthal in Bohemia. They noticed the ore was far more radioactive than its uranium content could explain, which pointed to an unknown element. To prove it existed, Marie processed several tonnes of ore to isolate just a fraction of a gram of radium chloride.

Ra.title: Named for its rays
Ra.text: The Curies named the element from the Latin word 'radius', meaning ray, because of the intense radiation it emits. Marie Curie even coined the word 'radioactivity' itself during this research. The discovery helped earn her two Nobel Prizes: Physics in 1903 (shared) and Chemistry in 1911 for isolating pure radium metal.

Ra.title: It glows in the dark
Ra.text: Radium emits enough energy that it makes nearby materials fluoresce, producing a faint blue-green glow without any external light source. The Curies described keeping glowing tubes of radium salts by their bedside and admiring their luminous beauty. This glow comes from the radiation exciting the surrounding air and any phosphors present, not from the radium giving off visible light directly.

Ra.title: Heavier than its family
Ra.text: Radium is the heaviest of the alkaline-earth metals, sitting at the bottom of Group 2 below barium, with atomic number 88. Like calcium and barium, it has two valence electrons and forms a +2 ion, so chemically it behaves much like its lighter relatives. Pure radium metal is silvery-white but quickly turns black when exposed to air as it reacts with nitrogen.

Ra.title: Every atom is unstable
Ra.text: Radium has no stable isotopes; every form of it is radioactive. The most common isotope, radium-226, has a half-life of about 1,600 years and decays by emitting an alpha particle. It is part of the natural decay chain of uranium-238, which is why radium is found wherever uranium ores occur in the Earth's crust.

Ra.title: The deadly Radium Girls
Ra.text: In the 1910s and 1920s, factory workers in the United States painted glow-in-the-dark watch and instrument dials with radium-based paint, often licking their brushes to a fine point. Many of these 'Radium Girls' developed severe bone damage, anemia, and cancers of the jaw and mouth. Their landmark lawsuits in the late 1920s helped establish modern labor safety rights and occupational health standards.

Ra.title: It mimics calcium in bone
Ra.text: Because radium chemically resembles calcium, the body mistakes it for calcium and deposits it in bones. There it irradiates surrounding tissue and bone marrow, which can cause cancers and blood disorders. This 'bone-seeking' behavior is exactly what made the radium dial painters so vulnerable to harm.

Ra.title: A pioneer of cancer therapy
Ra.text: Before safer alternatives existed, sealed radium needles and tubes were implanted near tumors to destroy cancerous cells with radiation, a technique called brachytherapy. This early form of radiotherapy saved lives and proved that radiation could fight as well as cause disease. Today radium has been almost entirely replaced by isotopes like cobalt-60 and iridium-192 that are easier and safer to handle.

Ra.title: Glowing paint and quack cures
Ra.text: In the early 20th century, radium was marketed in toothpaste, face creams, drinking water, and tonics promising health and vigor before its dangers were understood. The most infamous case was American socialite Eben Byers, who died in 1932 after drinking a radium tonic called Radithor, his jaw and bones destroyed. These tragedies pushed governments to regulate radioactive consumer products.

Ra.title: Still fighting cancer today
Ra.text: A modern medicine called Radium-223 dichloride, sold as Xofigo, was approved by the US FDA in 2013 to treat prostate cancer that has spread to the bones. Its calcium-like chemistry is now an advantage: it travels straight to bone tumors and delivers short-range alpha radiation that kills cancer cells while sparing nearby healthy tissue. This turns radium's old danger into a precisely targeted weapon.

Ac.title: Discovered Twice Over
Ac.text: Actinium was first isolated in 1899 by French chemist André-Louis Debierne, a close colleague of Marie and Pierre Curie, from residues of uranium ore. Just three years later, in 1902, German chemist Friedrich Oskar Giesel independently rediscovered it and proposed the name 'emanium.' The name 'actinium' won out, derived from the Greek word 'aktis,' meaning ray or beam.

Ac.title: It Literally Glows in the Dark
Ac.text: Actinium is so intensely radioactive that it makes the surrounding air glow with an eerie pale-blue light. This happens because its emitted radiation excites nitrogen and oxygen molecules in the air, which then release the absorbed energy as visible light. The effect is similar in cause to the blue glow seen in nuclear reactor pools.

Ac.title: Named the Whole Family
Ac.text: Actinium gives its name to the entire actinide series, the 15 elements running from actinium (Z=89) through lawrencium (Z=103). This group includes famous elements like uranium and plutonium, all of which share similar electron-filling behavior in the 5f subshell. Sitting at the head of the row, actinium is the namesake template for this part of the periodic table.

Ac.title: Vanishingly Rare on Earth
Ac.text: Natural actinium is incredibly scarce, occurring only as a fleeting decay product of uranium and thorium in their ores. A ton of uranium ore contains only about 0.2 milligrams of actinium-227. Because of this extreme rarity, almost all actinium used in research and medicine is produced artificially in reactors or accelerators.

Ac.title: A Promising Cancer Fighter
Ac.text: Actinium-225 is one of the most exciting isotopes in modern targeted alpha-particle cancer therapy. Attached to molecules that home in on tumor cells, it delivers a burst of alpha radiation that destroys cancer over a very short range while sparing nearby healthy tissue. Clinical studies, especially for prostate cancer, have shown striking results, fueling a global effort to produce more of this scarce isotope.

Ac.title: The 21-Year Clock
Ac.text: The most stable and commonly studied isotope, actinium-227, has a half-life of about 21.8 years. Other isotopes are far more fleeting: actinium-225 lasts only about 10 days, while many others decay in minutes or seconds. No isotope of actinium is stable, so every atom of it is steadily transforming into other elements.

Ac.title: Hotter Than You'd Expect
Ac.text: A sample of actinium-227 is warm to the touch because its radioactive decay continuously releases energy as heat. The element is roughly 150 times more radioactive than radium of the same mass, making even tiny quantities require careful shielding and remote handling. This self-heating is a direct, tangible demonstration of nuclear energy at work.

Ac.title: A Silvery, Reactive Metal
Ac.text: In pure form, actinium is a soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes quickly when exposed to air. It reacts with oxygen and moisture, forming a white coating of actinium oxide that actually helps protect the metal underneath from further corrosion. Its melting point is around 1,050 degrees Celsius, and chemically it behaves much like its lighter cousin, lanthanum.

Ac.title: No Job in Living Things
Ac.text: Actinium has no known biological role and is not needed by any living organism. If it enters the body, it tends to accumulate in the liver and especially the bones, where its alpha radiation can damage tissue over time. For this reason it is considered a serious radiological hazard rather than a nutrient or trace element.

Ac.title: A Standard Candle for Tools
Ac.text: Because actinium-227 decays in a well-characterized chain that includes a steady production of helium and other daughter products, it has been used as a neutron source when mixed with beryllium. These actinium-beryllium sources can be useful for instrument calibration and certain types of radiography. Researchers also value pure actinium-227 as a way to generate small, controlled amounts of its medically prized descendant, actinium-225.

Th.title: Named After the Thunder God
Th.text: Thorium was discovered in 1828 by the Swedish chemist Jons Jacob Berzelius, who isolated it from a black mineral sent to him from Norway. He named the new element after Thor, the Norse god of thunder, and named the mineral itself thorite. It was one of several elements Berzelius pioneered, alongside cerium and selenium.

Th.title: Radioactive Without Anyone Knowing
Th.text: For seventy years thorium was thought to be a perfectly ordinary metal, because radioactivity had not yet been discovered. In 1898 Marie Curie and, independently, Gerhard Carl Schmidt found that thorium emits radiation, making it one of the first elements ever recognized as radioactive. This work helped Curie coin the very term radioactivity.

Th.title: An Element That Glowed in Lamps
Th.text: From the 1890s into the 20th century, thorium dioxide was the key ingredient in the gas mantle, the little fabric mesh that made gas street lamps and camping lanterns shine brilliantly white. When heated in a flame, thoria glows intensely due to candoluminescence. Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach built an industrial empire on this invention.

Th.title: Almost Eternal Half-Life
Th.text: The main natural isotope, thorium-232, has a half-life of about 14 billion years, roughly the age of the universe itself. This means that nearly all the thorium present when Earth formed is still here today, having barely begun to decay. Its slow, steady decay is one of the main sources of the heat that keeps Earth's interior molten.

Th.title: More Abundant Than You'd Guess
Th.text: Thorium is about three to four times more common in Earth's crust than uranium, and roughly as abundant as lead. The richest deposits occur in the mineral monazite, mined from beach sands in India, Brazil, Australia, and the United States. A single tonne of ordinary granite contains enough thorium to hold meaningful amounts of energy.

Th.title: A Fuel That Isn't Quite Fuel
Th.text: Thorium-232 cannot directly sustain a chain reaction, but when it absorbs a neutron it transforms into uranium-233, which is an excellent nuclear fuel. This makes thorium a fertile material rather than a fissile one. Experimental molten-salt reactors, including one run at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the 1960s, were built to exploit exactly this conversion.

Th.title: One of the Densest Metals
Th.text: Pure thorium is a soft, silvery metal that is surprisingly dense, at about 11.7 grams per cubic centimetre, heavier than lead. It also has one of the highest melting points among the actinides, around 1750 degrees Celsius. Freshly cut, it is bright and ductile, but it slowly tarnishes to grey and then black in air.

Th.title: Pinpoint Beams for Surgeons
Th.text: Because thorium dioxide has an extremely high melting point and refractive index, it was once added to specialty optical glass for high-quality camera and scientific lenses. Thoriated tungsten is still used today in electrodes for TIG welding and in some vacuum tubes, where a trace of thorium dramatically improves electron emission. These uses rely on thorium's physical properties rather than its radioactivity.

Th.title: No Job in Living Things
Th.text: Thorium has no known biological role in any organism, and the human body neither needs nor uses it. When ingested, most thorium passes through, but a fraction can lodge in bone and the liver, where its radioactivity poses a long-term health risk. This is why a former medical contrast agent called Thorotrast, used for X-ray imaging in the early 20th century, was eventually abandoned.

Th.title: Forged in Colliding Stars
Th.text: Like gold and platinum, thorium is created in the cosmos through the rapid neutron-capture process, thought to occur in supernovae and in the violent mergers of neutron stars. Astronomers can even detect thorium's spectral lines in ancient stars and use its slow decay as a cosmic clock to estimate their ages. Finding thorium in a star is direct evidence of one of the universe's most extreme events.

Pa.title: A Name Forged in Decay
Pa.text: Protactinium means "parent of actinium" in Greek, because its most stable isotope, protactinium-231, decays by alpha emission into the element actinium. The name was officially adopted by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry in 1949, shortened from the earlier "protoactinium." It sits at atomic number 91, squeezed between thorium (90) and uranium (92) in the actinide series.

Pa.title: Discovered Twice in One Year
Pa.text: Long-lived protactinium-231 was identified in 1918 independently by Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner in Germany and by Frederick Soddy and John Cranston in Britain. A short-lived isotope, protactinium-234, had already been spotted in 1913 by Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring, who briefly called it "brevium" for its fleeting half-life of just over a minute. The race illustrates how rapidly radiochemistry advanced during and just after World War I.

Pa.title: One of the Rarest Natural Elements
Pa.text: Protactinium occurs naturally only as a trace decay product of uranium in ores like pitchblende, at roughly one part of protactinium for every ten million parts of uranium. Its concentration in the Earth's crust is on the order of a few parts per trillion, making it one of the scarcest naturally occurring elements. To get usable quantities, scientists must extract it painstakingly from large volumes of processed ore.

Pa.title: The 130-Kilogram Extraction
Pa.text: In 1961 the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority carried out a heroic separation, processing about 60 tonnes of waste material to recover roughly 125 grams of 99.9 percent pure protactinium-231. This single batch supplied most of the world's research-grade protactinium for decades afterward. The effort cost around fifty thousand pounds and remains the largest-ever isolation of the element.

Pa.title: A Bright, Heavy Metal
Pa.text: In its pure form protactinium is a silvery, malleable metal with a notably high density of about 15.4 grams per cubic centimetre, comparable to many of the heaviest metals. It melts at roughly 1568 degrees Celsius and is one of the few actinides known to become superconducting, transitioning at a temperature of about 1.4 kelvin. At room temperature it slowly tarnishes in air, developing an oxide coating.

Pa.title: A Chemist's Nightmare to Handle
Pa.text: Protactinium is famous among radiochemists for being awkward to work with because its ions readily hydrolyze and cling to the walls of glassware and to colloidal particles. This "sticky" behaviour means dissolved protactinium can vanish from solution onto container surfaces unless kept in strongly complexing acids like hydrofluoric acid. Its rich chemistry bridges the +5 oxidation state typical of tantalum-like elements and the +4 state seen in heavier actinides.

Pa.title: A Clock for the Oceans
Pa.text: Because protactinium-231 has a half-life of about 32,760 years and behaves differently in seawater than its relative thorium-230, the ratio between the two is used to date ocean sediments tens of thousands of years old. Oceanographers exploit this protactinium-thorium method to reconstruct past changes in ocean circulation, including the strength of Atlantic currents during ice ages. It is a powerful tool for understanding Earth's climate history.

Pa.title: Radioactive and Genuinely Dangerous
Pa.text: Every isotope of protactinium is radioactive, and protactinium-231 is both an alpha emitter and chemically toxic, making it hazardous if inhaled or ingested. It is considered one of the more dangerous radiotoxic substances because the body retains it in bone, where its radiation can damage tissue over long periods. Handling requires sealed gloveboxes and strict radiological controls, which is one reason it has almost no commercial use.

Pa.title: No Job in Everyday Life
Pa.text: Despite decades of study, protactinium has essentially no industrial or commercial applications because it is too rare, too expensive, and too radioactive to be practical. Its use is confined almost entirely to basic scientific research, such as studies of actinide chemistry and the geological dating mentioned above. In this sense it is a purely "academic" element, valuable for what it teaches rather than what it builds.

Pa.title: A Fleeting Member of the Decay Chain
Pa.text: Protactinium-234 appears as a brief but important link in the natural decay chain of uranium-238, the most common uranium isotope on Earth. It exists in two forms, a ground state and a metastable state, with the metastable version decaying in just over a minute by emitting a high-energy beta particle. Studying these short-lived states helped early physicists map out how heavy elements transform step by step toward stable lead.

U.title: Named After a New Planet
U.text: German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth isolated a new substance from the mineral pitchblende in 1789 and named it after Uranus, the planet William Herschel had discovered just eight years earlier in 1781. Klaproth actually had an oxide, not the pure metal; pure uranium was first isolated by Eugène-Melchior Péligot in 1841 by reducing uranium tetrachloride with potassium. The naming linked the new element to the excitement of expanding the known solar system.

U.title: The Heaviest Natural Element
U.text: With atomic number 92, uranium is the heaviest element that occurs in significant amounts in nature. Heavier elements like plutonium and neptunium exist naturally only in vanishingly tiny traces, so uranium effectively marks the practical end of the natural periodic table. Its nucleus packs 92 protons, making it nearly 20 times denser to handle than water at about 19 grams per cubic centimetre.

U.title: It Discovered Radioactivity
U.text: In 1896 French physicist Henri Becquerel left uranium salts on a photographic plate in a dark drawer and found the plate fogged, revealing invisible rays coming from the uranium itself. This accidental observation was the discovery of radioactivity, a phenomenon later named and studied by Marie and Pierre Curie. Becquerel shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with the Curies for this work.

U.title: Almost All U-238
U.text: Natural uranium is overwhelmingly uranium-238, which makes up about 99.27 percent of every sample, while the fissile isotope uranium-235 accounts for only about 0.72 percent. Because reactors and weapons need more U-235, uranium must be enriched, a difficult process that exploits the tiny mass difference between the two isotopes. A third isotope, U-234, exists in trace amounts as a decay product of U-238.

U.title: A Clock for the Earth
U.text: Uranium-238 decays into lead-206 with a half-life of about 4.47 billion years, almost exactly the age of the Earth. Geologists use uranium-lead dating on minerals like zircon to measure the ages of the oldest rocks and even meteorites. This method gave the first reliable estimate of Earth's age at roughly 4.5 billion years, set by Clair Patterson in 1956.

U.title: One Pellet, Tonnes of Coal
U.text: A single ceramic fuel pellet of enriched uranium, about the size of a fingertip, can release energy equivalent to roughly a tonne of coal. This enormous energy density comes from nuclear fission, where splitting a U-235 nucleus liberates millions of times more energy than any chemical reaction. Today nuclear power supplies around a tenth of the world's electricity, almost all of it from uranium fuel.

U.title: Nature's Own Reactor
U.text: About 1.7 billion years ago in Oklo, Gabon, natural uranium deposits became concentrated enough, with groundwater as a moderator, to sustain self-regulating nuclear fission chain reactions. These natural reactors ran on and off for hundreds of thousands of years, long before humans existed. Scientists discovered them in 1972 when uranium from the site showed a strangely low U-235 content, the telltale sign it had already been fissioned.

U.title: It Once Colored Glass
U.text: Long before its radioactivity was understood, uranium compounds were prized for coloring glass and ceramic glazes brilliant green and yellow, sometimes called Vaseline glass for its fluorescent glow under ultraviolet light. Ancient Roman mosaics near Naples contain glass tinted yellow with uranium oxide. The practice declined in the 20th century once the metal became a strategic and regulated material.

U.title: More Common Than Silver
U.text: Despite its fearsome reputation, uranium is a fairly common element in the Earth's crust, present at around 2.7 parts per million, which makes it about 40 times more abundant than silver. It is found in rocks, soil, and dissolved in seawater, where the oceans hold an estimated 4 billion tonnes. The heat from uranium's slow radioactive decay, alongside thorium and potassium, helps keep the Earth's interior hot and drives plate tectonics.

U.title: Fuel of the First Bomb
U.text: On 6 August 1945 the bomb dropped on Hiroshima, nicknamed Little Boy, used highly enriched uranium-235 in a gun-type design that slammed two sub-critical pieces together. It was so confidently expected to work that it was used in combat without a prior test. This same fission physics, harnessed slowly and safely in reactors, also powers submarines and produces medical isotopes that diagnose and treat disease.

Np.title: The First Synthetic Transuranic
Np.text: Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium ever created, synthesized in 1940 by Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson at the Berkeley Radiation Laboratory in California. They produced it by bombarding uranium-238 with neutrons, which captured a neutron and then beta-decayed into element 93. This discovery opened the door to the entire family of transuranic elements, and McMillan shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the work.

Np.title: Named for a Planet
Np.text: Neptunium is named after the planet Neptune, following the pattern set by uranium, which was named for Uranus. Because Neptune is the planet just beyond Uranus in the Solar System, it was the natural choice for the element that sits just beyond uranium on the periodic table. This celestial naming tradition continued with the very next element, plutonium, named for Pluto.

Np.title: A Surprisingly Dense Metal
Np.text: Pure neptunium is a silvery, lustrous metal that is remarkably dense, with the alpha form reaching about 20.45 grams per cubic centimeter, making it one of the densest of all the actinides. It melts at a relatively low 644 degrees Celsius and exists in three different crystal structures depending on temperature. Like many actinides, it is chemically reactive and slowly tarnishes in air.

Np.title: It Glows With Radioactivity
Np.text: All isotopes of neptunium are radioactive, with the longest-lived being neptunium-237, which has a half-life of about 2.14 million years. This isotope decays through a long chain of alpha and beta emissions, eventually ending at stable bismuth-209 (or thallium-205 by very recent measurements). Because of its long half-life, neptunium-237 is the form that accumulates and persists in nuclear waste.

Np.title: Hiding in Uranium Ore
Np.text: Although neptunium is essentially a man-made element, trace amounts occur naturally in uranium ores, formed when uranium atoms capture stray neutrons from natural fission and radioactive decay. These quantities are minuscule, measured in parts per trillion, far too small to mine. This makes neptunium one of the rarest naturally occurring elements on Earth.

Np.title: Fuel for Deep-Space Power
Np.text: Neptunium-237 can be irradiated with neutrons to breed plutonium-238, the isotope that powers radioisotope thermoelectric generators used on spacecraft. These generators turn the heat of radioactive decay into electricity and have powered missions like the Voyager probes, the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, and the New Horizons mission to Pluto. Thus neptunium plays a quiet but vital role in exploring the outer Solar System.

Np.title: It Can Sustain a Chain Reaction
Np.text: Neptunium-237 is fissile enough to sustain a nuclear chain reaction, and scientists have calculated its critical mass at roughly 60 kilograms in a bare sphere. In 2002, researchers at Los Alamos National Laboratory experimentally confirmed that neptunium can go critical, which is why the element is carefully tracked under international nuclear safeguards. Despite this capability, it has never been used to build a weapon.

Np.title: A Chemist's Color Palette
Np.text: In solution, neptunium can exist in an unusually wide range of oxidation states, from +3 all the way up to +7, and each state shows a distinct, vivid color. Neptunium(III) is purple, neptunium(IV) is yellow-green, neptunium(V) is green-blue, and neptunium(VI) is pink-red. This rainbow of oxidation states makes neptunium chemistry especially rich and a favorite subject for studying actinide behavior.

Np.title: The Neptunium Decay Series
Np.text: Neptunium-237 is the parent of one of the four major radioactive decay chains, known as the neptunium series. Unlike the other three chains, this series has largely vanished from nature because its longest-lived member decays far faster than the age of the Earth, about 4.5 billion years. Studying the surviving traces of this series helps scientists understand the history of radioactive elements in the cosmos.

Np.title: Captured in Tiny Amounts
Np.text: It took years after its discovery before anyone isolated a visible, weighable sample of neptunium metal, which was first prepared in 1944. Today a typical large nuclear reactor produces several hundred kilograms of neptunium-237 per year as a byproduct of uranium fuel. Managing this steady supply is a major challenge for nuclear waste storage, since its long half-life means it remains hazardous for over a hundred thousand years.

Pu.title: Born in a Berkeley Lab
Pu.text: Plutonium was first produced in December 1940 and chemically identified in February 1941 by Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy and Arthur Wahl at the University of California, Berkeley. They made it by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons in a 60-inch cyclotron, creating neptunium-238 that decayed into plutonium-238. It was the second transuranium element ever discovered, right after neptunium.

Pu.title: Named After a Dwarf Planet
Pu.text: Following the pattern of uranium (Uranus) and neptunium (Neptune), the new element was named after Pluto, then the outermost planet of the solar system. Seaborg deliberately chose the symbol Pu instead of the more logical Pl, partly as a playful joke that he expected to be rejected but which slipped through unnoticed. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, long after the element's name was set.

Pu.title: A Metal That Has Six Forms
Pu.text: Solid plutonium is one of the most structurally complex metals known, existing in six distinct crystal phases (allotropes) between room temperature and its melting point of 640 degrees Celsius. These phases have wildly different densities, so a sample can expand or shrink dramatically with small temperature changes. Engineers add a few percent of gallium to stabilize the workable delta phase, a trick essential to fabricating plutonium parts.

Pu.title: It Is Warm to the Touch
Pu.text: A lump of plutonium-238 feels noticeably warm because its intense alpha radioactivity releases about 0.56 watts of heat per gram. This self-heating is so reliable that the metal can glow a dull red and stay hot for decades without any external power. The property turns a chemical curiosity into a long-lived, compact energy source.

Pu.title: Powering Spacecraft for Decades
Pu.text: Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) convert the heat of decaying plutonium-238 directly into electricity using thermocouples, with no moving parts. This technology powers NASA's Voyager 1 and 2 probes (launched 1977 and still transmitting), the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, and the New Horizons mission to Pluto. With a half-life of about 88 years, Pu-238 keeps instruments running where sunlight is too weak for solar panels.

Pu.title: The Engine of Nuclear Reactors
Pu.text: Plutonium-239 is fissile, meaning a single neutron can split its nucleus and release more neutrons to sustain a chain reaction. Just a few kilograms can reach critical mass, releasing enormous energy. This is why Pu-239 became central to both nuclear power and weapons, and the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in 1945 used a plutonium core.

Pu.title: Almost Absent From Nature
Pu.text: Although plutonium is overwhelmingly a man-made element, vanishingly tiny amounts occur naturally. Trace Pu-239 forms in uranium ores when uranium-238 captures stray neutrons from spontaneous fission or cosmic rays. Far larger natural deposits existed about two billion years ago at Oklo in Gabon, where uranium concentrations were high enough to run natural fission reactors that bred plutonium.

Pu.title: Forged in Dying Stars
Pu.text: Heavy elements like plutonium are created in the cosmos by the rapid neutron-capture process, which requires the violent neutron flux of merging neutron stars and possibly some supernovae. The isotope plutonium-244 has a half-life of about 80 million years, long enough that scientists search deep-sea sediments for traces deposited by ancient nearby explosions. Such measurements help reveal how often these cataclysmic events seeded our region of the galaxy.

Pu.title: A Surprising Chemical Chameleon
Pu.text: In water, plutonium can simultaneously exist in four different oxidation states, from +3 to +6, each with its own color, ranging from blue-violet to orange. This makes its solution chemistry among the most complex of any element and a genuine headache for engineers reprocessing nuclear fuel. The behavior stems from its 5f electrons, which sit on a knife-edge between being chemically active and locked away.

Pu.title: Dangerous Mainly When Inhaled
Pu.text: Plutonium emits alpha particles that cannot penetrate skin or even a sheet of paper, so handling sealed sources is far less hazardous than its reputation suggests. The real danger comes if fine particles are inhaled or enter the bloodstream, where the radiation can damage nearby tissue and lodge in bones and the liver. Because of this, plutonium work demands sealed gloveboxes and strict containment rather than thick external shielding.

Am.title: Born in the Manhattan Project
Am.text: Americium was first produced in late 1944 at the University of Chicago's Metallurgical Laboratory by Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso. They made it by bombarding plutonium-239 with neutrons in a reactor, building up to americium-241 through successive neutron captures and beta decay. Because the work was wartime-classified, the discovery was not publicly announced until 1945, partly revealed by Seaborg on a children's radio quiz show.

Am.title: Named for a continent
Am.text: The element sits directly below europium in the periodic table, so Seaborg's team named it after the Americas, echoing how europium was named after Europe. This deliberate parallel highlighted the chemical similarity between the actinide and lanthanide series. The naming logic helped cement Seaborg's then-controversial idea that the actinides form their own family at the bottom of the table.

Am.title: It glows in the dark
Am.text: Freshly prepared americium metal is silvery-white, but it is so intensely radioactive that the material warms itself and can glow faintly in the dark from its own radiation. A single gram releases over 100 milliwatts of heat continuously from alpha decay. This self-heating means a visible piece of americium is never truly at room temperature with its surroundings.

Am.title: Inside millions of smoke detectors
Am.text: The most common ionization smoke detector contains a tiny source of americium-241, typically only about 0.3 micrograms, sealed in a metal foil. Its alpha particles ionize the air in a small chamber, creating a steady current that smoke particles disrupt, triggering the alarm. This makes americium one of the very few synthetic elements that ordinary people keep in their homes.

Am.title: A 432-year clock
Am.text: Americium-241, the workhorse isotope, has a half-life of about 432 years, decaying by alpha emission into neptunium-237. That timescale is long enough to give a stable, predictable output for decades yet short enough to be intensely radioactive. The much rarer americium-243 lasts far longer, with a half-life of roughly 7,370 years.

Am.title: Gauging thickness and moisture
Am.text: Industry uses americium-241 in radioactive gauges that measure the thickness of glass, paper, and metal sheets as they roll off production lines, without ever touching the material. Mixed with beryllium, it also becomes a portable neutron source used in oil-well logging to detect water and oil-bearing rock underground. These americium-beryllium sources let engineers see into places no probe could reach.

Am.title: A candidate to power spacecraft
Am.text: The European Space Agency has developed americium-241 as a fuel for radioisotope heater units and generators on deep-space missions. Although it produces less heat per gram than plutonium-238, americium can be extracted from aged civil nuclear waste, making it cheaper and more available in Europe.
