A spacecraft running on americium could keep working for centuries far from the Sun.

Am.title: Many faces of one metal
Am.text: Americium is chemically versatile, forming compounds in oxidation states from +2 all the way up to +7, more than most of its actinide neighbors. In water its ions paint a palette of colors, with the americium(III) ion appearing pink and higher states giving yellows and tans. This rich chemistry makes americium a favorite test case for scientists studying how heavy elements bond.

Am.title: Not found in nature
Am.text: Americium does not occur naturally on Earth in any meaningful amount, because even its longest-lived isotopes decay away in mere thousands of years, far shorter than the planet's age. Every atom of americium in existence today was manufactured in reactors or detonated in nuclear tests. Traces were indeed scattered worldwide by atmospheric weapons testing in the 1950s and 1960s.

Am.title: Heavier than lead, denser than steel
Am.text: Americium metal has a density of about 12 grams per cubic centimeter, heavier than lead and roughly one and a half times denser than steel. It melts at around 1,176 degrees Celsius and exists in several crystal structures depending on temperature and pressure. Despite being a heavy, hard-to-handle radioactive metal, chemists have purified it into shiny ingots for careful study.

Cm.title: Named for the Curies
Cm.text: Curium was named in honor of Marie and Pierre Curie, the pioneers of radioactivity research. The naming deliberately echoes its lighter chemical cousin gadolinium, which honors the chemist Johan Gadolin, since curium sits directly below gadolinium in the periodic table's structure. It is one of the few elements named after specific people who were themselves scientists.

Cm.title: Born in wartime Berkeley
Cm.text: Curium was first synthesized in the summer of 1944 by Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, and Albert Ghiorso at the University of California, Berkeley, by bombarding plutonium-239 with alpha particles in a cyclotron. The work was part of the secret Manhattan Project, so the discovery stayed classified for years. Seaborg famously first hinted at the new elements during a children's radio quiz show in 1945 before any formal publication.

Cm.title: A metal you can never hold
Cm.text: Curium is intensely radioactive, and a sizable sample glows with a soft purple or lilac light in the dark, caused by the energy released as its own radiation excites the surrounding air and the metal itself. The decay is so energetic that a chunk of curium grows noticeably warm to the touch. Handling it requires sealed gloveboxes and remote tools, because even small amounts are dangerous to living tissue.

Cm.title: Hotter than its surroundings
Cm.text: A single gram of curium-244 releases roughly 3 watts of heat continuously from its radioactive decay, far more thermal power per gram than plutonium-238. This makes curium a candidate fuel for radioisotope thermoelectric generators that could power spacecraft for decades. The intense self-heating is a direct consequence of its short half-life packing a lot of decays into a small time.

Cm.title: It explored Mars
Cm.text: Curium-244 has served as the alpha-particle source in alpha particle X-ray spectrometers carried aboard NASA Mars rovers, including Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity. The instrument bathes a rock in alpha particles and reads the X-rays that bounce back to identify which elements the rock contains. In a sense, a man-made element helped decode the natural chemistry of another planet.

Cm.title: Once thought impossible to separate
Cm.text: Curium and its neighbor americium were so chemically similar and so hard to purify that the Berkeley chemists privately nicknamed them pandemonium and delirium during the frustrating separation work. Curium's strong tendency to exist in the +3 oxidation state, like the lanthanides, is exactly what makes it cling to its chemical cousins. Modern ion-exchange techniques finally tamed the separation.

Cm.title: A half-life rivaling Earth's age
Cm.text: While most curium isotopes vanish quickly, curium-247 has a half-life of about 15.6 million years, and curium-248 lasts roughly 348,000 years. These long-lived forms are valued for research because they stay around long enough to study without constant replenishment. Even the longest-lived curium, though, is far too short-lived to survive from the formation of the solar system to today.

Cm.title: Extinct in nature, alive in starlight
Cm.text: Curium does not occur naturally on Earth today, but evidence in ancient meteorites suggests curium-247 was present in the early solar system and has since completely decayed away. Astronomers have also detected signs that curium is produced in violent cosmic events such as neutron star mergers, where extreme neutron bombardment builds up heavy elements. So while we make it in reactors, the universe forges it in cataclysms.

Cm.title: Seven shifting crystal forms
Cm.text: Under increasing pressure, curium metal transforms through several distinct crystal structures, and one of its high-pressure phases is remarkable because its magnetism actively helps stabilize the structure. This is unusual, since magnetism rarely controls the basic atomic arrangement of a metal. Studying these phase changes helps physicists understand how the 5f electrons of the actinides behave under extreme conditions.

Cm.title: A stepping stone to heavier elements
Cm.text: Curium is not just an endpoint but a launchpad: bombarding curium targets with light ions has been used to create even heavier elements, and curium is itself made by neutron irradiation of plutonium in reactors. Only gram-scale quantities are produced worldwide each year, making it precious and tightly controlled. Its place at atomic number 96 makes it a key rung on the ladder toward the superheavy elements.

Bk.title: Named For Berkeley
Bk.text: Berkelium was named after the city of Berkeley, California, home of the University of California laboratory where it was created. The naming deliberately echoes terbium, the element named after the Swedish village of Ytterby, because berkelium sits directly below terbium on the periodic table. The team noted the parallel openly, paying homage to the periodic table's vertical relationships.

Bk.title: Born From A Cyclotron
Bk.text: Berkelium was first synthesized in December 1949 by Glenn Seaborg, Stanley Thompson, and Albert Ghiorso. They bombarded a tiny sample of americium-241 with accelerated alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron at Berkeley, producing berkelium-243. It was the fifth transuranium element ever discovered.

Bk.title: You Can't Find It In Nature
Bk.text: Berkelium does not occur naturally on Earth in any measurable amount, because all of its isotopes are radioactive and decay far faster than the age of our planet. Every atom of berkelium that exists has been made artificially in reactors or accelerators. Trace amounts were once spread globally by atmospheric nuclear weapons testing in the 20th century, but these have long since decayed.

Bk.title: A Metal You Could Hold (Briefly)
Bk.text: Berkelium is a silvery, soft metal that is malleable enough to be shaped, and it is dense at about 14.8 grams per cubic centimeter. It melts at roughly 986 degrees Celsius. Despite these tangible metallic properties, only microgram-to-milligram quantities have ever been produced, so no one has ever forged a visible lump of it for everyday handling.

Bk.title: It Glows With Its Own Heat
Bk.text: The most stable isotope, berkelium-247, has a half-life of about 1,380 years, but the isotope usually produced, berkelium-249, lasts only around 330 days. Berkelium-249's radioactivity is so intense that samples warm themselves and emit a faint glow. This self-heating also slowly damages the element's own crystal structure from within as it decays.

Bk.title: The Key To Element 117
Bk.text: Berkelium's most famous practical role was as a target for making tennessine, element 117. In 2009 Oak Ridge National Laboratory produced about 22 milligrams of berkelium-249 over roughly a year, then shipped it to Russia. There, scientists bombarded it with calcium-48 ions to create the first atoms of tennessine in 2010.

Bk.title: A Race Against Radioactive Decay
Bk.text: Because berkelium-249 decays with a half-life of under a year, experiments using it are a race against time. The Oak Ridge berkelium shipped for the tennessine experiment was losing usable material every single day. Scientists had to carefully schedule the international transport and the irradiation to finish before too much of the precious target vanished.

Bk.title: Hard To Make, Rarely Made
Bk.text: Berkelium is one of the rarest synthetic elements, produced only at a handful of facilities such as Oak Ridge's High Flux Isotope Reactor. Making it requires bombarding curium or plutonium targets with neutrons for long periods, building up heavier nuclei step by step. The world's total production has historically amounted to only a fraction of a gram at a time.

Bk.title: It Likes To Be +3
Bk.text: In chemical compounds berkelium most commonly adopts the +3 oxidation state, behaving much like other actinides and the lanthanide terbium above it. However, it can also reach an unusually accessible +4 state, which is rarer among the heavier actinides. This +4 chemistry helps chemists separate and purify berkelium from neighboring elements.

Bk.title: Purely A Tool For Science
Bk.text: Berkelium has no biological role and no commercial or medical uses; it is too scarce, too costly, and too radioactive to be practical for anything outside research. Its entire value lies in fundamental science, especially as a stepping-stone to forge superheavy elements at the very edge of the periodic table. Studying its bonding and electron behavior also tests our theories of how relativity reshapes the chemistry of heavy atoms.

Cf.title: Born in a Berkeley Cyclotron
Cf.text: Californium was first created in 1950 at the University of California, Berkeley, by Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg. They produced it by bombarding a tiny target of curium-242 with alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron. The very first batch contained only about 5,000 atoms, far too few to see, yet enough to identify a brand-new element.

Cf.title: Named for a State and a School
Cf.text: The element honors both the U.S. state of California and the University of California. The discoverers noted with some humor that, unlike earlier explorers who had to cross an ocean to reach California, scientists searching for element 98 faced the much harder journey of crossing the periodic table. It remains one of the few elements named after a specific university.

Cf.title: A Neutron Factory in Your Hand
Cf.text: One microgram of californium-252 spits out about 2.3 million neutrons every second through spontaneous fission. This makes it one of the most powerful portable neutron sources known, with no reactor or accelerator required. A single gram would release roughly 2.3 trillion neutrons per second, a staggering output for a speck of metal.

Cf.title: Finding Gold and Oil Underground
Cf.text: Because it floods its surroundings with neutrons, Cf-252 is used in well-logging tools that scan rock formations for oil, water, and minerals. The neutrons interact with atoms in the rock, and the returning radiation reveals what lies underground. The same neutron flood is used in portable scanners that detect gold, silver, and even explosives or landmines.

Cf.title: Jump-Starting Nuclear Reactors
Cf.text: Californium-252 serves as a reliable startup neutron source for nuclear reactors, providing the initial burst of neutrons needed to kick off a controlled chain reaction. It is also used to calibrate radiation detectors and to study how materials behave under intense neutron bombardment. Its predictable, steady neutron output makes it ideal for these precise jobs.

Cf.title: Treating Cancer With Neutrons
Cf.text: In medicine, californium-252 has been used in brachytherapy, where tiny sealed sources are placed inside or next to a tumor. The neutrons it emits can damage cancer cells that resist ordinary X-ray and gamma-ray treatments, including some cervical, brain, and oral cancers. This makes it a valuable option for certain hard-to-treat tumors.

Cf.title: Among the Most Expensive Substances
Cf.text: Californium is extraordinarily costly to make, with prices historically quoted around 27 million U.S. dollars per gram for Cf-252. Only fractions of a gram are produced worldwide each year, chiefly at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee and at a reactor in Dimitrovgrad, Russia. This scarcity places it among the priciest materials on Earth by weight.

Cf.title: It Glows From Its Own Decay
Cf.text: A concentrated sample of californium is so intensely radioactive that it actually glows, heated by the energy of its own constant decay. The radiation is hazardous enough that it can disrupt the formation of red blood cells in the body if mishandled. Researchers must handle it remotely behind heavy shielding using glove boxes and robotic arms.

Cf.title: Heavier Cousins Owe It Thanks
Cf.text: Californium is one of the few elements heavy enough to serve as a target for making even more exotic elements. Bombarding Cf-249 with calcium-48 ions was the method used to synthesize oganesson, element 118, the heaviest element currently known. Without enough californium to build a target, the bottom row of the periodic table could not have been completed.

Cf.title: Glimpsed in an Exploding Star
Cf.text: Californium does not occur naturally on Earth in any meaningful amount, since its longest-lived isotope, Cf-251, has a half-life of only about 900 years. However, its telltale signature was reported in the light of supernovae, where the violent collapse and explosion of dying stars can briefly forge such heavy elements. Studying these signatures helps astronomers understand how nature builds the heaviest atoms.

Es.title: Born in a Bomb's Fire
Es.text: Einsteinium was discovered in December 1952 in the radioactive debris of the first thermonuclear (hydrogen) bomb test, code-named 'Ivy Mike,' detonated over Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific. The intense neutron flux let uranium nuclei swallow many neutrons at once, building up to element 99 before beta decay raised the proton count. Because the work was tied to a classified weapons test, the discovery was kept secret and not published until 1955.

Es.title: Named for Einstein
Es.text: The element honors Albert Einstein, who was still alive when it was discovered but died in April 1955, shortly before the naming was made public. The team at the University of California, Berkeley, led by Albert Ghiorso, proposed the name; einsteinium and its neighbor fermium (element 100, for Enrico Fermi) were named for giants of physics. Einstein himself reportedly never knew an element had been named after him.

Es.title: It Glows in the Dark
Es.text: Einsteinium is so intensely radioactive that visible quantities glow with a soft blue light, caused by the energy released as its own radiation excites the surrounding air and material. This self-luminescence is a direct, eerie demonstration of just how much energy these unstable nuclei pour out. The same radioactivity heats the metal noticeably above room temperature.

Es.title: A Metal That Cooks Itself
Es.text: The decay of einsteinium-253 releases roughly 1,000 watts of heat per gram, enough to make a sample warm to the touch and to slowly damage the very crystal it forms. This intense self-heating, combined with radiation, makes the metal's properties extraordinarily hard to measure. Scientists must race against the clock because the material literally destroys itself from the inside.

Es.title: You Can't Find It in Nature
Es.text: Einsteinium does not occur naturally on Earth in any meaningful amount; every atom that exists has been made artificially in reactors or accelerators. Its longest-lived isotope, einsteinium-252, has a half-life of only about 472 days, far too short to have survived since the planet formed. Any primordial einsteinium vanished billions of years ago.

Es.title: Made by the Microgram
Es.text: Einsteinium is among the rarest synthesized elements: it is produced at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, and only fractions of a milligram are made per year. A typical research sample might contain just a few micrograms or even nanograms. This scarcity means most experiments use vanishingly small amounts handled with extreme care.

Es.title: The Bridge to Heavier Elements
Es.text: Einsteinium served as a crucial stepping stone in the hunt for new elements: bombarding an einsteinium target with alpha particles led to the 1955 discovery of mendelevium, element 101. Because einsteinium can be made in (barely) weighable quantities, it remains one of the heaviest elements usable as a target for creating even heavier ones. It is, in effect, a launchpad deeper into the periodic table.

Es.title: A Surprisingly Light Metal
Es.text: Despite sitting among the heavy actinides, einsteinium metal has a relatively low density of about 8.84 grams per cubic centimeter and a face-centered cubic crystal structure. Studies suggest its outer electrons are slightly more 'free' than in its neighbors, hinting at unusual bonding behavior at the edge of the actinide series. These quirks make it a valuable probe of how electron shells behave under extreme nuclear conditions.

Es.title: Chemistry Caught on Camera
Es.text: In 2021, scientists at Berkeley Lab and partner institutions performed some of the first detailed chemical bonding studies on einsteinium, using less than 250 nanograms of the element. They measured its bond distances and absorption behavior, revealing subtle departures from the trends seen in lighter actinides. The experiment was a tour de force, since the sample was decaying and damaging its container throughout the work.

Es.title: No Job, No Biology
Es.text: Einsteinium has no biological role whatsoever and is not part of any living organism; it exists purely as a tool for fundamental research. Because of its fierce radioactivity, it has no commercial or industrial applications and is studied only in specialized laboratories. Its entire reason for existing, from a human standpoint, is to help us understand the heaviest reaches of matter.

Fm.title: Born in a Hydrogen Bomb
Fm.text: Fermium was first discovered in the radioactive debris of "Ivy Mike," the first thermonuclear (hydrogen) bomb test, detonated by the United States in November 1952 over Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific. Scientists at Los Alamos, Argonne, and Berkeley found that uranium nuclei in the device had captured many neutrons in an instant, then beta-decayed up to element 100. The find was kept secret for years for Cold War security reasons and not announced until 1955.

Fm.title: Named for a Nuclear Pioneer
Fm.text: The element honors Enrico Fermi, the Italian-American physicist who built the world's first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, in 1942. Fermi won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on induced radioactivity using slow neutrons. He died of cancer in 1954, shortly before the element bearing his name was publicly revealed.

Fm.title: The Heaviest You Can Bombard
Fm.text: Fermium marks an important frontier: it is the heaviest element that can be made in weighable amounts by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons in a reactor. For elements beyond fermium (mendelevium and up), this neutron-capture route fails because the relevant fermium isotopes fission or decay too quickly. To make heavier elements, scientists must switch to firing whole atomic nuclei at targets in accelerators.

Fm.title: A Vanishingly Brief Existence
Fm.text: Every isotope of fermium is radioactive, and the most stable one, fermium-257, has a half-life of only about 100.5 days. More commonly studied fermium-255 lasts barely 20 hours. This means fermium can never accumulate; any sample is constantly decaying away into other elements.

Fm.title: Nowhere in Nature
Fm.text: Fermium does not occur naturally on Earth in any detectable quantity, and none is believed to exist naturally anywhere in the cosmos today. Although it can in principle form during the rapid neutron-capture (r-process) in supernovae and neutron-star mergers, its isotopes decay far too fast to survive the journey of cosmic time. Every fermium atom that has ever been studied was manufactured by humans.

Fm.title: Spontaneous Splitting
Fm.text: Fermium-256 has a striking decay habit: instead of just emitting an alpha particle, most of its atoms undergo spontaneous fission, literally splitting in two without any outside trigger. Its half-life for this process is only about 2.6 hours. This made fermium isotopes important test cases for physicists studying how and why heavy nuclei tear themselves apart.

Fm.title: Studied a Few Atoms at a Time
Fm.text: Because so little fermium can ever be made, much of its chemistry has been explored using "tracer" techniques with just a handful of atoms in solution. Researchers infer its behavior by watching how those atoms move through chemical separations rather than by handling a visible lump of metal. In water it normally forms the Fm3+ ion, like its neighboring actinides.

Fm.title: An Unusual Two-Plus State
Fm.text: Although fermium usually behaves with a +3 charge, chemists have shown it can be coaxed into a +2 oxidation state more easily than the actinides just before it. This reflects the growing stability of a filled 5f electron shell as you move across the actinide series. Such subtle electronic trends help scientists test theories about chemical periodicity at the very edge of the periodic table.

Fm.title: A Discovery Naming Dispute
Fm.text: The right to name elements 99 and 100 became entangled in Cold War politics and scientific rivalry. American teams led by Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg proposed honoring Fermi and Einstein, but the secrecy around the bomb test complicated the credit and timing of the announcement. The names einsteinium and fermium were eventually accepted internationally.

Fm.title: No Job Outside the Lab
Fm.text: Fermium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its extreme scarcity, high cost of production, and rapid radioactive decay make it useful only for fundamental scientific research. Studying it helps chemists and physicists understand the limits of nuclear stability and the behavior of the heaviest elements.

Md.title: Named For Mendeleev
Md.text: Mendelevium honors Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who published the first widely recognized periodic table in 1869. The name was a deliberate Cold War gesture: in 1955 American scientists chose to celebrate a Russian whose table had famously predicted undiscovered elements. It was the first element named after a person who created the periodic system itself.

Md.title: Discovered One Atom At A Time
Md.text: In 1955 a Berkeley team led by Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin and Stanley Thompson made mendelevium by bombarding einsteinium-253 with alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron. The experiment produced only about one atom of element 101 per bombardment, and the entire discovery rested on a total of just 17 atoms. It was the first element ever discovered by detecting single atoms, one event at a time.

Md.title: A Clever Chemistry Trick
Md.text: Because so few atoms existed, the team could not weigh or see mendelevium, so they identified it chemically using ion-exchange columns. They predicted that Md atoms would wash off the column in a specific order relative to other actinides and then watched for the telltale radioactive decay in exactly the predicted drops. This elegant elution method let them prove a brand-new element from a handful of invisible atoms.

Md.title: It Breaks The Actinide Rule
Md.text: Most actinides strongly prefer the +3 oxidation state in water, but mendelevium also forms a surprisingly stable +2 ion. This unusual stability comes from its nearly filled 5f electron shell, which makes the divalent state energetically favorable. Studying Md helped chemists understand how the actinide series differs from the lighter rare-earth elements above it.

Md.title: A Half-Life Of Weeks
Md.text: The longest-lived isotope, mendelevium-258, has a half-life of about 51.5 days, far longer than most isotopes of its neighbors. This relative stability makes it the workhorse isotope for laboratory chemistry experiments on the element. Even so, a sample would noticeably weaken within a couple of months as it radioactively decays.

Md.title: Vanishingly Rare On Earth
Md.text: Mendelevium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth and must be created atom by atom in particle accelerators or reactors. Scientists have never assembled a weighable, visible quantity of the metal, so its bulk appearance and melting point are estimated rather than measured. Everything humans have ever made of it would be invisible to the naked eye.

Md.title: Born From Other Synthetic Elements
Md.text: To make mendelevium, researchers first had to manufacture its target, einsteinium, which itself does not exist in nature. Einsteinium-253 was so precious that only a few billion atoms could be prepared, then coated onto a thin gold foil for bombardment. This made Md a synthetic element built from another synthetic element, a chain of human-made matter.

Md.title: Purely For Pure Science
Md.text: Mendelevium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications, and given its scarcity and rapid decay it likely never will. Its only real-world value is scientific: testing predictions about electron structure, oxidation states, and the limits of the periodic table. It is a classic example of research pursued to understand nature rather than to build a product.

Md.title: Self-Heating And Self-Destructive
Md.text: Like other heavy actinides, mendelevium is intensely radioactive, and its decay releases enough energy that a macroscopic lump would heat itself and damage its own crystal structure. The emitted radiation steadily breaks chemical bonds and disrupts any container holding it. This self-destruction is one reason no large sample has ever been kept intact.

Md.title: A Window Into Relativity
Md.text: In very heavy atoms like mendelevium, inner electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity measurably changes their energy levels. These relativistic effects help explain why Md favors its unusual +2 state and behaves differently from lighter elements with similar configurations. Element 101 thus serves as a real laboratory for testing how relativity reshapes chemistry.

No.title: Named For Alfred Nobel
No.text: Nobelium honors Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist and inventor of dynamite who endowed the Nobel Prizes. The name was proposed in 1957 by a team at the Nobel Institute for Physics in Stockholm. Even after that group's claim was disproven, the name stuck and was officially adopted, making Nobel one of the few people honored with an element.

No.title: A Three-Lab Naming Fight
No.text: Nobelium sits at the heart of the Cold War "Transfermium Wars" over who discovered the heaviest elements. Teams in Stockholm, Berkeley (USA), and Dubna (USSR) all claimed credit during the late 1950s and 1960s. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry eventually credited the Dubna group led by Georgy Flerov with the convincing discovery, but kept the Berkeley-backed name.

No.title: It Does Not Exist In Nature
No.text: Nobelium is entirely synthetic and is never found in the Earth's crust, oceans, or atmosphere. Every atom that has ever existed was made in a particle accelerator by smashing lighter nuclei together, such as firing carbon ions at a curium target. There is no natural source and no cosmic reservoir of it that we can collect.

No.title: Gone In Less Than An Hour
No.text: Nobelium's longest-lived isotope, nobelium-259, has a half-life of only about 58 minutes. Most other isotopes vanish in seconds or fractions of a second. This fleeting existence is why scientists have only ever produced it a handful of atoms at a time, never enough to see or weigh.

No.title: The Rebel Plus-Two Ion
No.text: In water, nobelium prefers the +2 oxidation state, which is highly unusual for an actinide since most of its neighbors favor +3. This stability comes from its filled 5f electron shell (a 5f14 configuration), which resists giving up an extra electron. This quirk makes nobelium chemically more like the alkaline-earth metal barium than like uranium.

No.title: Chemistry On Single Atoms
No.text: Because only a few atoms can be made at once, chemists study nobelium using "one-atom-at-a-time" techniques, repeating experiments thousands of times. Researchers track how lone atoms behave on ion-exchange columns to deduce properties like ionic charge. This pushes analytical chemistry to its absolute limit of sensitivity.

No.title: First Heavy Element Laser-Probed
No.text: In 2018, a team at the GSI laboratory in Germany measured nobelium's atomic energy levels using laser spectroscopy, a landmark for elements this heavy. It was among the first elements beyond fermium to have its atomic structure directly probed by light. The results tested how Einstein's relativity reshapes the electron orbitals of very heavy atoms.

No.title: A Window Into Nuclear Shells
No.text: Nobelium isotopes are prized by physicists for probing nuclear "magic numbers" and the predicted island of stability. Studying how nobelium nuclei spin and deform helps refine models of what holds super-heavy nuclei together. These experiments guide the search for even heavier, potentially longer-lived elements.

No.title: No Job Outside The Lab
No.text: Nobelium has no commercial, industrial, or medical uses whatsoever, and it plays no biological role in any living thing. Its extreme scarcity, rapid radioactive decay, and enormous production cost make it purely a subject of fundamental research. Its entire value lies in what it teaches us about the structure of matter.

No.title: A Heavyweight Actinide
No.text: With atomic number 102, nobelium is the second-to-last member of the actinide series, just before lawrencium. It is one of the transuranium elements, meaning it sits beyond uranium on the periodic table. Element 102 marks the near-completion of the 5f electron shell that defines the entire actinide family.

Lr.title: Last of the Actinides
Lr.text: Lawrencium, with atomic number 103, sits at the very end of the actinide series in the periodic table. As the final actinide, it bridges this f-block row to the transactinides that begin with rutherfordium (element 104). Its placement makes it a key marker for testing chemical periodicity in the heaviest elements.

Lr.title: Named for the Cyclotron Pioneer
Lr.text: The element honors Ernest O. Lawrence, the American physicist who invented the cyclotron particle accelerator in 1931 and won the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physics. The same Lawrence lends his name to two U.S. national laboratories, Lawrence Berkeley and Lawrence Livermore. Its symbol was originally 'Lw' before being changed to 'Lr' by IUPAC in 1963.

Lr.title: A Cold War Discovery Dispute
Lr.text: Lawrencium was first reported in 1961 by a team led by Albert Ghiorso at the Lawrence Berkeley laboratory in California. A Soviet group at Dubna also made claims to its discovery in the 1960s, fueling a Cold War priority dispute. IUPAC and IUPAP eventually credited both Berkeley and Dubna with shared roles in confirming the element.

Lr.title: It Vanishes in Hours
Lr.text: Lawrencium has no stable isotopes; every form is radioactive and short-lived. Its longest-lived isotope, lawrencium-266, has a half-life of only about 11 hours, while most others decay in seconds or minutes. This fleeting existence means scientists must study it within moments of creating it.

Lr.title: Made an Atom at a Time
Lr.text: Lawrencium does not occur in nature and can only be produced artificially in particle accelerators. It is made by bombarding targets of elements like californium or americium with light ions such as boron or oxygen nuclei. Only a few atoms have ever been created at once, making bulk samples impossible.

Lr.title: An Electron Out of Place
Lr.text: Lawrencium is predicted to have an unusual ground-state electron configuration ending in 7s2 7p1, rather than the 6d1 that simple patterns might suggest. This anomaly arises from relativistic effects, where the heavy nucleus accelerates inner electrons to a large fraction of light speed and reshuffles energy levels. It makes lawrencium a fascinating test case for relativistic quantum chemistry.

Lr.title: The Easiest Electron to Remove
Lr.text: In 2015, an international team working in Japan measured lawrencium's first ionization energy as roughly 4.96 electron volts. This is one of the lowest ionization energies of any element, reflecting that loosely bound 7p electron predicted by theory. The experiment was a landmark, directly probing the chemistry of an element available only as single atoms.

Lr.title: Prefers the +3 State
Lr.text: Like most actinides, lawrencium's most stable and characteristic oxidation state in solution is +3. Studies of its aqueous chemistry suggest its ionic radius and behavior fit smoothly into the trends of the heavier actinides. This consistency helps chemists confirm that the actinide series genuinely ends at element 103.

Lr.title: Purely a Research Element
Lr.text: Lawrencium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications whatsoever. Because only a handful of atoms can be made and they decay almost immediately, it exists solely as a subject of fundamental scientific research. Its value lies entirely in what it teaches us about the structure of matter at the edge of the periodic table.

Lr.title: A Window Into Atomic Limits
Lr.text: Studying lawrencium helps scientists understand how relativistic effects increasingly distort chemistry as nuclei grow heavier and more crowded with protons. These insights guide predictions about even heavier superheavy elements and the theorized 'island of stability.' In this way, a barely-existing element illuminates the rules that govern all atoms.

Rf.title: First Of The Superheavies
Rf.text: Rutherfordium, element 104, is the first of the transactinide (superheavy) elements, sitting just past the actinide series. Its discovery marked the start of the 6d transition metals, making it the heaviest element widely treated as a true transition metal. Every atom of it ever made has been produced artificially in a particle accelerator.

Rf.title: A Cold War Naming Feud
Rf.text: Soviet scientists at Dubna proposed the name 'kurchatovium' (Ku) in 1964 after Igor Kurchatov, while American teams at Berkeley pushed for 'rutherfordium' in 1969. This clash was part of the decades-long 'Transfermium Wars' over priority. IUPAC finally settled the dispute and made 'rutherfordium' official in 1997.

Rf.title: Named For The Atom's Father
Rf.text: The element honors Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911 with his famous gold-foil experiment. Fittingly, an element that exists only as fleeting nuclei is named after the man who proved the nucleus exists. Rutherford also won the 1908 Nobel Prize, but in Chemistry, not Physics.

Rf.title: Made By Slamming Nuclei Together
Rf.text: Rutherfordium is created by fusing lighter nuclei in an accelerator, for example firing carbon-12 ions at californium-249, or neon-22 at plutonium-242. Only a handful of atoms are produced at a time, sometimes just one. The atoms must be detected almost instantly because they vanish within seconds.

Rf.title: A Half-Life Of Just Over An Hour
Rf.text: The longest-lived known isotope, rutherfordium-267, has a half-life of about 1.3 hours, while most isotopes survive only seconds or less. There are roughly 16 known isotopes, ranging in mass number from about 253 to 270. Because of this fleeting existence, rutherfordium can never be collected as a visible, weighable sample.

Rf.title: Chemistry With Single Atoms
Rf.text: Scientists study rutherfordium's chemistry one atom at a time using rapid gas-phase and liquid-phase techniques before the atom decays. These heroic experiments confirmed that it behaves like a heavier cousin of hafnium and zirconium, forming compounds such as the volatile chloride RfCl4. It is one of the few elements whose chemistry is explored atom-by-atom rather than in bulk.

Rf.title: Relativity Bends Its Behavior
Rf.text: In such a heavy atom, inner electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity noticeably reshapes the electron orbitals. These relativistic effects can make rutherfordium deviate from the simple predictions of its periodic-table position. Studying it is therefore a real-world test of how relativity influences chemistry.

Rf.title: A Predicted Dense Metal
Rf.text: No one has ever seen bulk rutherfordium, but calculations predict it would be a solid silvery metal with a density around 17 to 23 grams per cubic centimeter. That would make it roughly twice as dense as lead and comparable to some of the densest known metals. Its expected ground-state electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d2 7s2.

Rf.title: It Decays By Splitting Apart
Rf.text: Many rutherfordium isotopes disappear through spontaneous fission, literally tearing into two smaller nuclei, while others undergo alpha decay. This behavior near the edge of nuclear stability helps physicists map the limits of how big an atomic nucleus can be. Such studies guide the search for the theorized 'island of stability' of longer-lived superheavy elements.

Rf.title: No Role In Nature Or Life
Rf.text: Rutherfordium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth and has no known biological role; it exists purely as a product of human-made nuclear reactions. Because only a few atoms are ever made and they decay almost instantly, it has no practical industrial or medical uses. Its sole value is scientific, helping us understand the structure of matter at the heaviest known extreme.

Db.title: Born From a Cold War Feud
Db.text: Dubnium sat at the heart of the 'Transfermium Wars,' a decades-long dispute between scientists in Dubna, Russia, and Berkeley, USA, over who first made element 105 in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Both groups claimed priority and proposed rival names, and the argument grew so heated it took an international committee to settle it. The element became a symbol of how political tension could spill into the laboratory.

Db.title: Named for a Russian Science City
Db.text: The official name 'dubnium' honors Dubna, the town north of Moscow that hosts the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR). IUPAC settled the name in 1997 after years of debate, partly as a diplomatic compromise to credit the Russian contribution. Element 105 had earlier carried proposed names like 'nielsbohrium' and the American favorite 'hahnium' before dubnium won out.

Db.title: It Does Not Exist in Nature
Db.text: Dubnium is entirely synthetic and has never been found in Earth's crust, in meteorites, or anywhere in the cosmos. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured by smashing lighter nuclei together in particle accelerators. Because of this, there is no naturally occurring sample of the element anywhere on the planet.

Db.title: Made by Atomic Collisions
Db.text: To create dubnium, physicists fire a beam of light ions at a heavier target, fusing the nuclei into a single super-heavy atom. The Dubna team famously bombarded americium-243 with neon-22 ions, while Berkeley used californium targets struck by nitrogen. Successful fusion events are extraordinarily rare, sometimes producing only a handful of atoms after weeks of running an accelerator.

Db.title: Gone in Hours at Most
Db.text: Dubnium has no stable isotopes, and even its longest-lived form, dubnium-268, has a half-life of only about a day (roughly 28 hours). Many other isotopes vanish in seconds or fractions of a second through radioactive decay. This fleeting existence means scientists must study the element almost the instant it is created.

Db.title: Studied a Single Atom at a Time
Db.text: Because dubnium is produced in such tiny quantities, chemists pioneered 'single-atom chemistry' to investigate it. They perform rapid chemical tests on one atom before it decays, repeating the experiment many times to build statistical evidence about its behavior. This is one of the most demanding forms of experimental chemistry ever attempted.

Db.title: A Heavyweight Transition Metal
Db.text: Dubnium sits in group 5 of the periodic table, directly below tantalum, so chemists expect it to behave like a heavy transition metal. Experiments have indeed shown it forms chemical compounds and tends toward a +5 oxidation state, consistent with its periodic neighbors. Studying whether it truly matches tantalum tests how well the periodic table holds up at its extreme edge.

Db.title: Relativity Bends Its Chemistry
Db.text: In super-heavy atoms like dubnium, electrons near the dense, highly charged nucleus move at a sizable fraction of the speed of light. These relativistic effects can shift electron energy levels and subtly alter the element's expected chemical behavior. Dubnium is therefore a real-world laboratory for testing how Einstein's relativity reshapes the periodic table.

Db.title: Surprising Family Resemblances
Db.text: When chemists studied dubnium's compounds, they found it did not always behave exactly like tantalum as a simple reading of the periodic table would predict. In some experiments its chemistry more closely resembled that of niobium or even the element protactinium. These unexpected results reveal that periodic trends can break down in subtle ways among the heaviest elements.

Db.title: Purely a Tool for Discovery
Db.text: Dubnium has no practical, industrial, medical, or biological uses, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its entire value is scientific: it helps physicists and chemists probe the limits of nuclear stability and the structure of matter. Every atom ever made has been used to answer fundamental questions rather than to build anything.

Sg.title: Named for a Living Legend
Sg.text: Seaborgium is named after the American nuclear chemist Glenn T. Seaborg, who co-discovered plutonium and nine other elements. It was the first element ever officially named after a person who was still alive at the time of naming in 1997. Seaborg reportedly said it was the greatest honor of his life, even greater than his 1951 Nobel Prize.

Sg.title: Born in a Berkeley Lab
Sg.text: Seaborgium was first created in 1974 by a team led by Albert Ghiorso and Kenneth Hulet at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California. They bombarded a target of californium-249 with oxygen-18 ions to produce a few atoms of seaborgium-263. A competing Soviet team in Dubna had reported related work, sparking a years-long naming dispute known as the 'Transfermium Wars.'

Sg.title: A Fleeting Existence
Sg.text: Seaborgium is intensely radioactive and exists only for the briefest moments before decaying. Its longest-lived known isotope, seaborgium-269, has a half-life of roughly two to three minutes, while many isotopes vanish in fractions of a second. Because of this, every seaborgium atom ever made has long since decayed away.

Sg.title: Counted Atom by Atom
Sg.text: Scientists have never assembled a visible, weighable sample of seaborgium; it has only been produced a handful of atoms at a time. Researchers must study its chemistry using single atoms before they decay, a field called 'atom-at-a-time' chemistry. This makes seaborgium one of the most experimentally challenging substances to investigate.

Sg.title: It Behaves Like Tungsten
Sg.text: Despite being a synthetic superheavy element, seaborgium sits in group 6 of the periodic table, directly below chromium, molybdenum, and tungsten. Pioneering experiments in the late 1990s confirmed it forms volatile oxide and oxychloride compounds much like tungsten does. This was a triumph for the periodic law, showing chemical patterns hold even for element 106.

Sg.title: A Carbonyl Surprise
Sg.text: In 2014, an international team at the GSI laboratory in Germany synthesized seaborgium hexacarbonyl, Sg(CO)6, the first complex of a superheavy element with carbon monoxide. This showed seaborgium can form a stable metal-carbonyl bond just like its lighter cousins. It was a landmark in proving that classic coordination chemistry extends to the heaviest known metals.

Sg.title: Made One Nucleus at a Time
Sg.text: Creating seaborgium requires slamming heavy ions into a target inside a particle accelerator at enormous energies. Even with a beam delivering trillions of projectiles per second, only a few atoms might be produced over days of running. The product atoms are then whisked away by gas-filled separators to be detected before they decay.

Sg.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Electrons
Sg.text: In superheavy atoms like seaborgium, electrons near the nucleus move at a sizable fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity noticeably alters their orbitals. These relativistic effects can subtly shift bonding and stability compared with lighter group-6 metals. Studying seaborgium tests how well our quantum models hold up at the extreme edge of the periodic table.

Sg.title: No Place in Nature
Sg.text: Seaborgium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in stars or supernovae in any lasting amount. It is entirely human-made, existing only inside laboratories with powerful accelerators. With no natural source and no stable isotope, it has zero biological role and no presence in living organisms.

Sg.title: Purely a Research Element
Sg.text: Seaborgium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications and almost certainly never will, because it cannot be made in useful quantities and decays too fast. Its entire value is scientific: it lets chemists probe the limits of the periodic table and the behavior of matter at extreme atomic numbers. In that sense, seaborgium is a tool for understanding nature rather than a material to be used.

Bh.title: Born in a German Lab
Bh.text: Bohrium was first created in 1981 at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany, by a team led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg. They fused chromium-54 ions into a bismuth-209 target, producing a single atom of bohrium-262. The same lab also discovered elements like hassium, meitnerium, darmstadtium, and roentgenium.

Bh.title: Named for a Quantum Pioneer
Bh.text: The element honors Danish physicist Niels Bohr, whose 1913 model of the atom introduced quantized electron orbits and earned him the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. The name was formally approved by IUPAC in 1997 after a long naming dispute over several heavy elements. Its earlier placeholder name was 'unnilseptium', literally Latin-Greek for 'one-zero-seven'.

Bh.title: It Vanishes in Seconds
Bh.text: Every isotope of bohrium is intensely radioactive and exists only fleetingly. The most stable known isotope, bohrium-270, has a half-life of roughly 61 seconds, while many others decay in mere milliseconds. This means no measurable quantity of bohrium has ever been accumulated; it is studied one atom at a time.

Bh.title: A Single Atom Chemistry Experiment
Bh.text: In 2000, scientists performed actual chemistry on just six atoms of bohrium-267, forming the volatile compound bohrium oxychloride (BhO3Cl). This remarkable feat showed bohrium behaves as a Group 7 element, chemically resembling its lighter cousins technetium and rhenium. It stands as one of the most extreme examples of doing chemistry with almost nothing.

Bh.title: Sits Beneath Rhenium
Bh.text: On the periodic table, bohrium occupies Group 7, directly below manganese, technetium, and rhenium. Theory predicts its outer electron configuration ends in 6d5 7s2, fitting the transition-metal pattern. Its measured volatility was actually lower than rhenium's, matching predictions that periodic trends still hold even for superheavy elements.

Bh.title: Made by Smashing Nuclei
Bh.text: Bohrium can only be produced in particle accelerators through 'cold fusion' reactions, where a beam of medium-weight ions is fired at a heavy target nucleus. The fused nucleus must shed energy by emitting a neutron to survive, and successful events are extraordinarily rare. Detectors then identify bohrium by tracking its chain of alpha-particle decays.

Bh.title: Decays in a Domino Chain
Bh.text: Bohrium isotopes mostly disappear through alpha decay, ejecting helium nuclei and transforming step by step into lighter elements such as dubnium and lawrencium. Scientists confirm a bohrium atom existed by reading this signature 'decay chain' backward. Some heavier isotopes can also break apart through spontaneous fission.

Bh.title: A Predicted Dense Metal
Bh.text: Although no one has ever held bohrium, calculations estimate it would be a solid metal with an astonishing density near 37 grams per cubic centimeter. That would make it almost twice as dense as lead and among the densest substances ever predicted. Its appearance, likely silvery, remains purely theoretical since a visible sample will probably never exist.

Bh.title: Absent From the Natural World
Bh.text: Bohrium is entirely synthetic and has never been found on Earth or detected anywhere in the cosmos. Because its isotopes decay so quickly, any bohrium forged in ancient stars or supernovae would have vanished billions of years ago. It belongs to the family of elements that exist only because humans deliberately build them.

Bh.title: A Member of the Superheavies
Bh.text: With 107 protons, bohrium sits deep in the 'superheavy' region of the periodic table, where atomic nuclei are pushed toward the limits of stability. Studying it helps physicists test the theory of the 'island of stability', a predicted zone where certain superheavy nuclei might last far longer. Bohrium has no biological role and no commercial use, serving purely as a frontier of fundamental science.

Hs.title: Forged in Darmstadt, 1984
Hs.text: Hassium was first created on 14 March 1984 by a team led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research near Darmstadt, Germany. They fired a beam of iron-58 ions at a lead-208 target, and the fusion of these nuclei produced just three atoms of hassium-265. This same laboratory was responsible for discovering six elements in total, from bohrium to copernicium.

Hs.title: Named After a German State
Hs.text: The name hassium comes from the Latin word "Hassia," the old name for the German state of Hesse, where the GSI laboratory that created it is located. The IUPAC officially approved the name in 1997 after a long international naming dispute over several heavy elements. This makes Hesse one of only a handful of places on Earth to have a chemical element named after it.

Hs.title: It Vanishes in Seconds
Hs.text: Hassium is intensely radioactive, and even its most stable known isotope, hassium-277m, has a half-life of only about 11 minutes, while many isotopes survive mere milliseconds. Because it decays so quickly, only a few hundred atoms of hassium have ever been made in the entire history of science. It does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth and must be synthesized one atom at a time in a particle accelerator.

Hs.title: A Predicted Island of Stability
Hs.text: Hassium sits near the theorized "island of stability," a region of the periodic table where superheavy nuclei with certain magic numbers of protons and neutrons are predicted to live unusually long. The isotope hassium-270 is doubly magic in some models and lives longer than its neighbors, supporting the theory. Studying hassium therefore helps physicists test the fundamental shell structure of the atomic nucleus.

Hs.title: The Heaviest Element Chemically Studied
Hs.text: In 2001 scientists in Germany achieved a remarkable feat: they confirmed the chemistry of hassium by making just seven atoms and reacting them with oxygen. At the time this made hassium the heaviest element whose chemical behavior had ever been experimentally measured. Doing chemistry with a handful of atoms that each survive only seconds is one of the great technical triumphs of modern science.

Hs.title: It Behaves Like Osmium
Hs.text: As element 108, hassium sits directly below osmium in group 8 of the periodic table, and experiments confirmed it acts as a heavier chemical cousin. When reacted with oxygen, hassium forms a volatile tetroxide, HsO4, exactly mirroring the behavior of osmium tetroxide, OsO4. This was a stunning confirmation that the periodic law still holds even among the heaviest superheavy elements.

Hs.title: Probably the Densest Element
Hs.text: Although a visible lump of hassium has never been made and never will be, calculations predict it would be one of the densest substances in the universe. Its theoretical density is around 41 grams per cubic centimeter, nearly double that of osmium and roughly twice the density of solid gold. This extreme density comes from packing 108 protons into a tiny, heavy atom with tightly bound electrons.

Hs.title: Built One Atom at a Time
Hs.text: Creating hassium requires smashing nuclei together in a heavy-ion accelerator, where the chance of two nuclei fusing instead of bouncing apart is vanishingly small. Researchers may run a beam for weeks just to detect a single atom, identifying it by the unique chain of alpha-particle decays it leaves behind. This decay-chain fingerprinting is how scientists prove a brand-new element was truly made.

Hs.title: Einstein Hidden in Its Electrons
Hs.text: In hassium the innermost electrons whip around the nucleus at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's theory of relativity reshapes the atom's structure. These relativistic effects subtly alter how hassium bonds and how volatile its compounds are compared to lighter group 8 metals. Measuring these effects in real experiments turns a single atom into a tiny test of fundamental physics.

Hs.title: No Job, Pure Knowledge
Hs.text: Hassium has absolutely no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological use, and because it decays in minutes it never will. It plays no role in any living organism and is not part of the natural chemistry of the body or the environment. Its entire value lies in pure research, where each fleeting atom helps map the very edge of the periodic table and the limits of matter itself.

Mt.title: Born From a Single Atom
Mt.text: Meitnerium was first created on 29 August 1982 at the GSI Helmholtz Centre in Darmstadt, Germany, by a team led by Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg. They detected just one single atom, produced by firing iron-58 ions at a bismuth-209 target in the SHIP velocity filter. Confirming a brand-new element from one atom required meticulous tracking of its radioactive decay chain.

Mt.title: Named for a Pioneer Physicist
Mt.text: The element honors Lise Meitner (1878-1968), the Austrian-Swedish physicist who, with Otto Frisch, provided the theoretical explanation for nuclear fission. Although her collaborator Otto Hahn won the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery, Meitner was controversially overlooked. Meitnerium is one of the few elements named after a woman, alongside curium (partly for Marie Curie).

Mt.title: A Synthetic Element, Never Found in Nature
Mt.text: Meitnerium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in the cosmos. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured in a particle accelerator. This is because all its isotopes are intensely radioactive and decay far too quickly to have survived since the elements formed in stars and supernovae.

Mt.title: Gone in the Blink of an Eye
Mt.text: All known isotopes of meitnerium are extremely unstable, with very short half-lives. The longest-lived isotope identified so far, meitnerium-278, has a half-life of only about 4 to 8 seconds. Most others vanish in fractions of a second, decaying mainly through alpha emission or spontaneous fission.

Mt.title: A Member of Group 9
Mt.text: On the periodic table meitnerium sits in group 9, directly below cobalt, rhodium, and iridium, making it a transition metal. Chemists predict it should behave somewhat like iridium, possibly favoring a +3 or +1 oxidation state. However, these properties remain theoretical because no one has ever assembled enough atoms to study its chemistry directly.

Mt.title: Probably a Dense, Heavy Metal
Mt.text: Theoretical calculations suggest meitnerium would be a solid metal at room temperature with an extraordinarily high density, estimated at roughly 27-28 grams per cubic centimeter. That would make it one of the densest substances ever, rivaling or exceeding osmium and iridium. Because samples never exist in bulk, this density has only been predicted, never weighed.

Mt.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Atoms
Mt.text: In superheavy elements like meitnerium, the innermost electrons move at a substantial fraction of the speed of light. This triggers relativistic effects that contract some electron orbitals and expand others, subtly altering the element's predicted chemistry. Scientists study meitnerium precisely to test whether Einstein's relativity bends the rules of the periodic table at its extreme edge.

Mt.title: Cooked Up by Cold Fusion
Mt.text: The original synthesis used a technique called cold fusion, which here means fusing two medium-weight nuclei gently enough that the merged nucleus survives rather than instantly flying apart. Iron-58 striking bismuth-209 produced meitnerium-266 plus a single neutron. This careful, low-energy approach was pioneered at GSI and helped create several other superheavy elements.

Mt.title: A Name That Took 15 Years
Mt.text: Although GSI proposed the name meitnerium soon after the 1982 discovery, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry did not officially approve it until 1997. During the interim it carried the placeholder systematic name unnilennium, symbol Une, simply meaning one-zero-nine in Latin-Greek roots. Such delays were common amid disputes over who deserved credit for the heaviest elements.

Mt.title: Purely a Research Curiosity
Mt.text: Meitnerium has no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological uses whatsoever, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its sole value is scientific: it helps researchers map the limits of nuclear stability and search for the theorized island of stability, where some superheavy nuclei might last much longer. Studying it deepens our understanding of how matter behaves at the frontier of the periodic table.

Ds.title: Forged in Darmstadt, 1994
Ds.text: Darmstadtium was first created on 9 November 1994 at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. A team led by Sigurd Hofmann and Peter Armbruster fused lead-208 with nickel-62 nuclei accelerated to enormous speeds. Only a single atom of darmstadtium-269 was detected in that first run, identified by the chain of alpha particles it emitted as it decayed.

Ds.title: Named for a German city
Ds.text: The element takes its name from Darmstadt, the city where it was discovered, making it one of the few elements named after the specific town of its creation rather than a country or person. The name was officially approved by IUPAC in 2003. Before that, it carried the placeholder systematic name ununnilium (Uun), simply meaning 'one-one-zero' in Latin-Greek numbering.

Ds.title: An atom-by-atom element
Ds.text: Darmstadtium has never been produced in weighable amounts; scientists have only ever made a few dozen atoms total. Creating it requires firing trillions of projectile ions at a target for days or weeks just to score one successful fusion event. This is why almost everything we 'know' about it is inferred from theory and the behaviour of lighter relatives like platinum, not from direct measurement of a sample.

Ds.title: Vanishes in a flash
Ds.text: Every isotope of darmstadtium is intensely radioactive and decays almost instantly. Its most stable known isotope, darmstadtium-281, has a half-life of only about 11 seconds, while the original Ds-269 lasted under a thousandth of a second. Because it disappears so fast, no one will ever hold a visible piece of it.

Ds.title: Predicted to be ultra-dense
Ds.text: Although a real lump has never existed, calculations suggest darmstadtium would be one of the densest substances imaginable, with an estimated density around 26 to 34 grams per cubic centimetre. That is roughly 1.5 times denser than gold or lead. The huge density comes from packing 110 protons and many neutrons into each tiny, heavy nucleus.

Ds.title: Platinum's heavy cousin
Ds.text: Darmstadtium sits directly below platinum, palladium and nickel in group 10 of the periodic table, so chemists expect it to behave like a noble, unreactive transition metal. If a sample could ever be assembled, it would likely be a silvery or grey solid that resists corrosion. Relativistic effects on its fast-moving inner electrons, however, might make its chemistry subtly different from platinum's.

Ds.title: A doorway to superheavies
Ds.text: Darmstadtium was a crucial stepping stone in the race to fill the bottom of the periodic table. The same GSI 'cold fusion' technique that produced it was used to discover its neighbours roentgenium (111) and copernicium (112) within just two years. Each new element pushed scientists closer to the theorised 'island of stability,' a region where superheavy nuclei might survive much longer.

Ds.title: Born only in laboratories
Ds.text: Darmstadtium does not occur anywhere in nature, not on Earth, in meteorites, or in stars. Any darmstadtium that might have formed in violent cosmic events like neutron-star collisions would have decayed away in seconds, long before it could be detected. It is a purely synthetic, human-made element that exists only when a particle accelerator manufactures it.

Ds.title: Read by its decay signature
Ds.text: Because you cannot see or weigh a single atom, scientists identify darmstadtium by the unique 'fingerprint' of radiation it leaves behind. The atom emits a precise sequence of alpha particles, each with a characteristic energy, as it transforms step-by-step into lighter known elements. Matching that decay chain to predictions is how the GSI team proved they had truly made element 110.

Ds.title: No jobs, only knowledge
Ds.text: Darmstadtium has zero industrial, medical, or biological uses, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its entire value is scientific: studying how it forms and decays tests our theories of nuclear structure and the limits of the periodic table. In that sense it is a pure 'curiosity' element, made to answer the question of how big an atom can get.

Rg.title: Born in a Darmstadt Lab
Rg.text: Roentgenium was first created on December 8, 1994, at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. The team led by Sigurd Hofmann and Peter Armbruster fired nickel-64 ions at a bismuth-209 target, and a single atom of roentgenium-272 was detected. The same lab also discovered its neighbors bohrium, hassnium, meitnerium, darmstadtium, and copernicium.

Rg.title: Named After an X-ray Pioneer
Rg.text: The element honors Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen, the German physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895 and won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The name was officially approved by IUPAC on November 1, 2004, on the 109th anniversary of Roentgen's discovery. Before that it carried the placeholder name unununium with the temporary symbol Uuu.

Rg.title: An Element That Vanishes Instantly
Rg.text: Roentgenium is intensely radioactive and has no stable isotopes whatsoever. Its longest-lived known isotope, roentgenium-282, has a half-life of only about two minutes, while most others survive for mere milliseconds. This fleeting existence means every atom decays almost as soon as it is made.

Rg.title: Made One Atom at a Time
Rg.text: Unlike everyday metals mined by the ton, roentgenium has only ever existed as a handful of individual atoms produced in particle accelerators. The original 1994 experiment yielded just three atoms over many days of bombardment. Because so few atoms have ever been created, scientists have never accumulated a visible, weighable sample.

Rg.title: A Superheavy Transition Metal
Rg.text: With atomic number 111, roentgenium sits in group 11 of the periodic table, directly below copper, silver, and gold. Chemists therefore predict it should behave as a transition metal and possibly form a +3 oxidation state as its most stable, unlike gold which favors +1 and +3. It is one of the so-called superheavy elements, all of which lie beyond the naturally occurring lineup.

Rg.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Chemistry
Rg.text: In such a massive atom, the innermost electrons travel at a large fraction of the speed of light, triggering Einstein's relativistic effects. Calculations suggest these effects make roentgenium's chemistry diverge sharply from gold's, even though they are neighbors in the same group. This is a vivid reminder that for the heaviest elements, the rules of ordinary chemistry start to bend.

Rg.title: Predicted to Be Denser Than Gold
Rg.text: Theoretical models estimate roentgenium's density at roughly 22 to 28 grams per cubic centimeter, rivaling or exceeding osmium and iridium, the densest known stable elements. It is also predicted to be a solid metal at room temperature. These figures remain calculations, however, because no bulk sample has ever been produced to measure directly.

Rg.title: Completely Absent From Nature
Rg.text: Roentgenium is not found anywhere in Earth's crust, oceans, or atmosphere, nor has it been detected in stars or cosmic material. It is a purely synthetic element that exists only when human-built accelerators force lighter nuclei to fuse together. Any roentgenium that might have formed in the early universe would have decayed away billions of years ago.

Rg.title: No Job Outside the Laboratory
Rg.text: Because it is so scarce and decays in moments, roentgenium has no commercial, industrial, or medical uses at all. Its sole value is scientific, helping researchers test the limits of nuclear stability and the periodic table itself. Studying it deepens our understanding of how the strong nuclear force holds extreme atoms together.

Rg.title: A Stepping Stone to the Island
Rg.text: Roentgenium lies near the theorized "island of stability," a predicted region of superheavy elements that might possess unusually long half-lives. Each new isotope scientists create, including the relatively long-lived roentgenium-282, helps map the shoreline of that island. The hunt drives the development of ever more sensitive detectors and powerful accelerators worldwide.

Cn.title: Born in a German Lab
Cn.text: Copernicium was first created on February 9, 1996, at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. A team led by Sigurd Hofmann fired zinc-70 ions at a lead-208 target, fusing two nuclei to make a single atom of element 112. It took years more of careful experiments and independent confirmation before the discovery was officially accepted in 2009.

Cn.title: Named for an Astronomer
Cn.text: The element honors Nicolaus Copernicus, the Renaissance scholar who placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the solar system. The name was proposed by the GSI discovery team and made official by IUPAC on February 19, 2010, the 537th anniversary of Copernicus's birth. It is one of the few elements named after a person who was not himself a chemist or physicist.

Cn.title: Gone in an Instant
Cn.text: Copernicium is intensely radioactive and decays almost as soon as it forms. Its most stable known isotope, copernicium-285, has a half-life of roughly 28 to 30 seconds, while many other isotopes survive for only milliseconds. This fleeting existence is why scientists have only ever made a handful of atoms at a time.

Cn.title: A Superheavy Heavyweight
Cn.text: With 112 protons packed into its nucleus, copernicium sits deep in the realm of "superheavy" elements. Atoms this large are held together against enormous electrical repulsion, and they exist near the predicted "island of stability" where certain proton and neutron counts may grant longer lifetimes. Studying them tests the very limits of how big an atom can be.

Cn.title: Maybe a Liquid Metal
Cn.text: Copernicium sits below mercury in the periodic table, and theory predicts it could be a volatile metal, possibly even a gas or liquid at room temperature. The reason is Einstein's relativity: electrons in such a heavy atom move at a large fraction of light speed, which contracts their orbitals and weakens the metallic bonding. This would make copernicium behave more like a noble gas than a typical transition metal.

Cn.title: Tested Atom by Atom
Cn.text: Because only single atoms can be made, chemists study copernicium using a technique called gas-phase chromatography, watching where one atom sticks to a gold-coated surface. In 2006 and later experiments, researchers compared how copernicium and mercury atoms deposited on cold detectors. The results hinted that copernicium is indeed more volatile and less metallic than mercury, just as relativity predicts.

Cn.title: Not Found in Nature
Cn.text: Copernicium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth, in meteorites, or in the stars we can observe. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured in a particle accelerator. Because its isotopes decay so quickly, even if it once formed in a cosmic explosion, none could have survived to the present day.

Cn.title: A Stepping Stone in Decay Chains
Cn.text: Copernicium often appears not as a target but as a product, born when heavier elements decay. Isotopes of flerovium (element 114), for example, shed an alpha particle and transform into copernicium on their way down to lighter atoms. Tracking these alpha-decay chains is exactly how scientists confirm that a new superheavy element was really created.

Cn.title: From Placeholder to Real Name
Cn.text: Before it had a permanent name, element 112 was called ununbium, a Latin-Greek placeholder literally meaning "one-one-two." IUPAC uses such systematic names for any element that has been claimed but not yet officially confirmed and named. Copernicium's journey from "ununbium" to a proper name shows how rigorously new elements must be verified.

Cn.title: No Use Outside the Lab
Cn.text: Copernicium has no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological role, and it plays no part in any living organism. Its only value is scientific: each atom helps physicists and chemists understand nuclear structure and how relativity reshapes the chemistry of the heaviest elements. In that sense, copernicium is a pure research element, made solely to expand human knowledge.

Nh.title: Asia's First Element
Nh.text: Nihonium was the first chemical element discovered in Asia, synthesized by a team led by Kosuke Morita at the RIKEN institute near Tokyo, Japan. Its name comes from "Nihon," one of the Japanese words for Japan, meaning "Land of the Rising Sun." The name and symbol Nh were officially approved by IUPAC in November 2016.

Nh.title: Three Atoms in Nine Years
Nh.text: Confirming nihonium's existence took extraordinary patience: the RIKEN team produced just three single atoms over nine years of experiments, in 2004, 2005, and 2012. They fired a beam of zinc-70 ions at a bismuth-209 target roughly 10 to the 19th power times, and only a handful of atoms ever fused. This made the discovery one of the most painstaking confirmations in the history of element-hunting.

Nh.title: A Fleeting Existence
Nh.text: Nihonium is intensely radioactive and exists for only a tiny fraction of a second. Its most stable known isotope, nihonium-286, has a half-life of about 10 seconds, while the isotopes RIKEN actually made survived for only milliseconds. Because it decays so fast, scientists identify it not by seeing the atom directly but by tracking the chain of alpha-decay products it leaves behind.

Nh.title: The Long Naming Battle
Nh.text: Before it had a real name, element 113 was called by the placeholder "ununtrium" (Uut), Latin-Greek for "one-one-three." A Russian-American collaboration at Dubna also claimed to have produced it, sparking a priority dispute. After review, IUPAC credited the RIKEN team with the discovery in 2015, giving Japan the honor of naming it.

Nh.title: Born From Nuclear Fusion
Nh.text: Nihonium is a synthetic element that does not occur anywhere in nature, on Earth or in the cosmos. It can only be created in particle accelerators by smashing lighter nuclei together so they fuse into a heavier one. This places it among the "superheavy" elements that exist solely because humans built machines powerful enough to forge them.

Nh.title: Member of Element 7's Family
Nh.text: Nihonium sits in group 13 of the periodic table, directly below thallium, alongside familiar elements like boron, aluminium, gallium, and indium. Chemists therefore expect it to behave loosely like a heavy post-transition metal. However, no one has ever gathered enough of it to see, weigh, or chemically test in bulk, so most of its properties are predictions rather than measurements.

Nh.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Chemistry
Nh.text: In superheavy atoms like nihonium, electrons whip around the nucleus at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's theory of relativity becomes important to chemistry. These relativistic effects are predicted to make nihonium's outer electrons behave unusually, possibly giving it a strong preference for the +1 oxidation state. Studying such effects is a major reason scientists bother to make these almost impossibly rare atoms.

Nh.title: Hunting the Island of Stability
Nh.text: Nihonium research is tied to the search for a theoretical "island of stability," a region where certain superheavy nuclei might last far longer than their neighbors. The trend in nihonium isotopes, with heavier ones living longer, offers tantalizing hints that this island could be real. Reaching it would mean creating nuclei with "magic numbers" of protons and neutrons that resist radioactive decay.

Nh.title: A Predicted Heavyweight Solid
Nh.text: Although it has never been seen as a visible substance, theory predicts nihonium would be a solid metal at room temperature with a high density, estimated around 16 grams per cubic centimeter, denser than lead. Calculations also suggest a melting point near 430 degrees Celsius. These figures remain purely computational, since not even a single visible speck of the metal has ever existed.

Nh.title: No Job in Biology or Industry
Nh.text: Nihonium has no biological role and no practical applications outside the laboratory, and it almost certainly never will. It is produced one atom at a time, costs an astronomical amount of effort to make, and vanishes within seconds. Its true value is to pure science: testing the limits of the periodic table and our understanding of how atomic nuclei and electrons behave at the extremes.

Fl.title: Named For Russia's Atom Lab
Fl.text: Flerovium honors the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, which in turn is named after Soviet physicist Georgy Flyorov. Flyorov is famous not only for nuclear science but for writing a 1942 letter to Stalin pointing out that physics journals had suddenly stopped publishing on fission, a clue that helped spark the Soviet atomic program. The name and symbol Fl were officially approved by IUPAC in May 2012.

Fl.title: Born In A Calcium Beam
Fl.text: Flerovium was first created in December 1998 at Dubna by bombarding a plutonium-244 target with a beam of calcium-48 ions. This 'hot fusion' approach, fusing a calcium nucleus into a heavy actinide, became the workhorse method for making superheavy elements. The collaboration between Russian and U.S. (Lawrence Livermore) scientists was key to confirming the discovery.

Fl.title: A Member Of Element 114
Fl.text: With 114 protons, flerovium sits in group 14 of the periodic table, directly below lead. That places it among carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, and lead, suggesting it could behave like a very heavy metal. Its position made it a prime test case for how chemistry changes when atoms get this enormous.

Fl.title: Brush With The Island Of Stability
Fl.text: Theorists long predicted an 'island of stability' near 114 protons, where certain superheavy nuclei would resist radioactive decay far better than their neighbors. Flerovium isotopes do show a hint of this: lifetimes that are surprisingly long for such heavy atoms. While no flerovium isotope is truly stable, it sits near the shore of this predicted island, making it a flagship for the theory.

Fl.title: Seconds, Not Eternities
Fl.text: Even flerovium's longest-lived known isotope, flerovium-289, has a half-life of only about 1.9 seconds. Most other isotopes vanish in milliseconds, decaying mainly by emitting alpha particles or by splitting apart in spontaneous fission. Studying something that disappears so fast requires detecting the chain of decay products atom by atom.

Fl.title: Maybe A Noble Gas In Disguise
Fl.text: Because relativistic effects make flerovium's outer electrons cling tightly to the nucleus, some scientists predicted it might be chemically inert and even behave like a noble gas rather than a metal. Experiments in the 2000s and 2010s, where single atoms were sent down gold-coated detector channels, suggested flerovium is at least less reactive than its neighbor lead. The debate over whether it is a volatile metal or nearly gas-like is still alive.

Fl.title: Relativity You Can Almost See
Fl.text: In flerovium, electrons near the nucleus move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's special relativity strongly reshapes the atom's structure. These relativistic effects contract the inner electron shells and alter chemical behavior in ways that simple periodic-table logic does not predict. Flerovium is one of the clearest natural laboratories for seeing relativity rewrite chemistry.

Fl.title: One Atom At A Time
Fl.text: Flerovium has never existed in a weighable amount; scientists have produced only a few dozen atoms in total since 1998. Each atom must be identified by its unique signature of decay energies and timings as it falls apart. This means all 'chemistry' done with flerovium is single-atom chemistry, an extreme frontier of experimental science.

Fl.title: Not Found In Nature
Fl.text: Flerovium does not occur anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in stars, supernovae, or cosmic rays in detectable amounts. It is entirely synthetic, existing only for moments inside particle accelerators. Any flerovium that might have formed in the early universe would have decayed away billions of years ago.

Fl.title: No Jobs, Only Knowledge
Fl.text: Flerovium has zero industrial, medical, or biological uses, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its entire value is scientific: it tests our theories about nuclear structure, the limits of the periodic table, and how matter behaves at the extreme edge of atomic size.
