Pursuing elements like flerovium drives advances in accelerator technology and ultra-sensitive detection that ripple into other fields.

Mc.title: Born in a Russian Lab
Mc.text: Moscovium was first created in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia, by a Russian-American team led by Yuri Oganessian. Researchers fired a beam of calcium-48 ions at a target of americium-243, and the fusion of these nuclei produced a few atoms of element 115. The discovery was a collaboration between JINR and the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States.

Mc.title: Named for Moscow Region
Mc.text: The element was officially named Moscovium in 2016 by IUPAC, honoring the Moscow Oblast where Dubna and the JINR laboratory are located. Before that, it carried the placeholder name 'ununpentium' (literally 'one-one-five' in Latin) and the symbol Uup. The name follows a tradition of naming superheavy elements after the places or institutions that discovered them, just like dubnium, also named for Dubna.

Mc.title: Vanishes in a Heartbeat
Mc.text: Moscovium is extraordinarily unstable and radioactive, with even its longest-lived known isotope, moscovium-290, having a half-life of only about 0.65 seconds. Most isotopes decay in mere milliseconds by emitting alpha particles. Because of this fleeting existence, scientists have only ever made a handful of atoms at a time, never enough to see with the naked eye.

Mc.title: A Stepping Stone to Other Elements
Mc.text: When moscovium atoms undergo alpha decay, they transform into atoms of nihonium (element 113). In fact, the very experiments that confirmed moscovium also provided important evidence for nihonium's existence by observing the decay chains. This makes moscovium a kind of nuclear ancestor, helping researchers map out the behavior of several superheavy elements at once.

Mc.title: Predicted to Be a Metal
Mc.text: Moscovium sits in group 15 of the periodic table, directly below bismuth, so chemists expect it to behave as a heavy post-transition metal rather than like the nonmetals nitrogen and phosphorus higher in the column. Calculations suggest it could be a solid at room temperature with a density several times that of water. Because so few atoms exist for fractions of a second, almost everything we 'know' about its chemistry comes from theory, not laboratory measurement.

Mc.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Atom
Mc.text: In atoms as heavy as moscovium, the innermost electrons move at a substantial fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's theory of relativity strongly alters their behavior. These relativistic effects are predicted to change moscovium's expected chemistry, potentially making certain oxidation states more or less stable than simple periodic trends would suggest. Studying such effects is one of the main scientific reasons for creating superheavy elements at all.

Mc.title: Edge of the 'Island of Stability'
Mc.text: Moscovium lies near a long-theorized 'island of stability,' a region of the chart of nuclides where certain superheavy isotopes might survive far longer than their neighbors. Physicists hope that isotopes with just the right balance of protons and neutrons could last minutes, days, or even longer. Moscovium's measurable, sub-second half-lives are seen as encouraging hints that this island may really exist nearby.

Mc.title: Made One Atom at a Time
Mc.text: Creating moscovium is staggeringly inefficient: experimenters may run a particle accelerator for weeks, sending trillions upon trillions of calcium ions at the target, just to produce a single detectable atom. The successful fusions are identified not by seeing the element directly but by detecting the precise sequence and energy of alpha particles it emits as it decays. This detective-like analysis of decay chains is how its discovery was ultimately confirmed.

Mc.title: Not Found in Nature
Mc.text: Moscovium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth, in meteorites, or, as far as we know, in stars. It is entirely synthetic, existing only briefly inside specialized accelerator laboratories. Even the violent nuclear processes in supernovae are not thought to leave behind any lasting moscovium, because any that formed would decay almost instantly.

Mc.title: No Uses Beyond Research
Mc.text: Because it can only be made a few atoms at a time and disappears in under a second, moscovium has no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological role of any kind. Its entire value is scientific: it helps physicists test the limits of the periodic table and refine theories about how atomic nuclei hold together. Studying elements like moscovium deepens our fundamental understanding of matter, even though you will never find it in any product.

Lv.title: Born in a Russian lab
Lv.text: Livermorium was first created in July 2000 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, by a team led by Yuri Oganessian. They bombarded a curium-248 target with calcium-48 ions, and a single atom of element 116 appeared and decayed within milliseconds. The discovery was the product of a long Russia-United States collaboration rather than a lone-genius moment.

Lv.title: Named for a place, not a person
Lv.text: The element honors the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in Livermore, California, whose scientists supplied target material and expertise for the experiments. The name was officially approved by IUPAC in May 2012, alongside flerovium for element 114. Naming an element after a town is unusual, putting Livermorium in the small club that includes berkelium, dubnium and darmstadtium.

Lv.title: A truly synthetic element
Lv.text: Livermorium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth or, as far as we know, in the cosmos, because every isotope is wildly radioactive and decays almost instantly. It exists only when physicists deliberately fuse lighter nuclei in a particle accelerator. In its entire history, only a handful of atoms have ever been made.

Lv.title: Gone in the blink of an eye
Lv.text: The longest-lived known isotope, livermorium-293, has a half-life of only about 60 to 80 milliseconds. That is faster than a human eye blink, which takes roughly 100 to 150 milliseconds. This fleeting existence is why scientists study the element by detecting its radioactive decay products rather than ever holding a visible sample.

Lv.title: Member of the oxygen family
Lv.text: Livermorium sits in group 16 of the periodic table, directly below polonium, making it the heaviest known member of the chalcogen family that begins with oxygen, sulfur and selenium. Based on this position, chemists predict it could in principle form compounds resembling those of its lighter cousins. Whether it actually behaves that way is unknown, since there is never enough of it to do real chemistry.

Lv.title: Relativity reshapes its electrons
Lv.text: In superheavy atoms like Livermorium, the innermost electrons move at a sizeable fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity significantly alters their energy levels. These relativistic effects are predicted to make Livermorium behave less like textbook polonium than a simple periodic-table reading would suggest. Studying such elements is partly a test of how well our deepest theories of the atom hold up at the extremes.

Lv.title: A stepping stone to element 117
Lv.text: When scientists later created tennessine (element 117), some of its decay chains passed through isotopes of Livermorium on their way to lighter elements. In this sense Livermorium served as a recognizable signpost confirming that even heavier elements had truly been made. Reading these decay chains, like footprints, is the main way researchers prove a new superheavy element existed at all.

Lv.title: Calcium-48: the magic bullet
Lv.text: Livermorium is made using calcium-48, a rare, mildly radioactive isotope of calcium prized because its nucleus is doubly magic and unusually stable for fusion experiments. This isotope makes up under one percent of natural calcium and must be painstakingly enriched, making it extraordinarily expensive. Without this special projectile, creating element 116 would be far harder.

Lv.title: Probing the island of stability
Lv.text: Livermorium lies near a long-predicted region of the chart of nuclides called the island of stability, where certain superheavy isotopes might survive far longer than their neighbors. Each new measurement of Livermorium's isotopes helps physicists refine where that island actually sits. Confirming it would be a landmark discovery about the fundamental limits of how big an atomic nucleus can be.

Lv.title: No uses, and that is the point
Lv.text: Livermorium has no commercial, industrial, medical or biological applications, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its value is entirely scientific: each atom is a data point that tests our understanding of nuclear forces and the structure of matter at the heaviest extreme. Pure curiosity-driven research like this is exactly how the boundaries of the periodic table keep expanding.

Ts.title: The Newest Halogen Group
Ts.text: Tennessine sits at the bottom of Group 17, the halogens, directly below astatine. Although it is classified as a halogen by its position in the periodic table, scientists predict its chemistry would be very different from chlorine or iodine because of extreme relativistic effects on its electrons. Some models suggest it might behave more like a semi-metal than a typical reactive nonmetal.

Ts.title: Named After Tennessee
Ts.text: Tennessine was named in honor of the U.S. state of Tennessee, recognizing the contributions of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Vanderbilt University, and the University of Tennessee to superheavy element research. The name was officially approved by IUPAC in November 2016. It is one of only two elements named after a U.S. state, the other being californium.

Ts.title: A 2010 Russian-American Team
Ts.text: Tennessine was first created in 2010 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, Russia, through a collaboration with American laboratories. The team was led by Yuri Oganessian, after whom element 118, oganesson, is named. The discovery was officially confirmed by IUPAC and IUPAP in late 2015.

Ts.title: Made From Rare Berkelium
Ts.text: To create tennessine, scientists bombarded a target of berkelium-249 with a beam of calcium-48 ions. The berkelium itself was extraordinarily difficult to obtain, requiring about 250 days of production at Oak Ridge's High Flux Isotope Reactor plus months of purification. Only around 22 milligrams of this precious material were available, and it decays with a half-life of just 330 days.

Ts.title: Vanishingly Few Atoms Ever Made
Ts.text: Only a handful of tennessine atoms have ever existed since its discovery. Across multiple experiments, scientists have detected merely a few dozen atoms in total. Each one is identified not by seeing it directly, but by tracing the chain of alpha-particle decays it produces as it falls apart.

Ts.title: Gone in Milliseconds
Ts.text: Tennessine is intensely radioactive and extraordinarily short-lived. Its most stable known isotope, tennessine-294, has a half-life of only about 51 milliseconds, while tennessine-293 lasts around 22 milliseconds. Because it disappears almost instantly, no one has ever accumulated a weighable sample or directly studied its bulk properties.

Ts.title: Sitting in the Eighth Row
Ts.text: Tennessine is one of the elements completing the seventh period of the periodic table, alongside nihonium, moscovium, livermorium, and oganesson. With 117 protons, its electrons are predicted to fill orbitals up to the 7p shell. Filling the entire seventh row was a major milestone announced by IUPAC in 2016.

Ts.title: A Probe of the Island of Stability
Ts.text: Tennessine research is part of the search for the theorized island of stability, a region of superheavy elements predicted to have unusually long lifetimes. Adding neutrons toward the magic number of 184 is thought to boost stability, and tennessine isotopes help map the approach to that island. Studying its decay chains gives physicists clues about nuclear shell structure at the extreme edge of matter.

Ts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Electrons
Ts.text: In superheavy atoms like tennessine, inner electrons move at a significant fraction of the speed of light, triggering Einstein's relativistic effects. These effects are predicted to split tennessine's outer 7p electrons into two energy groups, weakening its ability to form the classic minus-one ion typical of halogens. This is why chemists suspect tennessine would break the neat trends seen in fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine.

Ts.title: Purely Synthetic and Practical-Use Free
Ts.text: Tennessine does not occur anywhere in nature, not on Earth and not in stars, because any atoms formed would decay far too quickly to persist. It exists only when deliberately forged atom-by-atom in particle accelerators. It has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications, and its sole value is advancing fundamental science about the limits of the periodic table.

Og.title: Heaviest Element Ever Made
Og.text: Oganesson is element 118, the heaviest element confirmed to exist and the one with the highest atomic number on the periodic table. With 118 protons crammed into its nucleus, it completes the seventh period of the table. No element beyond it has yet been officially recognized.

Og.title: Named for a Living Scientist
Og.text: Oganesson honors the Russian-Armenian physicist Yuri Oganessian, a pioneer of superheavy-element research at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna. When it was named in 2016, he became only the second person ever to have an element named after them while still alive, after Glenn Seaborg (seaborgium). The symbol Og and the '-on' ending mirror the noble gases like neon and argon.

Og.title: Made by Fusing Calcium and Californium
Og.text: Scientists created oganesson by firing a beam of calcium-48 ions at a target of californium-249 at the Dubna cyclotron in Russia, in collaboration with the U.S. Lawrence Livermore and Oak Ridge labs. Out of trillions upon trillions of collisions, only a handful of atoms were ever produced. The discovery was first reported in 2002 and 2005, and confirmed in the years that followed.

Og.title: Only a Few Atoms Exist
Og.text: In total, scientists have detected only about five or six atoms of oganesson in history. Each one was identified not directly but by tracing the chain of alpha-particle decays it left behind. This makes it one of the rarest substances humans have ever observed.

Og.title: Vanishes in Under a Millisecond
Og.text: Oganesson is extraordinarily unstable: its most studied isotope, oganesson-294, has a half-life of roughly 0.7 milliseconds before it decays by emitting an alpha particle. That is far less than the blink of an eye, which lasts about a tenth of a second. Such fleeting lifetimes are why superheavy atoms must be detected almost the instant they form.

Og.title: A Noble Gas That May Not Be Noble
Og.text: Oganesson sits beneath radon in the noble-gas column, so by tradition it should be chemically inert. But theory suggests relativistic effects on its electrons could make it surprisingly reactive, unlike helium or neon. Some calculations even predict it would be a solid, not a gas, at room temperature.

Og.title: Where Relativity Rewrites Chemistry
Og.text: In such a heavy atom, the innermost electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity must be used to describe them. These relativistic effects are predicted to smear out oganesson's electron shells, possibly blurring the neat shell structure seen in lighter elements. Physicists study it precisely because it tests the limits of our quantum and relativistic theories of the atom.

Og.title: Not Found Anywhere in Nature
Og.text: Oganesson does not occur naturally on Earth, in meteorites, or anywhere known in the cosmos, because it decays far too quickly to persist. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured by physicists in a particle accelerator. It is a purely human-made addition to the universe's catalogue of matter.

Og.title: No Uses Beyond Pure Science
Og.text: Because it exists only as a few short-lived atoms, oganesson has no industrial, medical, or commercial applications whatsoever. Its entire value is scientific: helping researchers probe how the periodic table behaves at its extreme edge. Studying it guides the search for even heavier, possibly more stable elements.

Og.title: Hunting the Island of Stability
Og.text: Oganesson lies near a long-theorized 'island of stability,' a region where certain superheavy nuclei with special numbers of protons and neutrons might survive far longer than their neighbors. While oganesson itself is fleeting, its creation is a stepping stone toward isotopes that could last seconds, minutes, or more. This quest drives laboratories in Russia, Germany, the United States, and Japan to keep pushing the periodic table's frontier.
